profileDesc.creation:
Initially created: 2025-12-06T12:10:26.972+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.
Input text:

p.seg: Sīmǎ Guāng
compiled by imperial command.
Later Study Tiān Tái
The First Record of Suí.
Beginning in the year Túwéi Zuò'è (jǐyǒu),
ending in Chongguāng Dàyuānxiàn (xīnhài),
a total of three years.
Suí
was the State of Suí during the Spring and Autumn period.
It was destroyed by Chǔ
and made into a county.
During the Qín and Hàn dynasties, it belonged to Nányáng Commandery.
During the Jìn dynasty, it belonged to Yìyáng Commandery.
Later, Suí Commandery was established separately.
During the Liáng dynasty, it was called Suí Prefecture,
then later it was annexed by Western Wèi.
Yáng Zhōng followed Zhōu Tàizǔ,
and for his achievements, he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Suíguo.
His son, Jiān, inherited the title.
He received the abdication from Zhōu,
and thus used Suí as the name of his state.
Also, because the character [AS-FEB8] [AS-FBEC] [AS-FEE2] of Zhōu and Qí did not afford peace and tranquility,
he removed
“ [AS-FEB8] [AS-FBEC] [AS-FEE2] ”
and made it
because [AS-FEB8] [AS-FBEC] [AS-FEE2] means to run, hence unstable.
[AS-FEB8] [AS-FBEC] [AS-FEE2]
is pronounced chuò.
Gāozǔ Wén Huángdì, first of the first rank.
His taboo name was Jiān,
his surname was Yáng.
The Suí Shū states: He was a native of Huáyīn County, Hóngnóng Commandery.
Zhèn, Grand Commandant of Hàn, had a descendant eight generations removed named Xuàn,
who begot Yuánshòu.
During the Later Wèi period, Yuánshòu served as a Sīmǎ in Wǔchuān Garrison,
and his descendants settled there.
Yuánshòu's great-great-grandson, Zhōng,
followed Zhōu Tàizǔ in his uprising in Guānxī,
and was indeed the father of the emperor.
From the 13th year of Tàijiàn of Chén Xuāndì to the 9th year of Kāihuáng,
the Suí had controlled the northwest for eight years.
As the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn begins its chronology for these nine years as the start of the Suí chronology,
it is therefore written as "first of the first rank."
In the 9th year of Kāihuáng
(jǐyǒu, 589),
the Emperor received the abdication from Zhōu in the 13th year of Tàijiàn of Chén Gāozōng.
By this year, he had pacified Chén,
unifying the realm.
The Tōngjiàn records events
by dating them according to Kāihuáng.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the day yǐchǒu, the first of the month,
the Chén ruler held court with his officials.
A great fog filled all four directions,
entering people's noses,
and everyone felt a sharp, pungent sensation.
The Chén ruler fell into a stupor,
and did not awaken until the pū hour.
Pū is when the sun reaches shēn.
Pū
is pronounced bēnmó.
On this day,
Hèruò Bì led his troops from Guǎnglíng to cross the Jiāng (Yangtze River).
Earlier, Bì had used old horses to buy many Chén boats and concealed them,
and bought fifty or sixty worn-out boats,
placing them in the channels.
The Chén people spied on them,
believing that the inner country had no boats.
Bì also requested that the river defense guards, at each change of shift,
must gather in Guǎnglíng.
Thus, he displayed a large array of banners,
and tents covered the fields.
The Chén people thought that a large Suí army had arrived,
and urgently dispatched troops to prepare.
Once they knew it was merely a change of shift for the guards,
their troops dispersed again.
Later, this became customary,
and they no longer set up defenses.
He also sent troops to hunt along the river from time to time,
with much noise from men and horses.
Therefore, when Bì crossed the Jiāng,
the Chén people did not notice.
Hán Qínhǔ led five hundred men from Héngjiāng to cross the river by night at Cǎishí.
Héngjiāng Pǔ
is in the territory of Hézhōu.
Cǎishí Jī
is thirty lǐ north of present-day Tàipíng Prefecture, at the ferry crossing opposite.
Jiāng
is pronounced liàng;
the same applies to jiāng bīng below.
They then captured it.
The incident at Shāwǔkǒu in the 12th month of the jiǎxū year of Déyòu was also similar to this.
The Suí Zhì states: Liùhé County, Jiāngdū Commandery,
was formerly named Wèishì.
Qín Commandery was established.
Later, Qí established Qín Prefecture.
Later, Zhōu changed the prefecture's name to Fāng Prefecture,
and the commandery's name to Liùhé.
In the early years of Kāihuáng,
the commandery was abolished.
In the 4th year,
Wèishì was renamed Liùhé.
Zhāng Shùnmín said: Táoyè Mountain
is the location of present-day Guābù Town.
Shuài
is read as shuài.
On the day bǐngyín,
Xú Zǐjiàn, the commander of Cǎishí garrison, urgently reported the change.
On the day dīngmǎo,
public ministers were summoned to discuss military matters.
On the day wùchén,
the Chén ruler issued an edict saying:
“The dogs and sheep are rampant,
invading and plundering the suburbs and capital region.
Hornets and scorpions are poisonous;
they should be swept away and pacified without delay.
I shall personally lead the six armies
to clear and pacify the eight directions.
All within and without should be on high alert.”
He appointed General of Agile Cavalry Xiāo Móhē, General of the Guard Fán Yì, and Central Army Commander Lǔ Guǎngdá as Dūdū.
Sīkōng Sīmǎ Xiāonàn and Governor of Xiāng Prefecture Shī Wénqìng were appointed Grand Supervising Generals.
In the winter of the previous year,
the Chén ruler promoted Shī Wénqìng to supervise Xiāng Prefecture,
but before he could take up his post, the Suí army crossed the Jiāng.
Nàn
is pronounced nǎidàn.
Jiàn
is pronounced gōnghán.
The Chén Nányù Prefecture's seat was Xuānchéng,
but at that time, it was moved to Gūshú.
Báixià City, together with Báishí Lěi,
during the Táng Wǔdé era, Jiāngníng County was moved here,
and named Báixià County.
Shuài
is read as shuài.
He re-established the reward system,
and ordered all monks, nuns, and Daoist priests
to perform labor.
On the day gēngwǔ,
Hèruò Bì attacked and captured Jīngkǒu,
and seized Huáng Kè, Governor of Nánxú Prefecture.
Nánxú Prefecture was governed from Jīngkǒu.
Not a single autumn hair was harmed.
When a soldier was found buying wine from commoners,
Bì immediately beheaded him.
Of the more than six thousand captives,
Bì released them all,
providing them with food and provisions, and sending them away,
giving them imperial edicts
to spread the message along their respective routes.
Thus, wherever they went, they were welcomed enthusiastically.
Fán Měng was in Jiànkāng,
and his son Xún was acting Governor of Nányù Prefecture.
On the day xīnwèi,
Hán Qínhǔ advanced to attack Gūshú.
Within half a day,
he captured it,
and seized Xún and his family.
Two lǐ south of present-day Dāngtú County, Tàipíng Prefecture, there is Gūshú Stream,
which flows west into the Great River,
likely named after the old garrison.
They returned to the south of the Jiāng.
The elders, who had long heard of Qínhǔ's prestige,
came to visit his military camp day and night without interruption.
Lǔ Guǎngdá's son Shìzhēn was in Xīncài,
and together with his younger brother Shìxióng and their subordinates, surrendered to Qínhǔ.
During Hóu Jǐng's rebellion,
Lǔ Xīdá gathered his fellow villagers to protect Xīncài,
and the Lǔ clan subsequently inherited this to serve Chén.
The note for Xīncài can be found in Volume 154, the first year of Chéngshèng of Liáng Shìzǔ.
Jiàng
is pronounced hùjiāng.
Guǎngdá was garrisoned in Jiànkāng at the time.
He impeached himself
and went to the Court of Judicial Review to request punishment.
The Chén ruler consoled him,
bestowed additional gold upon him,
and sent him back to his camp.
Fán Měng and Jiǎng Yuánsùn, General of the Left Guard, led eighty qīnglóng boats to patrol at Báixià
to defend against the Liùhé troops.
The Chén ruler, knowing that Měng's wife and children were with the Suí army,
feared he had other intentions,
and wanted to replace him with Rèn Zhōng, General Who Pacifies the East.
He ordered Xiāo Móhē to subtly persuade Měng.
Měng was displeased.
The Chén ruler then reconsidered hurting his feelings and stopped.
Zhòng
is pronounced as written,
meaning difficulty.
Thereupon, Hèruò Bì (賀若弼) advanced from the northern route,
and Hán Qínhǔ (韓擒虎) advanced from the southern route simultaneously.
Jīngkǒu (京口) was north of Jiànkāng (建康),
while Gūshú (姑孰) was south of Jiànkāng.
They fled at the mere sight of them;
Bì (弼) divided his troops to cut off the strategic point of Qǔ'ē (曲阿) and entered.
Qǔ'ē,
originally Yúnyáng (雲陽),
during the Qín (秦) dynasty,
people said that the land had the qi (氣) of a Son of Heaven.
Shǐhuáng (始皇) dug a northern pit to destroy its influence,
cut a straight road to make the ‘a’ (阿) crooked,
and renamed it Qǔ'ē.
Its land was between Wǔjìn (武進) and Dāntú (丹徒) counties.
Bì (弼) divided his troops to cut off its strategic point
for fear that the troops from Sānwú (三吳) would come to the rescue of Jiànkāng,
flanking them from the rear.
Duàn (斷)
is pronounced 'duǎn'.
Xiāo Móhē (蕭摩訶) was stationed at Lèyóuyuàn (樂遊苑),
Fán Yì (樊毅) was stationed at Qíshé Sì (耆闍寺),
Lǔ Guǎngdá (魯廣達) was stationed at Báitǔ Gāng (白土岡),
and Zhōngwǔ Jiāngjūn (忠武將軍) Kǒng Fàn (孔範) was stationed at Bǎotián Sì (寶田寺).
Zhōngwǔ Jiāngjūn,
established by the Liáng (梁) dynasty,
ranked nineteenth;
the Chén (陳) dynasty ranked it fourth in official grade,
with a salary of two thousand dàn (石) of grain,
its position was inferior to the Sìpíng Jiāngjūn (四平將軍).
On the day of Jǐmǎo (己卯),
Rèn Zhōng (任忠) entered from Wúxīng (吳興) to respond.
The previous year, Rèn Zhōng had been sent to guard Wúxīng.
Emperor Xiàowǔ (孝武) of Jìn (晉) built the Zhūquè Mén (朱雀門),
which had two bronze sparrows on top,
directly facing the Grand Bridge (大航) in front,
hence it was called Zhūquè Háng (朱雀航).
On Xīnwèi (辛未),
Hèruò Bì advanced to occupy Zhōngshān (鍾山).
Zhōngshān is eighteen lǐ (里) northeast of present-day Shàngyuán (上元) county.
The Yúdì Zhì (輿地志) states: In ancient times, it was called Jīnlíng Shān (金陵山),
and the county name derived from it.
It was also called Jiǎng Shān (蔣山);
at the end of the Hàn (漢) dynasty, Jiǎng Zǐwén (蔣子文), the prefect of Mòlíng (秣陵), died fighting rebels at the foot of this mountain.
The Sūn (孫) clan made Mòlíng their capital,
and because their ancestor's taboo name was Zhōng (鍾),
they renamed it Jiǎng Shān.
Jìn Wáng Guǎng (晉王廣) dispatched Zǒngguǎn (總管) Dù Yàn (杜彥) to join forces with Hán Qínhǔ (韓擒虎),
with twenty thousand infantry and cavalry stationed at Xīnlín (新林).
Xīnlín Pǔ (新林浦)
is twenty lǐ from present-day Jiànkāng city,
extending west directly to Báilù Zhōu (白鷺洲).
They defeated the Chén (陳) general Jì Zhèn (紀瑱) at Qíkǒu (蘄口).
Qíshuǐ (蘄水) enters the river at this mouth.
Jiāng (將),
is pronounced 'liàng';
same below.
Zhèn (瑱),
is pronounced 'diàn',
also 'zhèn'.
Those who surrendered followed one after another.
Jìn Wáng Guǎng submitted a report,
and the Emperor was greatly pleased,
hosting a banquet and bestowing gifts upon his ministers.
At that time, Jiànkāng still had more than one hundred thousand armored soldiers.
The Chén (陳) ruler was naturally timid and weak,
and not skilled in military affairs.
He only wept day and night,
and all decisions within the palace
were entrusted to Shī Wénqìng (施文慶).
Wénqìng, knowing that the generals resented him,
and fearing their success,
then reported:
"These disgruntled individuals
have never submitted to officials.
With the urgency of this situation,
how can they be fully trusted!"
Because of this, any requests from the generals
were mostly rejected.
When Hèruò Bì attacked Jīngkǒu,
Xiāo Móhē requested to lead troops to meet him in battle,
but the Chén (陳) ruler refused.
When Bì (弼) reached Zhōngshān,
Móhē again said:
"Bì's forces are deeply entrenched far from home,
their ramparts and trenches are not yet firm.
If we sally out and attack them by surprise,
we can certainly defeat them."
This was again refused.
The Chén (陳) ruler summoned Móhē and Rèn Zhōng to the inner palace to discuss military affairs.
Zhōng (忠) said:
"Military strategy dictates: the attacker values swift battle,
while the defender values caution.
Currently, our state has ample troops and provisions.
We should firmly defend Táichéng (臺城),
erect barricades along the Huái (淮) River,
and even if the northern army comes,
do not engage them in battle.
Divide troops to cut off the river route,
so that their communications cannot get through.
Give me ten thousand elite soldiers
and three hundred Jīncì (金翅) ships,
and I will go down the river to attack Lùhé (六合) directly.
Their main army will surely think that their crossing generals and soldiers have been captured,
and their morale will naturally be crushed.
The local people of Huáinán (淮南) have long been acquainted with me.
Now hearing of my arrival,
they will surely follow like shadows.
Shīgǔ (師古) said: Jǐngcóng (景從) means following like a shadow follows a form.
Cutting off their retreat,
then all their armies will depart without being attacked.
Xúzhōu (徐州) is the path to Péngbiàn (彭汴).
Fù (復),
is pronounced 'fú yòu'.
Duàn (斷),
is pronounced 'dīng guǎn'.
The forces of Zhōu Luóhóu (周羅睺) and others upriver will certainly move downstream to reinforce.
Zhōu Luóhóu was then supervising the navy
at Yǐnghàn (郢漢)."
The Chén (陳) ruler could not follow this advice.
The next day,
he suddenly said:
"This protracted war makes me anxious.
Call Xiāo Láng (蕭郎) to go out and attack them."
Rèn Zhōng kowtowed and earnestly pleaded against battle.
Kǒng Fàn (孔範) again reported:
"Please make a decisive move.
I will engrave a stele on Yànrán (燕然) for Your Majesty."
Kǒng Fàn compared himself to Dòu Xiàn (竇憲) defeating the Xiongnú (匈奴),
such was the deceit and flattery that misled the state and destroyed the family.
Wéi (為),
is pronounced 'yú wěi';
same below.
Yàn (燕),
is pronounced 'yú xián'.
He said to Móhē:
"Can you make this decisive move for me!"
Móhē replied:
"In past battles,
it was for the state and for myself;
today's matter
is also for my wife and children."
The Chén (陳) ruler distributed much gold and silk to the armies as rewards.
Fù (賦)
means to give or distribute.
On Jiǎshēn (甲申),
he sent Lǔ Guǎngdá to array his troops on Báitǔ Gāng,
south of the other armies;
Rèn Zhōng was next,
Fán Yì and Kǒng Fàn were next after him,
and Xiāo Móhē's army was at the northernmost.
The armies stretched twenty lǐ from north to south,
their head and tail unable to communicate with each other during advance or retreat.
Hèruò Bì led light cavalry up the mountain.
Seeing the massed armies,
he then galloped down
and, with his seven Zǒngguǎn (總管) Yáng Yá (楊牙), Yuán Míng (員明) and others,
totaling eight thousand armored soldiers,
formed a formation to await them.
The Chén (陳) ruler had an affair with Xiāo Móhē's wife,
so Móhē initially had no intention of fighting.
Only Lǔ Guǎngdá and his followers fought bravely,
engaging Bì (弼).
The Suí (隋) forces retreated several times.
Two hundred seventy-three men of Bì's (弼) command died.
Bì (弼) used smoke to conceal himself,
distressed but recovered.
The Chén (陳) soldiers, having captured heads,
all rushed to present them to the Chén (陳) ruler to claim rewards.
Bì (弼), knowing their arrogance and laziness,
led his troops to attack Kǒng Fàn (孔範).
Fàn's (範) troops fled after a brief engagement.
The Chén (陳) armies looked on,
and their cavalry and infantry scattered and collapsed,
unable to be stopped.
Five thousand men died.
Yuán Míng captured Xiāo Móhē
and sent him to Bì (弼).
Bì (弼) ordered him to be dragged out and executed,
but Móhē's expression remained unchanged.
Bì (弼) then released him and treated him with respect.
Rèn Zhōng (任忠) galloped into the imperial palace.
He saw the Chén (陳) sovereign and reported the defeat,
saying:
" 'Guān (官)' means 'to live well,'
'hǎo (好)' means 'good,'
which is fitting;
'zhù (住)' means 'to stop.'
This is also 'to stop.'
Today, southerners still use this expression."
The Chén (陳) sovereign gave him gold and two bundles of silk,
ordering him to recruit men to fight.
Zhōng (忠) said:
"Your Majesty should only prepare boats and oars
and join the main army upstream."
This meant going to join Zhōu Luóhóu (周羅睺) and others.
The Chén (陳) sovereign believed him
and ordered Zhōng (忠) to go out and organize.
He commanded the palace women to dress up and wait for him,
wondering why he was taking so long.
At that time, Hán Qínhǔ (韓擒虎) advanced his army from Xīnlín (新林).
Zhōng (忠) had already led a few horsemen to surrender at Shízǐgāng (石子岡).
Commander Cái Zhēng (蔡徵) guarded Zhūquè Háng (朱雀航).
Hearing that Qínhǔ (擒虎) was about to arrive,
his troops became terrified and dispersed.
Zhōng (忠) led Qínhǔ's (擒虎) army directly into Zhūquè Mén (朱雀門).
The Chén (陳) people wanted to fight.
Zhōng (忠) waved at them and said:
"Even this old man has surrendered,
why are you soldiers still fighting!"
"Jūn (軍)" (army)
is sometimes written as
"jūn (君)" (lord).
Thereupon, all the civil and military officials within the city fled.
Only the President of the Board of Civil Office, Yuán Xiàn (袁憲), remained in the palace hall,
and President of the Imperial Secretariat Jiāng Zǒng (江總) and a few others stayed in the provincial government office.
The Chén (陳) sovereign said to Yuán Xiàn (袁憲):
"I have never treated you better than others,
but today I am filled with regret."
This is like Liú Shàn (劉禪) with Xí Zhèng (郤正).
It also means the customs of the prominent families in Jiāngdōng (江東) have reached their end.
The Chén (陳) sovereign, in a panic,
was about to hide.
Xiàn (憲) said sternly:
"The northern troops, once they enter,
will certainly not commit any offenses.
With such a great matter, where does Your Majesty wish to go to find safety!
Your
subject wishes Your Majesty to straighten your clothes and cap,
and ascend the main hall,
following the precedent of Emperor Wǔ of Liáng (梁武帝) when he met Hóu Jǐng (侯景)."
This event can be found in Volume 162, Emperor Wǔ of Liáng (梁武帝) in the third year of Tàiqīng (太清).
(The Chén sovereign) got off the couch and rushed away,
saying:
"Under the edge of a blade,
it is not advisable to confront them directly.
I have my own plan!"
He led more than ten palace women out through the rear hall, Jǐngyáng Diàn (景陽殿),
intending to throw himself into a well.
Xiàn (憲) earnestly remonstrated, but he would not listen.
Xiàhóu Gōngyùn (夏侯公韻), a Palace Attendant of the Rear Apartments, covered the well with his body.
The Chén (陳) sovereign struggled with him,
and after a long time,
he finally managed to get in.
Soon, soldiers peered into the well,
called out,
but received no answer.
They were about to throw stones
when a cry was heard.
They pulled him up with a rope,
surprised by how heavy he was.
When he came out,
it was with Zhāng Guì (張貴) and Kǒng Guìpín (孔貴嬪), tied together, that he ascended.
Zhù Mù (祝穆) said: "The Jǐngyáng (景陽) well is in Fǎbǎo Sì (法寶寺)."
Or it is said:
"Below the Báilián Gé (白蓮閣) there is a small pond,
about ten square feet."
Or it is said:
"It is beside the Lǎnhuī Tíng (覽輝亭) in Bǎoníng Sì (保寧寺)."
It was traditionally said: "The railing has a stone vein.
If one wipes it with silk,
it leaves a rouge mark."
It was also called Yānzhī Jǐng (胭脂井) (Rouge Well),
and also Rǔ Jǐng (辱井) (Well of Disgrace).
The Liáng (梁) system had Diànzhōng Shèrén (殿中舍人) and Shǒu Shèrén (守舍人).
The Chén (陳) system designated Diànzhōng Shèrén (殿中舍人) as a third-rank position,
and Shǒu Shèrén (守舍人) as a third-rank honorary title,
outside the nine ranks.
Hòugé Shèrén (後閤舍人) (Palace Attendant of the Rear Apartments)
was probably a Diànzhōng Shèrén (殿中舍人) who guarded the rear apartments.
Prince Shēn (深), at fifteen years old,
sat behind closed doors,
with the attendant Kǒng Bóyú (孔伯魚) at his side.
This was a Crown Prince's attendant.
The Liáng (梁) system had four Tàizǐ Zhōngshèrén (太子中舍人) (Central Palace Attendants to the Crown Prince),
who managed the prohibitions of his residence;
and sixteen Shèrén (舍人) (Palace Attendants),
who managed documents.
The Zhōngshèrén (中舍人) were divided into eight classes,
and the Shèrén (舍人) into three classes.
The Chén (陳) system designated Zhōngshèrén (中舍人) a salary of 600 *shí* (石),
and the Shèrén (舍人) likewise.
Shēn (深) sat calmly
and consoled them, saying:
"The barbarians are on the move;
there is no need to worry!"
The soldiers all paid their respects to him.
At that time, there were over a hundred members of the Chén (陳) imperial clan, princes, and marquises in Jiànkāng (建康).
The Chén (陳) sovereign, fearing they might cause trouble,
summoned them all
and had them stationed in the imperial court,
with Prince Shūyīng (叔英) of Yùzhāng (豫章) supervising them.
He also secretly made preparations for them.
When Táichéng (臺城) fell,
they led each other out to surrender.
Hèruò Bì (賀若弼), riding on his victory, reached Lèyóu Yuàn (樂遊苑).
Lǔ Guǎngdá (魯廣達) still commanded his remaining troops, fighting fiercely and without rest.
He killed and captured several hundred people.
As night fell,
he finally unarmored himself,
bowed twice towards the imperial palace and wept bitterly,
saying to his men:
"My body could not save the nation,
my guilt is profound!"

The prefecture was named after Jiǎngshān (蔣山).
Jìn Wáng Guǎng (晉王廣) returned with his army.
He left Wáng Sháo (王韶) to guard Shítóu Chéng (石頭城)
and entrusted him with subsequent affairs.
In the third month,
on the *jǐsì* (己巳) day,
Chén Shúbǎo (陳叔寶) and his princes, dukes, and all officials departed from Jiànkāng (建康)
for Cháng'ān (長安).
The large and small groups on the road
stretched continuously for five hundred *lǐ* (里).
The emperor ordered that the residences of Cháng'ān's (長安) commoners be temporarily divided to accommodate them.
Everything, inside and out, was renovated and prepared.
Envoys were dispatched to welcome and comfort them.
The Chén (陳) people who arrived felt as if they were returning home.
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the *xīnhài* (辛亥) day,
the emperor visited Lí Shān (驪山).
Lí Shān (驪山) is in Xīnfēng Xiàn (新豐縣).
On the *yǐsì* (乙巳) day,
should probably be
the triumphal music was played upon entry.
Chén Shúbǎo (陳叔寶) and all the princes, marquises, generals, and ministers, along with the imperial carriages, regalia, astronomical charts, and records, were arranged in sequence.
They were surrounded by iron cavalry
and entered with Jìn Wáng Guǎng (晉王廣) and Qín Wáng Jùn (秦王俊),
lining up in the palace courtyard.
Guǎng (廣) was appointed Tàiwèi (太尉)
and bestowed with a grand carriage, riding horses, court robes and crowns, a dark jade *guī* (圭), and a white jade *bì* (璧).
On the *bǐngchén* (丙辰) day,
the emperor sat on the viewing platform of Guǎngyáng Mén (廣陽門).
Guǎngyáng Mén (廣陽門) had a viewing platform and watchtowers.
Guān (觀) is pronounced *gǔwán*.
He and the crown prince, along with twenty-eight other princes,
Sīkōng (司空) Sīmǎ Xiāonàn (司馬消難), and down to the Shàngshū Láng (尚書郎), numbering over two hundred people,
were addressed by the emperor, who had a Nàyán (納言) proclaim an edict to comfort them.
Next, he had a Nèishǐ Lìng (內史令) proclaim an edict,
blaming them for the inability of monarch and subjects to assist each other,
which led to their downfall.
Shúbǎo (叔寶) and all his officials were ashamed and terrified, prostrating themselves on the ground,
holding their breath and unable to respond.
Soon after, they were pardoned.
At first,
Wǔyuán Dì (武元帝) had welcomed Sīmǎ Xiāonàn (司馬消難)
(This refers to the 167th scroll of Chén Gāozǔ Yǒngdì's (陳高祖永定) second year).
The emperor's deceased father, Zhōng (忠), was posthumously titled Wǔyuán Dì (武元帝).
Their relationship was very close,
and the emperor always treated him with the respect due to an uncle.
When Chén (陳) was pacified and
Xiāonàn (消難) arrived,
he was specially exempted from death
and assigned to the household of musicians.
He was exempted after twenty days
and was still granted an audience due to their old friendship.
He soon died at home.
On the *gēngxū* (庚戌) day,
the emperor presided over Guǎngyáng Mén (廣陽門).
Guǎngyáng Mén (廣陽門) was the main south gate of Dàxīng (大興) Palace City.
The *Táng Liù Diǎn* (唐六典) states: "During the Suí (隋) dynasty, it was called Guǎngyáng Mén (廣陽門), built in the second year of Kāihuáng (開皇).
In the first year of Rénshòu (仁壽),
it was renamed Zhāoyáng Mén (昭陽門).
In the first year of Wǔdé (武德) of the Táng (唐) dynasty,
it was renamed Shùntiān Mén (順天門).
In the first year of Shénlóng (神龍),
it was renamed Chéngtiān Mén (承天門)."
Outside the gate, along the road, piles of silk and cloth were arrayed,
reaching to the southern suburbs.
These were distributed with varying amounts,
totaling over three million bolts.
Within the former territory of Chén (陳),
corvée labor was remitted for ten years,
and other prefectures were exempted from their year's rent and taxes.
Yuán Xié (元諧), Duke of Lè'ān (樂安), stepped forward and said:
"Your Majesty's prestige and virtue are far-reaching.
Your servant previously requested that the Turkic Khagan be made a border guard and
Chén Shúbǎo (陳叔寶) be made a clerk.
Now, your servant's words can be put into practice."
The emperor said:
"When I pacified the Chén (陳) state,
it was originally to eliminate rebellion,
not to boast.
Your memorial is quite contrary to my wishes.
The Turks do not know the mountains and rivers,
how could they guard the borders?
Shúbǎo (叔寶) is muddled and drunk,
how could he be put to use!"
Xié (諧) withdrew in silence.
On the *xīnyǒu* (辛酉) day,
Yáng Sù (楊素) was advanced in peerage to Duke of Yuè (越公).
According to the *Suí Shū* (隋書),
Yáng Sù (楊素) was promoted from Duke of Qīnghé Jùn (清河郡公) to Duke of Yǐng Guó (郢國公).
Sù (素) said:
"The rebel Wáng Yì (王誼) was previously enfeoffed in Yǐng (郢).
I do not wish to share that title with him."
He was then re-enfeoffed as Duke of Yuè (越公).
Xuán Jiǎng (玄獎) was made Duke of Qīnghé Jùn (清河郡公).
He was bestowed with ten thousand bolts of cloth
and ten thousand *shí* (石) of grain.
Hèruò Bì (賀若弼) was ordered to ascend the imperial seat,
bestowed with eight thousand bolts of cloth,
promoted to Shàng Zhùguó (上柱國),
and advanced in peerage to Duke of Sòng (宋公).
Each was also bestowed with gold, jewels, and a sister of Chén Shúbǎo (陳叔ǎo) as a concubine.
Hèruò Bì (賀若弼) and Hán Qínhǔ (韓擒虎) disputed their achievements before the emperor.
Bì (弼) said:
"Your servant fought fiercely at Jiǎng Shān (蔣山),
defeated their elite troops,
captured their brave generals,
and displayed our formidable might,
thereby pacifying the Chén (陳) state.
Hán Qínhǔ (韓擒虎) barely engaged with Chén (陳),
how can he compare to your servant!"
Qínhǔ (擒虎) said:
"I originally received a clear imperial edict
instructing me and Bì (弼) to combine our forces simultaneously to capture the false capital.
Bì (弼) dared to act ahead of schedule,
encountered the enemy, and fought,
causing many soldiers to be wounded and killed.
Your servant, with five hundred light cavalry,
without shedding a drop of blood,
directly captured Jīnlíng (金陵),
received the surrender of Rèn Mánnú (任蠻奴),
captured Chén Shúbǎo (陳叔寶),
seized their treasury,
and overturned their stronghold.
Bì (弼) only knocked on the Běiyè Mén (北掖門) in the evening.
Your servant opened the gate and admitted him.
This was merely an act of saving himself from punishment,
how can he compare to your servant!"
The emperor said:
"Both generals have achieved top merits."
Thereupon, Qínhǔ (擒虎) was advanced to Shàng Zhùguó (上柱國)
and bestowed with eight thousand bolts of cloth.
However, the authorities impeached Qínhǔ (擒虎) for allowing his soldiers to run wild
and defile the Chén (陳) palace.
Because of this, he was not granted additional peerage or fiefdom.
Gāo Jǐng (高熲) was promoted to Shàng Zhùguó (上柱國)
and advanced in peerage to Duke of Qí (齊公),
bestowed with nine thousand bolts of cloth.
The emperor comforted him, saying:
"After you conquered Chén (陳),
people said you were rebellious,
but I have already executed them.
The path of monarch and minister is in harmony,
not something that 'green flies' can sow discord in."
The emperor casually ordered Jǐng (熲) to discuss the pacification of Chén (陳) with Hèruò Bì (賀若弼).
Jǐng (熲) said:
"Hèruò Bì (賀若弼) first offered ten strategies
and then fought hard at Jiǎng Shān (蔣山) to defeat the enemy.
Your servant is merely a civil official,
how dare I discuss merits with a great general!"
The emperor laughed heartily,
commending his modesty.
When the emperor was campaigning against Chén (陳),
he had Gāo Jǐng (高熲) consult Lǐ Délín (李德林), Shàng Yí Tóng Sān Sī (上儀同三司), for strategies,
which were then given to Jìn Wáng Guǎng (晉王廣).
Now,
the emperor rewarded his achievements
by bestowing him with Zhùguó (柱國)
and enfeoffing him as a Commandery Duke,
with a reward of three thousand bolts of cloth.
After the imperial edict had been proclaimed,
someone advised Gāo Jǐng (高熲), saying:
"If credit is now given to Lǐ Délín (李德林),
the generals will surely be indignant.
Moreover, later generations will see your achievements as mere empty gestures."
Jǐng (熲) then went in and spoke about this,
so the order was rescinded.
Qín Wáng Jùn (秦王俊) was appointed Zǒngguǎn (總管) of forty-four prefectures' military affairs in Yángzhōu (揚州),
and stationed in Guǎnglíng (廣陵).
Jìn Wáng Guǎng (晉王廣) returned to Bìngzhōu (幷州).
When Jìn Wáng Guǎng-Zhī (晉王廣之) executed the Five Corrupt Officials of Chén,
the Five Corrupt Officials
were Shī Wén-Qìng (施文慶), Shěn Kè-Qīng (沈客卿), Yáng Huì-Lǎng (陽慧朗), Xú Xī (徐析), and Jì Huì-Jǐng (暨慧景).
Therefore, he was spared;
but upon arriving in Cháng'ān,
his deeds were fully exposed.
On the yǐwèi day,
the Emperor revealed his transgressions and wickedness,
casting him to the remote frontiers
to apologize to the people of Wú and Yuè.
Tuō (瑳) was harsh, mean, greedy, and vulgar,
jealous of and harmful to talent;
Yí (儀) was manipulative and fawning,
offering two daughters to seek intimacy;
sǎn (散),

qí (騎),

tuō (瑳),

He spoke deceptively and obsequiously,
and was therefore equally guilty.
The Emperor bestowed generous gifts upon Chén Shú-Bǎo (陳叔寶),
frequently granting him audiences,
and his rank was equivalent to a third-grade official;
whenever he attended a banquet,
out of fear of causing him sadness,
Wú music was not played.
Later, his supervisor reported:
"Shú-Bǎo (叔寶) said,
'Since I have no official position,
whenever I attend court assemblies,
I wish to obtain an official title.'"
The Emperor said:
"Shú-Bǎo (叔寶) has no heart or liver at all!"
The supervisor then said:
"Shú-Bǎo (叔寶) is often drunk,
rarely sober."
The Emperor asked:
"How much does he drink?"
The reply was:
"He drinks one shí (石) daily with his sons and younger brothers."
The Emperor was greatly astonished and
ordered his alcohol consumption to be restricted,
but then said:
"Let him follow his nature;
otherwise,
how can he pass the days!"
Alas,
this is why Chén Shú-Bǎo (陳叔寶) was able to die in his bed!
Fearing he might cause trouble in the capital city,
he was relocated to border prefectures,
given fields and property to make a living,
and granted clothes annually to ensure his safety.
An imperial edict appointed Chén Shàngshūlìng (陳尚書令) Jiāng Zǒng (江總) as Shàng Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (上開府儀同三司);
Púyè (僕射) Yuán Xiàn (袁憲), Piàojì (驃騎) Xiāo Mó-Hé (蕭摩訶), and Lǐngjūn (領軍) Rèn Zhōng (任忠) were all made Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司);
Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書) Yáo Chá (姚察) of Wúxìng (吳興) was made Mìshū Chéng (祕書丞).
The Emperor praised Yuán Xiàn's (袁憲) refined conduct
and issued an edict,
considering him the foremost figure south of the Yangtze,
appointing him as Cìshǐ (刺史) of Chāngzhōu (昌州).
The Suí Zhì (隋志) states: Chōnglíng Jùn (舂陵郡),
Latar Wèi (後魏) established Nán Jīngzhōu (南荊州),
Xī Wèi (西魏) renamed it Chāngzhōu (昌州).
He was promoted and appointed Zhǔjué Shìláng (主爵侍郎).
sǎn (散),
read as sī dǎn fān.
qí (騎),

The Suí Zhì (隋志) states: Zhǔjué Shìláng (主爵侍郎)
belongs to the Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書).
"At the beginning of the conquest of Chén,
I regretted not killing Rèn Mán-Nú (任蠻奴).
Having received honor and emoluments from others,
and bearing a heavy responsibility,
he was unable to die for his country,
but instead claimed he could do nothing.
How far removed is that from Hóng Yǎn (弘演) offering his liver!"
Wèi Yì-Gōng (衞懿公) fought the Di (狄) people at Yíngzé (熒澤),
and was killed by the Di (狄) people.
Hóng Yǎn (弘演) offered his liver to die with him.
The Emperor met Zhōu Luó-Hóu (周羅睺),
comforted and encouraged him,
and promised him wealth and high rank.
Luó-Hóu (羅睺) replied tearfully:
"Your servant received great kindness from the Chén (陳) family;
with the demise of my former dynasty,
there is no integrity left to record.
That I was spared death
is a gift from Your Majesty,
how dare I hope for wealth and high rank!"
Hè Ruò-Bì (賀若弼) said to Luó-Hóu (羅睺):
"I heard you commanded troops in Yǐng (郢) and Hàn (漢),
and I immediately knew Yángzhōu (揚州) could be taken.
The royal army's successful crossing
indeed matched my estimation."
Luó-Hóu (羅睺) said:
"If I had been able to contend with you,
the outcome of victory or defeat would be unknown."
How did Zhōu Luó-Hóu (周羅睺) manage to say this to Hè Ruò-Bì (賀若弼)?
The historians merely exaggerated.
He was appointed Shàng Yítóng Sānsī (上儀同三司).
Previously,
Chén general Yáng Xiáng (羊翔) had surrendered.
During the campaign to conquer Chén,
he served as a local guide.
His position reached Shàng Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (上開府儀同三司),
with a rank above Luó-Hóu (羅睺).
Hán Qín-Hǔ (韓擒虎) joked with him in the imperial court:
"You lack adaptability,
and now stand beneath Yáng Xiáng (羊翔).
Can you not feel ashamed?"
Luó-Hóu (羅睺) said:
"In the past, in Jiāngnán (江南),
I long heard of your good reputation,
considering you a man of integrity under heaven;
what you say today
is far from what I expected."
Qín-Hǔ (擒虎) showed a look of shame.
When the Emperor reproached the Chén (陳) ruler and his ministers,
Chén Shú-Wén (陳叔文) alone appeared pleased and self-satisfied.
Dé sè (得色):
self-satisfied and showing it in one's expression.
"When I was in Bāzhōu (巴州),
I had already sent my submission in advance.
I beg you to consider this situation,
and hope for treatment beyond the usual!"
Although the Emperor disliked his disloyalty,
he wished to appease the region south of the Yangtze,
so he appointed Shú-Wén (叔文) as Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司),
and made him Cìshǐ (刺史) of Yízhōu (宜州).
Yízhōu (宜州) was established in Huáyúan (華原) County of Jīngzhào (京兆).
Initially,
Chén Sànqí Chángshì (陳散騎常侍) Wéi Dǐng (韋鼎) was sent as an envoy to Zhōu (周).
The biography of Wéi Dǐng (韋鼎) states: He was sent as an envoy to Zhōu (周) during the Tài Jiàn (太建) era of Chén.
sǎn (散),

and when noble, the whole world will be one family.
A cycle of the year,

zhì (質),

Chén Chángchéng-Gōng (陳長城公) ascended the throne,
changing the era name to Zhì Dé (至德).
He sold all his fields and residences.
Dàjiàngqīng (大匠卿) Máo Biāo (毛彪) asked him why,
Dǐng (鼎) replied:
'The imperial aura of Jiāngdōng (江東)
ends here!
You and I will be buried in Cháng'ān.'"
When Chén (陳) was pacified,
the Emperor summoned Dǐng (鼎) and made him Shàng Yítóng Sānsī (上儀同三司).
Dǐng (鼎) was the grandson of Ruì (叡).
Wéi Ruì (韋叡) established fame and achievements during the time of Liáng Wǔ-Dì (梁武帝).
On the rénxū day,
an imperial edict proclaimed:
"Now, the entire land is united,
and all living beings can fulfill their nature;
the law of great peace
can now be widely implemented.
All my officials and people
should cleanse their bodies and bathe in virtue,
with every family cultivating itself
and every person conquering their desires.
The Shū (書) says: 'Only by conquering madness does one become a sage.'
One must not fail to restrain;
punishment can assist transformation,
but must not be solely relied upon.
Beyond the nine layers of palace guards
and the garrisons protecting the four directions,
military forces and weapons
should all be abolished.
As the world is now peaceful
and all regions are without trouble,
sons of military families
can all study the classics;
private weapons and armor
shall all be removed and destroyed.
Proclaim this to all under heaven,
so that all may understand this intention."
Hèruò Bì 賀若弼 drafted his strategy and presented it,
calling it the 'Seven Strategies for Pacifying Chén 陳, Granted by the Emperor'.
The Emperor did not examine it,
saying,
"You wish to promote my name,
but I do not seek fame;
you should record it in your own family history."
Bì 弼 held a prominent and weighty position,
and his brothers were all ennobled as jùn gōng 郡公,
serving as cì shǐ 刺史 and senior generals.
The precious curiosities in his household
were innumerable,
and hundreds of his maids and concubines wore embroidered silk.
Luó 羅

Later, when the Tūjué 突厥 came to court,
the Emperor said to them,
"Have you heard of the Son of Heaven of the state of Chén 陳 south of the Jiāngnán 江南?"
They replied,
"We have heard of him."
The Emperor ordered his attendants to lead the Tūjué 突厥 to Hán Qínhǔ's 韓擒虎 presence and said,
"This is the one who captured the Son of Heaven of Chén 陳."
Qínhǔ 擒虎 looked at them sternly,
and the Tūjué 突厥 were terrified,
not daring to look up.
Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn 左衞將軍 Páng Huǎng 龐晃 and others slandered Gāo Jiǒng 高熲 to the Emperor,
and the Emperor, in anger,
dismissed them all.
Páng Huǎng 龐晃 had formed close ties with the Emperor during his period of obscurity,
and their relationship was very intimate.
However, he had a rift with Gāo Jiǒng 高熲,
and together with Guǎngpíng Wáng Xióng 廣平王雄, he repeatedly spoke ill of Jiǒng 熲,
which led to all of them being dismissed.
Jiǒng 熲,
pronounced 'Jū-yǒng'.
Then the Emperor said to Jiǒng 熲,
"Dúgū Gōng 獨孤公
is like a mirror;
the more it is polished,
the brighter it becomes."
Originally,
Jiǒng's 熲 father Bīn 賓 was a subordinate of Dúgū Xìn 獨孤信
and was granted the surname Dúgū 獨孤,
which is why the Emperor always called him Dúgū 獨孤 and did not refer to him by his personal name.
According to historical records, after Dúgū Xìn 獨孤信 was executed,
his wife and children were exiled to Shǔ 蜀.
Empress Dúgū 獨孤, being the daughter of Bīn's 賓 former colleague,
often visited his family.
How could Jiǒng's 熲 success
be solely due to his talent and strategy!
Externally, he gained the favor of the monarch, and internally, he received the gracious treatment of the monarch's mother.
But when externally one is resented by the monarch,
and internally one loses the affection of the monarch's mother,
one is immediately alienated and cast aside.
In the relationship between monarch and minister,
how can one not be cautious!
Yuán Xié 元諧, Prince of Lè'ān 樂安,
was chivalrous and spirited by nature.
He possessed a noble disposition,
and as a youth, he studied with the Emperor
and they were very fond of each other.
After the Emperor ascended the throne,
Xié 諧 successively held prominent official positions.
Xié 諧 enjoyed criticizing others
and was unable to curry favor with those around him.
He was on good terms with the Shàng Zhùguó 上柱國 Wáng Yì 王誼.
When Yì 誼 was executed,

someone accused Xié 諧, along with his cousin Shàng Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī 上開府儀同三司 Pāng 滂, Línzé Hóu Tián Luán 臨澤侯田鸞,

(Cóng 從

(Qí 祈 is a surname

was enfeoffed in Qí 祈,

The memorial stated,
"Xié 諧 plotted to have Qí Xù 祈緒 lead the Dǎngxiàng 党項 troops to cut off the Bā 巴 and Shǔ 蜀 regions.
Furthermore,
Xié 諧 once visited the Emperor with Pāng 滂,
and Xié 諧 privately said to Pāng 滂, 'I am the master,
the one on the throne is a thief.'
He then ordered Pāng 滂 to observe the qi 氣 (aura).
Pāng 滂 said, 'His cloud resembles a crouching dog and a running deer,
not as blessed as our fortune cloud.'"
The Emperor was furious,
and Xié 諧, Pāng 滂, Luán 鸞, and Xù 緒 were all executed.
The Kǎoyì 考異 states: The biography of Lǐ Déllín 李德林 says,
"Déllín 德林, seeing that Liáng Shìyàn 梁士彥 and Yuán Xié 元諧 repeatedly harbored rebellious intentions,
and that Jiāngnán 江南 was challenging the imperial court,
composed the Tiānmìng Lùn 天命論 and presented it."
Xié's 諧 biography says,
"Several years after the pacification of Chén 陳,
people accused Xié 諧 of plotting rebellion."
According to records, Xié 諧 requested that Chén Shúbǎo 陳叔寶 be made a nèishǐ 內史,
which means he was still alive when Chén 陳 fell.
Yáng Xióng 楊雄 was then in power,
and Xié 諧 wanted to slander him to have him removed,
which means Xióng 雄 had not yet become Sīkōng 司空.
Therefore, this account is appended here.

tenth month,
on the *wùzǐ* day,
Wéi Shìkāng, the Minister of Personnel, was appointed Governor-General of Jīng Prefecture.
Shìkāng was
the younger brother of Guāng.
Wéi Guāng pacified and settled Lǐngnán
and died in office.
According to Wéi Shìkāng's biography in the *Suíshū*: Shìkāng was
Guāng's elder brother.
Guāng is pronounced *guāng* (古黃翻).
He served in the Ministry of Personnel for over ten years,
and was praised at the time for his honesty and fairness.
According to Shìkāng's biography,
he transferred from Minister of Rites to Minister of Personnel
before the fourth year of Kāihuáng.
In the seventh year, he was appointed Inspector of Xiāng Prefecture,
then successively Governor-General of Ān Prefecture and Xìn Prefecture.
In the thirteenth year, he returned to court
and was reappointed Minister of Personnel.
He moved in and out of high positions,
serving for over ten years in total,
not exclusively in the Ministry of Personnel.
He said to his sons and nephews:
"Why must one's emoluments be excessive?
Retreat when you reach your peak;
do not wait until old age,
resign when illness strikes."
He then earnestly begged to retire.
The Emperor did not permit it
and sent him to guard Jīng Prefecture.
At that time, there were only four Governor-Generals in the empire:
Bīng, Yáng, Yì, and Jīng.
The three kings of Jìn, Qín, and Shǔ, and Shìkāng were appointed to these positions,
which was considered an honor at the time.
11 Eleventh month,
on the *xīnyǒu* day,
the Emperor visited Wēntāng.
This was the hot springs at Lí Mountain.
Chéng Dàchāng said: "The Huángtáng Stone Well
was built by Yǔwén Hù of the Later Zhōu dynasty.
Emperor Wén of Suí later renovated the buildings
and planted over a thousand pines and cypresses."
12 Twelfth month,
on the *wùzǐ* day,
an imperial edict stated:
"Anyone who steals one *shēng* or more of frontier grain
shall all be executed."
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Xíngfǎ Zhì* (Treatise on Penal Law) places this event in the sixteenth year.
This account now follows the *Dìjì* (Annals of Emperors).
13 On the *jǐchǒu* day,
an edict mandated that civil and military officials be replaced after four evaluations.
In the times of Táng and Yú, three years constituted one evaluation;
in later generations, one year constituted one evaluation.
14 Línghú Xī, the Inspector of Biàn Prefecture, came to court.
The *Suí Zhì* says: Jùnyí County, Yíngyáng Commandery,
was where Eastern Wèi established Liáng Prefecture,
which Later Zhōu renamed Biàn Prefecture.
The Línghú clan originated from the Wèi clan.
In the Spring and Autumn period, Wèi Kē, a grandee of Jìn, was enfeoffed in Línghú,
and his descendants adopted it as a surname.
Biàn is pronounced *biàn* (皮變翻).
He was bestowed three hundred bolts of silk
(mixed goods were measured in *duàn*,
pure goods in *pǐ*).
Xī was
the son of Zhěng.
Línghú Zhěng is mentioned in volume 159, during the first year of Zhōngdàtóng under Emperor Wǔ of Liáng.
1 Spring,
first month,
on the *dīnghài* day,
imperial grandson Yù was made Prince of Píngyuán,
Yún Prince of Ānchéng,
Ní Prince of Ānpíng,
Kè Prince of Xiāngchéng,
Gāi Prince of Gāoyáng,
Sháo Prince of Jiàn'ān,
Jiǒng Prince of Yǐngchuān.
All were the sons of Yǒng.
2 Summer,
sixth month,
on the *jiǎwǔ* day,
it was first decreed that merchants and artisans were not allowed to enter officialdom.
3 Autumn,
eighth month,
on the *bǐngxū* day,
an edict stated:
"For those condemned to death,
execution shall proceed only after three appeals."
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Xíngfǎ Zhì* places this event in the fifteenth year.
This account now follows the *Dìjì*.
4 In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day Jǐchǒu,
the Emperor went to Chángchūn Gōng.
The Suí Zhì states: In Cháoyì Xiàn, Tóngzhōu, there is Chángchūn Gōng.
On the day Rénzǐ,
he returned to Cháng'ān.
5 The Dǎngxiàng raided Huìzhōu.
The Suí Zhì states: Wénshān Jùn,
during the Later Zhōu, Wénzhōu was established.
In the early years of Kāihuáng, it was renamed Shǔzhōu,
and soon after, it became Huìzhōu.
Dǎng
is pronounced Dǐlǎng.
6 The Emperor married Princess Guānghuà to Mùróng Shìfú, the Khagan of Tǔyùhún.
Shìfú presented a memorial requesting to refer to the princess as Tiānhòu,
but the Emperor did not permit it.
1 In spring,
the second month,
on the day Guǐwèi,
Shǐ Wànsuì, Duke of Tàipíng, attacked the Nánníng Qiāng
and subdued them.
Shǐ Wànsuì inherited the title of County Duke of Tàipíng.
The Suí Zhì states: Tàipíng Xiàn
belonged to Jiàng Jùn.
The land of Nánníng
belonged to Zāngkē during the Hàn,
to Nánzhōng during Shǔ Hàn,
to Níngzhōu during the Jìn,
and became Nánníngzhōu during the Liáng.
Later, it was occupied by the Cuàn clan,
who claimed their ancestors were originally from Ānyì,
and that their seventh-generation ancestor was the Grand Administrator of Nánníng during the Jìn.
When China was in chaos,
they then ruled among the barbarians.
Upon examining the Jìn Zhì,
there was no Nánníng Jùn.
The Xīcuàn
were barbarians,
not Qiāng.
The Tōngjiàn, following the Suí Jì, forms this narrative.
When Liáng Ruì conquered Wáng Qiān,
it is recorded in volume 174, during the twelfth year of Tàijiàn of Emperor Xuān of Chén.
Only Cuàn Zhèn, the chieftain of Nánníngzhōu, relying on its remoteness, did not submit.
Ruì submitted a memorial,
stating:
"Nánníngzhōu,
the land of Zāngkē in the Hàn era,
has a dense population
and is rich in gold and treasures.
Xú Wénshèng, the Inspector of Nánníngzhōu during the Liáng, was summoned to Jīngzhōu by the Prince of Xiāngdōng
to raise troops to suppress Hóu Jǐng,
and Wénshèng went.
Before a distant strategy could be implemented,
the local leader Cuàn Zàn secretly occupied the region.
The state remotely bestowed upon him the title of Inspector,
and his son Zhèn succeeded him until now.
However, Zhèn has frequently failed in his duties as a subject,
and tribute has not been presented.
I request that, taking advantage of the troops that pacified Shǔ,
we swiftly subdue Nánníng."
Later, the Nánníng barbarian Cuàn Wán surrendered
and was appointed Inspector of Kūnzhōu,
and Kūnzhōu was established in his territory.
Jiàng
is pronounced Hùjiāng;
the same below.
Then, Shǐ Wànsuì, General of the Left Leader Cavalry, was appointed Overall Commander of the expeditionary force,
leading his troops to attack them,
entering from Qīnglíng Chuān
and reaching Nánzhōng.
Qīnglíng Chuān
was the land of Qīnglíng Xiàn during the Hàn.
Qīng
is pronounced Cāngjīng.
Líng
is pronounced Lángdīng.
Wànsuì defeated them all;
passing by Zhūgé Liàng's monument to his achievements,
the Táng Shǐ records: Nánzhào King Fèng Jiāyì built Zhédōng Chéng,
where Zhūgé Liàng's stone inscription was still present.
According to the Táng Shǐ,
Emperor Tàizōng attacked the Xīcuàn
and established Qīnglíng and Nòngdòng as counties.
West of Nòngdòng were the barbarians of Dà Bólòng and Xiǎo Bólòng prefectures,
and to their west, they bordered Huángguā, Yèyú, and Xī'ěrhé.
Xī'ěrhé
is also Yèyúhé.
Sū Shì said: Nánzhào has Xī'ěrhé,
which is Zāngkē Jiāng.
The river's shape is like a moon embracing an ear,
hence its name Xī'ěrhé.
Ěr
is pronounced Érzhǐ,
and also Érzhì.
He traveled over a thousand lǐ,
defeated more than thirty of their tribes,
and captured over twenty thousand men and women.
The various barbarians were greatly alarmed,
and sent envoys to surrender,
offering bright pearls an inch in diameter.
Thereupon, a stone tablet was erected to eulogize the virtues of Suí.
Wànsuì requested to bring Cuàn Wán to court,
and the Emperor granted permission.
Cuàn Wán secretly had second thoughts
and did not wish to proceed to the imperial court,
so he bribed Wànsuì with gold and jewels.
Wànsuì then let Wán go and returned.
This laid the groundwork for Shǐ Wànsuì's later disgrace.
Huán
is pronounced Cóngxuān,
and also as written.
2 On the day Gēngyín,
the Emperor went to Rénshòu Gōng.
3 Lǐ Guāngshì, the Lǐ chieftain of Guìzhōu, revolted.
Shǐ'ān Jùn,
Liáng established Guìzhōu.
Lǐ
is pronounced Lǐ.
Shuài
is pronounced Suǒlèi;
the same for Qúshuài below.
Fǎ Shàng dispatched troops from Lǐngnán,
and Shì Jī dispatched troops from Lǐngběi,
both converging at Yǐnzhōu.
The Suí Zhì states: Yùlín Jùn,
Liáng established Dìngzhōu,
later renamed Nándìngzhōu,
and after pacifying Chén, renamed Yǐnzhōu.
Unable to advance,
they halted at Héngzhōu.
The Suí Zhì states: Héngshān Jùn,
after pacifying Chén, Héngzhōu was established.
Guāngshì was defeated in battle,
and led his elite troops to flee and hold Bái shí Dòng.
Bái shí Dòng
is sixty lǐ south of present-day Xúnzhōu.
Shuài
is read as Shuài;
the same below.
Among his followers, there were those who came to surrender,
and their wives and children were immediately returned to them.
Within ten days,
several thousand people surrendered;
Guāngshì's forces disintegrated and fled,
and he was pursued and beheaded.
The Emperor also dispatched Yuánwài Sǎnqí Shìláng Hé Chóu to recruit soldiers to suppress Guāngshì.
Chóu persuaded Mò Chóng and other followers to surrender,
and, acting under imperial authority, appointed their leaders as officials of prefectures and counties.
Chóu
was the nephew of Tuǒ.
As the barbarians and Yuè people of Lǐngnán frequently rebelled,
the Emperor appointed Lìnghú Xī, Inspector of Biànzhōu, as Overall Commander of Seventeen Prefectures in Guìzhōu,
allowing him to act expediently,
and officials from Inspector downward could be appointed under his imperial authority.
Upon his arrival in the department, Xī
greatly extended benevolence and trust.
The chieftains of the streams and caves said to each other:
"Previously, all Overall Commanders threatened us with military might.
Now, this one persuades us with handwritten instructions;
how can we resist!"
Thereupon, they all submitted.
Previously, the prefectures and counties were rough and difficult to govern,
and most high officials could not hold their posts,
delegating governance to the Overall Commander's office.
Xī dispatched them all,
established cities and towns,
and opened schools.
Both Huá and Yi peoples were influenced and transformed.
The Lǐ chieftain
Níng Měnglì,
during the Chén era, had already occupied Nánhǎi.
The Suí then pacified him,
appointing him Inspector of Ānzhōu.
Měnglì, relying on the rugged terrain, was arrogant and proud,
never participating in court visits.
Xī persuaded him with benevolence and trust,
and Měnglì was moved,
came to the office for an audience,
and dared not commit wrongdoing.
Xī memorialized to change Ānzhōu to Qīnzhōu.
The Suí Zhì states: Níngyuè Jùn,
Liáng established Ānzhōu,
now renamed Qīnzhōu.
4 The Emperor believed that local subordinate officials did not respect or fear their superiors,
making it difficult to accomplish tasks.
In the third month,
on the day Rénchén,
an edict stated:
"For offenses committed by subordinate officials discussed by various departments,
if the law is lenient but the circumstances are serious,
it is permitted to mete out flogging beyond the standard legal provisions."
Thereupon, superiors and subordinates coerced each other,
alternately inflicting beatings and floggings,
considering cruelty and violence as capability,
and adherence to law as weakness.
The Emperor, seeing the proliferation of bandits,
decreed that all who stole even one *qián* should be executed in the marketplace.
Sometimes three people stealing a single melon,
if the matter was discovered, would immediately die.
Consequently, travelers would all rise late and retire early,
fearing that they might inadvertently commit a crime.
*Kǎo Yì* says: The *Xíngfǎ Zhì* writes
"晚宿" (retire late),
so the character *zǎo* (early) must be a mistake.
There were several men who seized an official and said to him:
"Are we seeking wealth?!
We have merely come for those who have been wronged.
Please memorialize the Supreme One for us: 'Since ancient times,
in structuring the state and establishing laws,
there has never been anyone who died for stealing one *qián*.
If you do not report this for us,
we will return,
and you and your kin will be exterminated!'"
The Emperor heard this,
and thus suspended this law.
Since ancient times,
there have been powerful and cunning individuals in villages and neighborhoods who exploited the weaknesses of officials,
but never
have we heard of anyone challenging their superiors to this extent.
No wonder there were so many bandits in the latter part of the Suí dynasty.
The wealth of the realm,
even the accumulation of one *qián*,
is why those who governed in ancient times
desired ease and accessibility for the people.
*Wéi* (為),
pronounced *yú wěi*.
The *ér* (而) in *ér wèi*, *ér bù*, and *ér shǔ*,
means "you."
The Emperor once, in a fit of rage,
wanted to execute someone by flogging in the sixth month.
Zhào Chuò of Hédōng, the Grand Judge Deputy, strenuously argued,
"According to the Suí system: each of the Nine Courts has one Minister and one Deputy Minister."
"Hédōng county,
the seat of Púzhōu's Hédōng commandery."
*Shǎo* (少),
pronounced *shǐ zhào*.
"In the month of midsummer,
heaven and earth nurture all living things;
one cannot execute people at this time."
The Emperor replied:
"Although the sixth month is a time of growth,
there are always thunder and lightning at this time;
I act in accordance with Heaven,
what is there that is not permissible!"
He then executed the person.
Lái Kuàng, an attendant of the Grand Judge, memorialized that the Grand Judge's office was too lenient.
"Attendant (掌固),
likely the same as the Han dynasty's *zhǎng gù*."
"The Tang dynasty's departments, bureaus, courts, and directorates all had attendants,
following the Suí system."
*Shàng* (上),
pronounced *shí zhǎng*.
He was ordered to attend the five-rank officials for consultation every morning.
*Qiǎn* (遣),
means "to send" or "to order."
*Háng* (行),
pronounced *hù gāng*.
*Jiàn* (見),
pronounced *xián biàn*.
The Emperor ordered a trusted minister to investigate,
and found no partiality or distortion.
The Emperor was enraged,
and ordered his execution.
Zhào Chuò strenuously argued,
believing Lái Kuàng should not die.
The Emperor brushed his robes and entered his private chambers.
Zhào Chuò falsely declared,
"I am no longer handling Lái Kuàng's case;
I have other matters
that I have not yet had time to memorialize."
The Emperor ordered him brought into the chambers.
Zhào Chuò bowed twice and requested:
"I have three death sentences upon myself:
as the Grand Judge Deputy,
I could not control my attendant,
causing Lái Kuàng to incur Heaven's punishment,
this is one.
The prisoner should not die,
but I could not argue to the death,
this is two.
I originally had no other matters,
but spoke falsely to gain entry,
this is three."
The Emperor's countenance softened.
Coincidentally, Empress Dúgū was present,
and ordered two golden cups of wine to be bestowed upon Zhào Chuò,
giving him the cups as well.
Lái Kuàng was thereby spared death,
and exiled to Guǎngzhōu.
Xiāo Móhē's son, Xiāo Shìlüè, rebelled in Jiāngnán.
Xiāo Móhē was to be implicated.
The Emperor said:
"Shìlüè is not yet twenty;
what can he accomplish?
As the son of a famous general,
he must have been coerced by others."
Consequently, he pardoned Xiāo Móhē.
Zhào Chuò firmly remonstrated against it.
The Emperor could not override him,
wishing Zhào Chuò to leave so he could pardon him,
and thus ordered Zhào Chuò to withdraw and eat.
Zhào Chuò said:
"My memorial on the case is not yet decided;
I dare not withdraw."
The Emperor said:
"The Grand Judge, please grant a special pardon to Xiāo Móhē for me!"
He then ordered his attendants to release him.
Xīn Dǎn, a Vice Minister of Punishments, once wore crimson trousers.
It was a popular belief that this was auspicious for official career;
the Emperor considered it a form of black magic,
and intended to execute him.
Zhào Chuò said:
"The law does not mandate death;
I dare not obey the edict."
The Emperor was extremely angry,
and said:
"You pity Xīn Dǎn and do not pity yourself!"
He ordered Zhào Chuò to be led away and executed.
Zhào Chuò said:
"Your Majesty may kill me,
but you cannot kill Xīn Dǎn."
When he reached the court hall,
he removed his robes, ready for execution.
The Emperor sent someone to ask Zhào Chuò:
"What will be the ultimate outcome?"
He replied:
"I uphold the law with a single heart;
I dare not fear death."
The Emperor brushed his robes and went inside.
After a long while,
he then released him.
The next day, he apologized to Zhào Chuò,
encouraged him,
and bestowed upon him three hundred bolts of silk.
At that time, the Emperor prohibited the circulation of counterfeit money.
There were two people in the marketplace
exchanging counterfeit money for good money.
A patrol officer arrested them and reported it.
"Patrol officers (武候),
belonged to the Left and Right Wǔhòu Generals,
responsible for day and night patrols, and arresting criminals."
Zhào Chuò came forward to remonstrate:
"The offense these people committed warrants flogging;
killing them is against the law."
The Emperor said:
"This does not concern you."
Zhào Chuò said:
"Your Majesty, not deeming me foolish and ignorant, placed me in the judiciary.
If you wish to kill people arbitrarily,
how can it not concern me!"
The Emperor said:
"Those who shake a large tree
and cannot move it should withdraw."
He replied:
"I hope to move the Heaven's heart;
what does moving a tree matter?"
The Emperor again said:
"One who sips soup and finds it hot sets it aside.
Does the Emperor's might
mean you wish to challenge me!"
Zhào Chuò bowed and stepped further forward,
rebuking him,
refusing to retreat.
The Emperor then went inside.
Liǔ Yù, the Investigating Censor, again submitted a strong remonstrance,
and the Emperor then stopped.
The Emperor, recognizing Zhào Chuò's sincere and upright heart,
would often bring him into his private chambers.
Sometimes, when the Emperor was seated with the Empress on the same couch,
he would immediately call Zhào Chuò to sit,
and discuss gains and losses.
He bestowed countless rewards upon him.
He served at the same time as Xuē Zhòu, the Grand Judge Minister,
and both were known for their fairness and magnanimity;
however, Xuē Zhòu judged cases based on circumstances while Zhào Chuò adhered to the law.
Both were considered competent.
Xuē Zhòu
was the son of Xuē Duān.
Xuē Duān served in the Zhōu dynasty,
as the Administrator of Càizhōu,
without other notable distinctions.
The Emperor's enforcement of the law became increasingly severe in his later years.
When a Censor failed to impeach a military official whose clothing and sword were not in order on New Year's Day,
the Emperor said,
"You are a Censor,
yet you act as you please."
He ordered the Censor's execution.
When Jiànyì Dàfū MáoSīzǔ remonstrated,
he too was executed.
The Suí dynasty's Ménxià Shěng established seven Jiànyì Dàfū.
The Wǔkù Lìng was punished for the wild growth in the court of the armory.
The Wǔkù Lìng
was subordinate to the Wèiwèi Sì.
Some were given horsewhips or parrots by their牧宰 (Mùzǎi) superiors.
When the Emperor discovered this,
he personally oversaw their execution.
The Emperor's moods were inconsistent,
and he no longer strictly adhered to the laws and statutes.
He placed his trust in Yáng Sù.
Yáng Sù, in turn, acted unjustly according to his whims.
He had a grudge against Hónglú Shàoqīng Chén Yán.
Once, when passing by a guesthouse for foreign envoys,
he saw horse droppings in the courtyard,
and several servants gambling with *chūpú* on a felt mat.
He reported this to the Emperor.
The Emperor was furious,
and ordered the Zhǔkè Lìng and all those gambling to be beaten to death.
Chén Yán was beaten almost to death.
The *Suí Zhì* states: The Hónglú Sì oversaw the Diǎnkè Lìng,
who was the Zhǔkè.
屎 (shǐ),
pronounced shì-ěr,
means excrement.
棰 (chuí),
pronounced zhǐ-ruǐ.
幾 (jī),
pronounced jū-yī,
also pronounced qí.
The Emperor dispatched Qīnwèi Dà Dūdū Qūtà Tōng of Cháng'ān to Lǒngxī to inspect the pastures.
The Suí dynasty established the Zuǒ Yòu Qīnwèi, Zuǒ Yòu Xūn Wèi, and Zuǒ Yòu Yì Wèi,
with officials such as Dà Dūdū, Shuài Dūdū, and Dūdū.
Emperor Yáng changed Dà Dūdū to Xiàowèi,
Shuài Dūdū to Lǚshuài,
and Dūdū to Duìzhèng.
Qūtú
is a barbarian compound surname.
Their ancestors were from Chānglí Tūhé,
and later moved their home to Cháng'ān.
Lǒngxī Commandery
is Wèizhōu.
屈 (qū),
pronounced jiǔ-wù.
The Emperor was enraged,
and intended to execute Tàipú Qīng Mùróng Xīdá and 1,500 other supervisory officials.
The Tàipú Qīng
was in charge of livestock administration, hence the desire to punish him.
"Human life is of the utmost importance.
How can Your Majesty kill over a thousand people
for the sake of livestock?
Your servant dares to beg with his life!"
The Emperor glared and shouted at him,
but Qūtú Tōng again kowtowed and said,
"Your servant's single life is forfeit,
in exchange for the lives of over a thousand people from Your Majesty."
The Emperor was moved and enlightened,
saying,
"My lack of discernment
has led to this!
It is fortunate to have your loyal words."
Thereupon, Xīdá and the others all had their sentences commuted from death,
and Qūtú Tōng was promoted to Zuǒ Wǔhòu Jiāngjūn.
The *Suí Zhì* states: The Zuǒ and Yòu Wǔhòu
were in charge of the imperial carriage's departure,
leading the vanguard and bringing up the rear,
patrolling day and night,
arresting criminals,
setting up signal fires along roads,
and positioning water and grass.
During imperial tours and field hunts,
they managed the camp's prohibitions.
5 Shàng Zhùguó
Liú Chǎng had a long-standing friendship with the Emperor,
who was very close to him.
His son, Jūshì,
was chivalrous and disregarded the law,
repeatedly committing crimes.
The Emperor, for Chǎng's sake,
always pardoned him.
Jūshì became increasingly arrogant and unrestrained.
He would select strong and valiant sons of high officials and noble families,
bring them to his house,
fasten their necks with a cartwheel and beat them.
Those who, almost to death, could not be subdued,
he called "brave warriors,"
released them, and befriended them.
His gang of three hundred followers
beat passersby
and committed many acts of robbery and extortion,
even against high officials and nobles,
none daring to challenge them.
Someone reported Jūshì for plotting rebellion.
The Emperor was enraged,
and had him executed.
A great many sons of high officials and nobles were dismissed from their posts due to their association with Jūshì.
6 Yáng Sù, Niú Hóng, and others again recommended Zhāng Zhòuxuán for his calendrical skills.
Last year, the Emperor had welcomed Zhòuxuán,
but later dismissed him.
復 (fù),
pronounced fú-yòu.
All these were old methods long difficult to understand.
He ordered Liú Huī and others to debate and analyze with Zhòuxuán and his group.
Liú Huī remained silent and offered no answers,
while Zhòuxuán solved fifty-four problems.
The Emperor then appointed Zhòuxuán Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng concurrently Tàishǐ Lìng,
bestowed upon him a thousand bolts of silk,
and ordered him to participate in finalizing the new calendar.
散 (sàn),
pronounced xī-dǎn.
騎 (qí),
pronounced qí-jì.
Zhòuxuán's calendar was completed.
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the *wùyín* day,
an imperial edict was issued to promulgate the new calendar.
The four previous calendar makers, including Liú Huī, were all dismissed from their posts.
7 In autumn, the seventh month,
Lǐ Shìxián from Guìzhōu rebelled.
The Emperor discussed suppressing him.
Several generals requested to go,
but the Emperor did not permit it.
He looked at Yòu Wǔhòu Dà Jiāngjūn Yú Qìngzé and said,
"You hold the position of prime minister,
and your noble rank is that of a grand duke.
At the beginning of Kaihuáng,
Qìngzé once served as Shàngshū Yòu Púyè,
a prime ministerial post.
He was granted Shàng Zhùguó,
and enfeoffed as the Duke of Lǔ,
a grand duke.
Yet you have no intention of going.
Why is that?"
Qìngzé bowed and apologized,
in fear.
Thereupon, Qìngzé was appointed Guìzhōu Dào Xíngjūn Zǒngguǎn,
and he suppressed the rebellion.
8 Qín Wáng Jùn,
was merciful and benevolent in his youth,
and fond of Buddhism.
He once requested to become a *śramaṇa*,
but was not permitted.
When he became Bìngzhōu Zǒngguǎn,
Jùn's appointment as Bìngzhōu Zǒngguǎn is mentioned in the previous volume, Year 10.
He violated regulations
by extensively building palaces.
Jùn was fond of women.
His consort, née Cuī,
was Hóngdù's younger sister.
She was jealous by nature,
and administered poison in a melon.
Due to this, Jùn fell ill
and was recalled to the capital.
The Emperor, seeing his extravagance and indulgence,
on the *dīnghài* day,
dismissed Jùn from his official post,
and ordered him to remain at his residence as a prince.
Cui, for poisoning the prince,
was deposed and exiled,
and ordered to commit suicide at home.
Liú Shēng, Zuǒ Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn,
The Cáo Wèi established the Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn.
From the Jìn to the Gāo Qí,
they were all subordinate to the Zuǒ and Yòu Wèi.
It was not until the Suí that they were on equal footing with the Zuǒ and Yòu Wèi within the Twelve Wèi Fǔ.
said, "Qín Wáng has no other fault
except for spending public funds
to build official residences.
Your servant believes he can be forgiven."
The Emperor said,
"The law cannot be violated."

"Qín Wáng's transgression
should not lead to such a severe punishment.
I beg Your Majesty to reconsider!"
The Emperor said,
"I am the father of five sons.

If it were as you suggest,
why not establish a separate law for the Emperor's children?
Even Zhōu Gōng, being who he was,
still executed Guǎn and Cài.
I am truly far inferior to Zhōu Gōng;
how can I undermine the law?"
He ultimately did not relent.
Yáng Sù was one who indulged the ruler's wickedness.
Later, he would support the decision to depose Yǒng and enthrone Guǎng,
having had insight into this matter.
卒 (zú),
pronounced zǐ-xù.

Tüli Kèhán of the Tujue came to receive the princess.

where she was taught the Six Rites.
The Six Rites were:
presenting betrothal gifts, inquiring the name, presenting a propitious divination, presenting the dowry, requesting the date of the wedding, and personal welcome of the bride.
The Emperor wished to sow discord between Tüli and Dūlán,
and so deliberately made the ceremonies very grand.
He dispatched Tàicháng Qīng Niú Hóng, Nàyán Sū Wēi, and Mínbù Shàngshū Húyù Xiàoqīng successively as envoys.
In the third year of Kāihuáng (583),
the Dùzhī Shàngshū was renamed Mínbù Shàngshū.
The character *shǐ* (使)
is pronounced *shūlì fān*.
Tüli originally lived in the north.
After marrying the princess,
Zhǎngsūn Shèng persuaded his chieftain to lead his people to migrate south,
to reside at the former stronghold of Dùjīn.
The former stronghold of Dùjīn
was probably Mount Dūjīn,
where Shābōlüè of the Tujue used to live.
The character *shuài* (帥)
is read *shuài*.
Dūlán angrily said:
"I am
the Great Kèhán!
Am I really inferior to Rǎngān?"
Thereupon, tribute payments ceased,
and they frequently came to raid the border regions.
Tüli, whenever he learned of their movements,
would immediately send a report,
and because of this, the border regions were always prepared in advance.
10 In the ninth month,
on the day *jiǎshēn*,
the Emperor arrived from Rénshòu Gōng.
11 When Hé Chóu returned from Lǐngnán,
in the second month of this year,
Hé Chóu had campaigned in Lǐngnán.
Chóu saw that his illness was critical,
and sent him back to Qīnzhōu,
making an agreement with him, saying:
"Between the eighth and ninth months,
you can come to the capital to meet me."
When the envoy returned
and presented the report,
the Emperor was displeased.
In winter,
the tenth month,
Měnglì died of illness.
The Emperor said to Chóu:
"You did not bring Měnglì earlier,
and now he has died!"
Chóu said:
"Měnglì made an agreement with your subject that
should he die,
he would send his son to serve.
The Yuè people are straightforward by nature,
so his son will surely come."
When Měnglì was dying,
he indeed instructed his son Zhǎngzhēn, saying:
"I made an agreement with the Great Envoy,
and it must not be broken.
After you have buried me,
you should immediately set out."
Zhǎngzhēn succeeded him as Cìshǐ,
and came to court as promised.
The Emperor was greatly pleased and said:
"Hé Chóu inspires such trust among the barbarians,
to this extent!"
12 When Lǔgōng Yú Qìngzé was campaigning against Lǐ Shìxián,
he appointed his wife's younger brother Zhào Shízhù as the Chángshǐ of his retinue.
Shízhù had an affair with Qìngzé's favorite concubine,
and fearing discovery,
he declared that Qìngzé did not want to undertake this expedition.
When the Emperor heard of it,
the rewards and gifts were very meager.
When Qìngzé returned,
he reached Línkuì Lǐng in Tánzhōu.
The *Suí Shū: Yú Qìngzé Zhuàn* writes
"Línkuì Lǐng in Tánzhōu."
Sòng Bái said: When Suí pacified Chén,
Xiāngzhōu was renamed Tánzhōu.
Dù Yòu said: It was named after Zhāotán.
He said:
"This is truly a dangerous and secure place,
moreover with ample provisions.
If a capable person is appointed to defend it,
it cannot be overcome by attack."
He sent Shízhù to rush to the capital to report,
and to observe the Emperor's countenance.
Shízhù then accused Qìngzé of treason,
and the case was handed to the authorities for investigation.
In the twelfth month,
on the day *rénzǐ*,
Qìngzé was executed,
and Shízhù was appointed Zhùguó.
13 Gāolì Wáng Tāng heard of the fall of Chén,
and was greatly frightened.
He organized troops and accumulated grain,
preparing a strategy for defense.
In this year,
the Emperor bestowed upon Tāng an imperial letter with a seal,
admonishing him that
"although you claim to be a vassal,
your loyalty and integrity are not fully demonstrated."
He further said:
"Although that region of yours
has limited land and few people,
if We now depose the King,
it cannot be left empty.
We will eventually have to select officials
to go there and pacify it.
If the King cleanses his heart and changes his ways,
acting according to the established laws,
then he is Our good minister;
why would We need to send other talented individuals?
King, how does the breadth of the Liáoshuǐ
compare to the Chángjiāng?
How many people of Gāolì
are there compared to the Chén state?
If We do not cherish and nourish,
and instead fault the King for his past transgressions,
We would only need to command one general;
why would We need many forces?
We earnestly admonish you,
permitting the King to renew himself."
When Tāng received the letter,
he was terrified
and was about to present a memorial expressing his gratitude and apology.
Coincidentally, he fell ill and died.
His son Yuán succeeded him.
The Emperor sent an envoy to appoint Yuán as Shàngkāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī
and inherited the peerage of Liáodōng Gōng.
The character *shǐ* (使)
is pronounced *shūlì fān*;
the same below.
He then requested to be enfeoffed as King,
and the Emperor permitted it.
From this time, Suí always had Gāolì in mind,
and later used its excellent army to destroy the kingdom.
14 Tǔyùhún was in great chaos.
The character *tǔ* (吐)
is pronounced *cóng tūn rùshēng*.
The character *gǔ* (谷)
is pronounced *yù*.
They installed his younger brother Fúyǔn as ruler,
and sent an envoy to report the matter of the deposition and installation,
and also to apologize for the crime of acting on their own authority,
and further requested to marry a princess according to their custom;
the Emperor agreed to it.
From then on, tribute arrived annually.
1 In spring,
the second month,
on the day *jiǎchén*,
the Emperor went to Rénshòu Gōng.
2 Gāolì Wáng Yuán led an army of over ten thousand Mòhé to raid Liáoxī.
The *Suí Shū* states: The Mòhé are north of Gāolì,
there are seven types in total: The first is called the Lìmò Department,
bordering Gāolì;
the second is called the Bódú Department,
north of the Lìmò;
the third is called the Ānchēgǔ Department,
northeast of the Bódú;
the fourth is called the Fúniè Department,
east of the Bódú;
the fifth is called the Hàoshì Department,
east of the Fúniè;
the sixth is called the Hēishuǐ Department,
northwest of the Ānchēgǔ;
the seventh is called the Báishān Department,
southeast of the Lìmò.
The Hēishuǐ Department was especially strong,
being the ancient Sùshèn clan.
The administrative seat of Liáoxī Commandery was Liǔchéng.
Suí established the Yíngzhōu Zǒngguǎnfǔ.
The character *mò* (靺)
is pronounced *mòbō fān*.
The character *hé* (鞨)
is pronounced *hùgè fān*.
When the Emperor heard this, he was greatly angered,
and on the day *yǐsì*,
appointed Hàn Wáng Liàng and Wáng Shìjī as commanders of the expeditionary force,
leading 300,000 troops by land and water to attack Gāolì.
Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè Gāo Jǐng was appointed Chángshǐ to Hàn Wáng,
and Zhōu Luóhóu was appointed Commander-in-Chief of the naval forces.
3 Yánzhōu Cìshǐ Dúgū Tuó
The Suí Shì records: Yán'ān Jùn,
was established as Dōngxià Zhōu by the Later Wèi dynasty.
The Western Wèi dynasty changed it to Yánzhōu.
Tuó,
pronounced like túhé.
He practiced cat-ghost sorcery,
and could make it kill people.
He said that each time it killed someone,
the wealth of the deceased's family would secretly transfer to the family that kept the cat-ghost.
It so happened that Empress Dúgū and Yáng Sù's wife, Zhèng Shì, both fell ill.
The doctors all said:
"It is a cat-ghost illness."
The Suí Shū biography of Tuó states: Xú Āní practiced cat-ghost sorcery.
She would sacrifice to it every midnight.
She said that "zǐ" [meaning midnight]
was a rat.
Tuó once asked for wine from his home.
His wife said:
"There's no money to buy it."
Tuó then said to Āní: "You can send the cat-ghost to Duke Yuè's house,
to get me enough money."
Āní then chanted a spell.
A few days later,
the cat-ghost went to Yáng Sù's house.
In the eleventh year,
the emperor had just returned from Bīngzhōu.
Tuó said to Āní:
"You can send the cat-ghost to the Empress,
so that she will bestow many things upon me."
Āní again chanted a spell,
and it then entered the palace.
Dàlǐ Chéng Yáng Yuǎn then, from outside the Mènxià, ordered Āní to summon the cat-ghost.
Āní then, in the middle of the night, placed a basin of fragrant porridge,
and tapping it with a spoon, called out:
"Cat-girl, please come,
do not stay in the palace."
After a long while,
Āní's face turned completely green,
as if being pulled.
She said the cat-ghost had arrived.
From this, the facts of the matter were fully ascertained.
Chù,
pronounced like xūyù;
the same below.
The Empress's half-brother,
Tuó's wife,
was Yáng Sù's half-sister.
Because of this, it was suspected that Tuó was responsible.
Gāo Jǐng and others were ordered to jointly investigate it,
and they fully uncovered the truth.
The emperor was enraged,
and ordered Tuó and his wife to be loaded into a calf-cart,
to be granted death.
Empress Dúgū did not eat for three days,
and pleaded for his life, saying:
"If Tuó were someone who corrupted the government and harmed the people,
I would not dare to speak;
but now, since it is because of my own person,
I dare to plead for his life."
Tuó's younger brother, Sīxūn Shìláng Zhěng, went to the palace gate to beg for mercy.
Sīxūn Shìláng was subordinate to the Lìbù Shàngshū.
Tuó was stripped of his official title and made a commoner,
and his wife, Yáng Shì, was made a nun.
Before this,
there was someone who sued, claiming his mother was killed by a cat-ghost.
The emperor considered it witchcraft and absurdity,
and angrily dismissed him.
By this time,
an edict was issued to execute the families accused of practicing cat-ghost sorcery.
Summer,
fourth month,
Xīnhài,
an edict stated:
"Families practicing cat-ghosts, gǔ-poison, yānmèi, or other illicit arts,
The Suí Shū Zhì records: In the southern regions, various prefectures often kept gǔ,
with Yíchūn being particularly prevalent.
The method involved gathering a hundred types of insects on the fifth day of the fifth month,
from large snakes
to small lice,
and placing them together in a vessel,
allowing them to devour each other.
The one remaining would be kept;
if it was a snake, it was called a snake-gǔ; if a louse, a louse-gǔ.
It was used to kill people,
entering the person's abdomen through food,
and consuming their vital organs.
When the victim died, their property would transfer to the gǔ master's family.
If no one else was killed for three years,
the keeper would suffer its ill effects themselves.
This was passed down through generations of descendants without interruption,
and sometimes even accompanied women upon marriage.
Yān,
pronounced like yūyǎn.
Mèi,
pronounced like mèi.
4 Sixth month,
Bǐngyín,
an imperial edict demoted Gāojùlí Wáng Yuán's official rank and titles.
Hàn Wáng Liàng's army marched out of Línyú Guān.
Línyú Guān,
was 480 lǐ west of Liǔchéng,
the so-called strategic pass of Lúlóng.
Yú,
pronounced like yù in the Hàn Shū.
Supplies and transport were interrupted,
the army lacked food,
and then encountered illness and plague.
Zhōu Luóhóu sailed from Dōnglái by sea towards Píngrǎng Chéng.
The Suí Shū records: Píngrǎng Chéng was six lǐ from east to west,
curving along the mountains,
with the Pèishuǐ river to its south.
Dù Yòu said: Píngrǎng Chéng was the old strategic city of the Cháoxiǎn kingdom.
Qù,
pronounced like qīyù.
Many ships were swept away and lost.
Autumn,
ninth month,
Jǐchǒu,
the army returned;
eight or nine tenths of the soldiers died.
Gāojùlí Wáng Yuán was also terrified and sent an envoy to apologize,
submitting a memorial stating
"Your subject Yuán, a piece of dung from Liáodōng."
The emperor then halted the military campaign,
treating him as before.
The King of Bǎijì, Chāng, sent an envoy with a memorial,
requesting to serve as a military guide.
The emperor issued an edict explaining that
"Gāojùlí has confessed its crimes,
and I have already pardoned it,
so it is not permissible to attack."
He handsomely rewarded the envoy and sent him back.
Gāojùlí was somewhat aware of this matter,
and invaded and plundered Bǎijì's borders with troops.
5 Xīnmǎo,
the emperor arrived back from Rénshòu Gōng.
6 Winter,
eleventh month,
Guǐwèi,

7 Twelfth month,
from the capital to Rénshòu Gōng,

8 The Southern Nánníng barbarians under Cuàn Wán rebelled again.
Shǔ Wáng Xiù reported
"Shǐ Wànsùi accepted bribes and released bandits,
leading to border troubles."
The emperor reprimanded Wànsùi.
Wànsùi slandered and falsely accused others;
the emperor was enraged,
and ordered his execution.
Gāo Jǐng and Zuǒwèi Dàjiàngjūn Yuán Mín and others strongly pleaded, saying:
"Wànsùi's heroic strategy surpasses others,
and soldiers are eager to serve him.
Even ancient famous generals
could not surpass him."
The emperor's anger slightly abated,
