1 Spring,
first month,
Guǐyǒu,
a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire.
2 Second month,
Jiǎyín,
the emperor visited Rénshòu Gōng.
Rénshòu Gōng was completed in the fifteenth year of Kāihuáng.
When it was completed,
Emperor Wén was angry and wanted to punish Yáng Sù.
Empress Dúgū was pleased and rewarded him.
Following this, the emperor frequently visited Rénshòu Gōng,
and at the end of his time in Rénshòu,
he eventually died in Rénshòu Gōng.
Benevolent ones have longevity;
the emperor exhausted the people's resources to build an detached palace.
Could this be called benevolence?
That he could not die in this palace
would have been appropriate.
The emperor was angry at Yáng Sù but did not punish him;
when the empress was pleased, he also became pleased.
Could it not be that extravagance can change people,
moving them upon encountering it,
to the point of indulging without knowing how to turn back,
and ultimately incurring the ridicule of ten thousand generations?
This shows that a ruler's virtue is valued in frugality.
3 The Tūjué Tūlì Kèhán, on account of Chángsūn Shèng's report that Dūlán Kèhán was preparing siege equipment,
intended to attack Dàtóngchéng.
The Suí Zhì states: "From Xiàzhōu, crossing the Wūshuǐ to the north,
traveling over five hundred and thirty lǐ,
passing Héngshuǐ,
and then traveling another one hundred and nineteen lǐ, one reaches Ānlèshù.
The garrison is on the western bank of the river;
on the eastern bank is old Dàtóngchéng.
The current Dàtóngchéng
is the old Yǒngjìzhà."
Jue (厥),
read as "jiù wù fān".
Ke (可),
from "kān rùshēng".
Hán (汗),
sound "hán".
Cháng (長),
read as "zhī liǎng fān".
Shèng (晟),
read as "chéng zhèng fān".
Gāo Gěng, the Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè, went out via the Shuòzhōu road.
The Suí Zhì states: "Mǎyìjùn
was formerly designated Shuòzhōu.
Língwǔjùn
was designated Língzhōu by the Later Wèi.
Both were to be under the command of the Hàn Wáng;
however, the Hàn Wáng never actually took the field."
Dūlán heard of this,
and allied with Dátóu Kèhán.
They combined their forces and launched a surprise attack on Tūlì.
A great battle ensued below the Great Wall,
and Tūlì suffered a crushing defeat.
Dūlán killed all of Tūlì's brothers, sons, and nephews,

The Suí Zhì states: "Língqiūxiàn of Yànménjùn
was designated Wèizhōu by the Later Zhōu."
Wèi (蔚),
read as "yú wù fān".
At night,
Tūlì and Chángsūn Shèng fled south with five horsemen.
By dawn,
having traveled over a hundred lǐ,
they had gathered several hundred horsemen.
Tūlì consulted with his subordinates, saying:
"Now that our army is defeated and we are submitting to the court,

How could the Son of Heaven of Dàsuí treat me with ceremony!
Although Diànjué has come,
there was originally no deep enmity;
Yuān (冤)
means 'resentment'.
He will surely spare and help us."
Shèng knew this,

When Tūlì saw four signal fires lit simultaneously,

Shèng deceived him, saying:
"The city is high and the terrain remote;

Our national law states that
if the enemy is few,
two signal fires are lit;
if many are coming,
three signal fires;
if they are pressing hard,
four signal fires.
They must see many enemies, and that they are close."
Tūlì was greatly alarmed,

we should surrender to the city."
Once they entered the garrison,

Jiāng (將),
as written.
In the fourth month,
on the Dīngyǒu day,

Piào (驃),
read as "pǐ miào fān".
Qí (騎),
read as "qí jì fān";
same below.
The Emperor ordered Tūlì to debate and question Dūlán's envoy, Yīntóu Tèlé.

Dūlán's younger brother, Yù
sùliù, abandoned his wife and children

Gāo Gěng dispatched Zhào Zhòngqīng, a Shàng Zhùguó, with three thousand soldiers as the vanguard.

The Tūjué then launched another major offensive.

Yáng Sù's army encountered Dátóu.
Previously, when generals fought the Tūjué,

they all combined battle chariots, infantry, and cavalry,

with the cavalry inside.
This was an ancient method;
even Wèi Qīng and Liú Yù could not change it,
which is to say, 'first make oneself invincible to await the enemy's vulnerability.'
Xiān (先),

Qí (騎),
read as "qí jì fān";
same below.
Yáng Sù said, "This is merely a way to secure oneself;

and was greatly pleased, saying:
"Heaven has granted this to me!"
He dismounted, bowed to heaven,
and led over a hundred thousand cavalry straight forward.
Zhōu Luóhóu, Shàng Yítóng Sānsī, said:

The Tūjué were utterly defeated,
Dátóu was severely wounded and fled,
and the number of dead and injured was immeasurable.
His followers cried out and departed.
Wèi Shū destroyed chariots and relied on infantry to defeat the Dí;
Yáng Sù abolished battle chariots and formed cavalry formations to defeat the Tūjué.
Both achieved victory by bravely advancing.
Shuài (帥),
read as "lǜ".
Shèng (勝),
sound "shēng".
Háo (號),
read as "hù gāo fān".

on the Dīngyǒu day,
Yùzhāngwáng Jiǎn was appointed Nèishǐ Lìng.
5 Wáng Shìjī, the Yíyáng Gōng, was appointed Liángzhōu Zǒngguǎn.

was designated Yíyángjùn by the Later Wèi.

6 Dúgū Hòu (獨孤后) was by nature jealous.
None in the imperial harem dared to approach the emperor.
A granddaughter of Yùchí Jǐng (尉遲迥),
possessed of great beauty,

The Emperor, at Rénshòu Gōng (仁壽宮), saw her and was pleased by her,

The Empress, watching for the Emperor to hold court,

The Emperor was greatly enraged by this,

Gāo Jǐng (高熲), Yáng Sù (楊素), and others pursued the Emperor

The Emperor sighed deeply and said:
"I am honored as the Son of Heaven,

Gāo Jǐng said:
"Your Majesty, how can you on account of one woman take the empire lightly!"
The Emperor's anger slightly abated.
He reined in his horse for a long time,
and only returned to the palace in the middle of the night.
The Empress awaited the Emperor inside her chambers.
Upon his arrival,

Jǐng (熲) and Sù (素) and others helped to reconcile them,

Previously, the Empress, considering Gāo Jǐng's (高熲) father to be a family retainer,

Jǐng's (熲) father, Bīn (賓),

When Xìn (信) was executed,

Hearing Jǐng (熲) refer to her as "one woman,"

At that time, Crown Prince Yǒng (勇) had lost the Emperor's affection.

Jǐng (熲) knelt and replied:

Dúgū Hòu (獨孤后) knew that Jǐng (熲) could not be swayed,

This laid the groundwork for the Empress to slander Jǐng (熲).

7. In the ninth month,

Hóng prioritized virtue and conduct over literary talent in his selections,

Although this caused delays,

Lìbù Shìláng Gāo Xiàojī had keen insight and quick discernment,

However, he was excessively spirited and bold,
and his conduct seemed frivolous,
which caused many high-ranking officials at the time to doubt him;
only Hóng deeply understood his true character
and trusted him wholeheartedly.
The Suí dynasty's selection of personnel was at its best during this time,
and contemporary opinion greatly admired Hóng's far-sighted discernment.

Another day,

4 Qín Xiàowáng Jùn (秦孝王俊) had been ill for a long time and could not get up.

The Emperor said to his envoy:

imbued with spirit and endowed with nature,
all know good and evil,
and all discern right from wrong.
If approached with utmost sincerity
and clearly guided and encouraged,
then customs will surely transform,
and people will all move towards goodness.
Previously, the realm was in chaos and disarray,
and moral education was abandoned.
Officials lacked compassion,
and the people harbored deceitful intentions.
I strive to follow the sagely laws
and transform the people with virtue.
And Gā deeply understood my intentions,
sincerely promoting and guiding.
The exiles were moved to realization,
and came to the judicial authorities of their own accord. This clearly shows that the people of this land
are not difficult to teach.
If all officials were like Wáng Gā,
and all common people were like Lǐ Cān and his group,
then punishment would be set aside and become unnecessary.
How far off would that be!"
Then he promoted Gā to be the Magistrate of Yōng.
Yōng County,
the seat of Qízhōu.
Yōng (雍)
is pronounced yú yòng fān.
9 Yuán Chōng, the Grand Astrologer, submitted a memorial stating:
"Since the rise of the Suí dynasty,
the daylight hours have gradually lengthened.
In the 1st year of Kāihuáng (581), the shadow length at winter solstice was one zhàng, two chǐ, seven cùn, and two fēn.
From then on, it gradually shortened.
By the 17th year (597),
it was shorter than the old measurement by three cùn and seven fēn.
When the sun is closest to the pole, the shadow is short and the day is long;
when it is farthest from the pole, the shadow is long and the day is short.
When it travels on the inner path, it is closest to the pole;
when it travels on the outer path, it is farthest from the pole.
Jí (極)
refers to the North Pole.
‘The xuánjī obtains its constant.’
Among the six wěi books,
there is the Chūnqiū Yuánmìng Bāo.
Kǒng Ānguó said: ‘Xuán (璇)
means beautiful jade.
Jī (璣) is an instrument for correcting astronomical observations.’
Xuán (璇)
is pronounced sì xuān fān.
‘The sun travels on the upper path;
during times of peace,
it travels on the middle path;
during times of tyranny,
it travels on the lower path.’
I humbly consider that the Suí dynasty, in commencing its rule,
was met with a response from the primeval force of Heaven.
The short shadow and long daylight
are phenomena rarely seen since antiquity."
The Shī says: "Zhèn gǔ rú zī (振古如茲)."
Máo Zhuàn says: "Zhèn (振)
means 'from'."
The Emperor said to his officials:
"This auspicious sign of longer daylight
is a blessing from Heaven.
Now that the Crown Prince has been newly established,
we should change the era name,
and take the meaning of 'long daylight' for the new era name."
Thereafter, all workers and laborers
had their tasks and quotas increased,
due to the longer daylight hours.
The artisans suffered greatly from this.
Historians say that Yuán Chōng falsely invoked Heaven to afflict the people.
Rénshòu 1st year
(Xīnyǒu, 601)
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the *yǐyǒu* day,
an amnesty was granted to all under Heaven,
and the era name was changed.
2 Yáng Sù, Shangshū Yòupúyè, was appointed Zuǒpúyè;
Sū Wēi, Nàyán, was appointed Yòupúyè.
3 On the *dīngyǒu* day,
Zhāo, Prince of Hénán, was moved and made Prince of Jìn.
4 Bùjiā Kèhán of the Tūjué tribe raided the frontier
and defeated Hán Hóng, Zǒngguǎn of Dàizhōu, at Héng'ān.
Yànmén Jùn
was the Suí Dàizhōu.
Jué,
read as "jiǔ wù fān".
Jiā,
read as "gǔ yá fān".
Kè,
from "kān" in entering tone.
Hán,
sound "hán".
Bài,
read as "bǔ mài fān".
Héng,
read as "hù dēng fān".
5 Zhāo, Prince of Jìn, was appointed Nèishǐlìng.
6 In the second month,
on the *yǐmǎo* day,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
7 In summer,
the fifth month,
on the *jǐchǒu* day,
ninety thousand Tūjué men and women came to surrender.
8 In the sixth month,
on the *yǐmǎo* day,
sixteen envoys were dispatched to inspect local customs.
9 On the *yǐchǒu* day,
an imperial edict stated that the students in schools throughout the empire were numerous but lacked refinement,
so only seventy students from Guózǐxué were to be retained;
Tàixué, Sìmen, and all prefectural and county schools were to be abolished.
The Hàn established Tàixué;
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn established Guózǐxué.
Later, Guózǐ and Tàixué each had *bóshì* to instruct students.
In the twentieth year of Tàihé of Hòuwèi,
schools were established at Sìmen,
and Sìmen Bóshì were appointed.
Since the Hàn dynasty,
commanderies had *wénxué*.
During the Suí, both commanderies and counties had *bóshì*.
Diànnèi Jiāngjūn
was Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn;
the Suí changed it to avoid a taboo name
and it belonged to the Zuǒ-Yòuwèi.
Héjiān Jùn
was Yíngzhōu.
Xuàn,
read as "yíng juàn fān".
Did not listen.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
Guózǐxué was renamed Tàixué.
10 Initially,
when the Emperor received the abdication from Zhōu,
fearing that the people's hearts were not yet subdued,
he often cited auspicious signs to impress them.
Those who fabricated and presented them
were countless.
In winter,
the eleventh month,
on the *jǐchǒu* day,
rites were performed at the southern suburb,
following the Fēngshàn ceremony,
and the inscribed text fully recounted the auspicious signs before and after to offer thanks.
11 The mountain láo rebelled.
Wèi Wénshēng of Luòyáng, Wèiwèi Shàogīng, was made Zīzhōu Cìshǐ.
Suízhi: Luòyáng Xiàn belonged to Hénán Jùn, Luòzhōu.
Zīyáng Jùn:
Xīwèi established Zīzhōu,
governed at Pánshí.
Shào,
read as "shǐ zhào fān".
Wénshēng's given name was Xuán,
but he was known by his courtesy name.
Upon arriving at his post,
the láo were attacking Dàláo Zhèn.
In the thirteenth year of Kāihuáng,
Dàláo Xiàn was established.
Sòng Bái said: Yíngzhōu Yìnglíng Xiàn
was originally Hàn Nán'ān Xiàn,
and the Suí established Dàláo Zhèn.
Jiǔyù Zhì: one hundred and fifty *lǐ* west of the prefecture.
He said:
“I am the Cìshǐ,
bearing the Son of Heaven's edict,
to care for you all.
Do not be alarmed or afraid!”
The láo dared not move.
Thereupon, he explained the advantages and disadvantages to them,
and their chieftains were moved and pleased.
They disbanded their troops and left.
More than one hundred thousand people submitted before and after.
The Emperor was greatly pleased
and bestowed two thousand bolts of silk.
On the *rénchén* day,
Wénshēng was made Suízhōu Zǒngguǎn.
Suízhi: Suíníng Jùn,
Hòuzhōu established Suízhōu.
12 The láo of Cháo, Chéng, and other five prefectures rebelled.
Féng Àng, chieftain of Gāozhōu, galloped to the capital
to request permission to suppress them.
Suízhi: Yì'ān Jùn,
Liáng established Dōngyángzhōu,
later changed to Yíngzhōu,
Cháozhōu was established after conquering Chén.
Cāngwú Jùn,
Liáng established Chéngzhōu,
the Suí later changed it to Fēngzhōu.
Gāoliáng Jùn,
Gāozhōu was established.
Qiú,
read as "cái yóu fān".
Zhǎng,
read as "zhī liǎng fān".
Sù sighed, saying:
“I did not expect there to be such a person among the barbarians!”
He immediately sent Àng to raise troops from Jiāng-Lǐng to attack them.
Jiāng-Lǐng
refers to Jiāngnán and Lǐngnán.
Àng was appointed Hànyáng Tàishǒu.
Suízhi: Hànyáng Jùn,
Hòuwèi called it Nánqínzhōu,
Xīwèi called it Chéngzhōu.
Shǒu,
read as "shǒu yòu fān".
13 An imperial edict appointed Yáng Sù as the Xíngjūn Yuánshuài of the Yúnzhōu Route,
Suízhi: Dìngxiāng Jùn,
in the fifth year of Kāihuáng, Yúnzhōu Zǒngguǎnfǔ was established,
governed at Dàlì.
He was to assist Qǐmín Kèhán in attacking Bùjiā to the north.
1 In spring,
the third month,
on the *jǐhài* day,
the Emperor visited Rénshòu Gōng.
2 Tūjué Sīlì Shìjīn and others
crossed the river to the south,
plundered six thousand Qǐmín men and women and over two hundred thousand livestock, and departed.
Yáng Sù led his armies in pursuit and attack,
fighting continuously for over sixty *lǐ*,
and utterly routed them.
The Tūjué fled north.
Sù advanced further in pursuit,
and at night,
caught up with them.
Fearing they might escape,
he ordered his cavalry to fall back slightly.
He personally led two riders and two surrendered Tūjué soldiers to travel alongside the enemy,
who did not notice them.
When the enemy had not yet settled into their camp,
he quickly ordered the rear cavalry to attack them by surprise,
utterly defeating them,
and recovered all the people and livestock to return to Qǐmín.
From then on, the Tūjué fled far away,
and there were no more raids south of the desert.
Qì,
read as "qī jì fān".
Chāo,
read as "chǔ jiāo fān".
Xuánzòng was granted the title Huáinán Gōng.
Huáinán Jùn Gōng.
3 Bīngbù Shàngshū Liǔ Shù
was the grandson of Qìng.
(For Liǔ Qìng, see volume 161, Liáng Wǔdì, Tàiqīng 2nd year.)
Relying on imperial favor, he became arrogant,
and even Yáng Sù and his ilk deferred to him.
The Emperor asked Fúxǐ Zhícháng Wànnián Wéi Yúnqǐ:
(The Fúxǐ Bureau
belonged to the Ménxià Shěng.
There were four Zhícháng.
Wànnián
belonged to Jīngzhào.)
(The character "xǐ" [璽]
is pronounced 'sī'.)
(The character "zhǎng" [長]
is pronounced 'zhī liǎng'.)
"If there are any inconvenient matters outside,
you may speak of them."
Shù was attending at the side at the time,
and Yúnqǐ reported:
"Liǔ Shù is arrogant and domineering,
having never experienced hardship.
Military matters are critical and important,
which he is not capable of handling.
Merely because he is the imperial son-in-law,
he occupies a crucial position.
I fear that public opinion will cause Your Majesty to be seen as 'not selecting the virtuous for office,
but rather favoring one's personal beloved,'
and this is indeed a great inconvenience."
The Emperor greatly approved of his words
and turned to Shù, saying:
"Yúnqǐ's words
are like medicine and stone for you;
you should treat him as a teacher and friend."
In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the day Bǐngxū,
an imperial edict ordered all officials, internal and external, to recommend those they knew to be capable.
Liǔ Shù recommended Yúnqǐ,
who was appointed Tōngshì Shèrén.
(In Cáo Wèi, the Zhōngshū [Chancellery] established one Tōngshì,
responsible for presenting memorials and documents.
During the Zhèngshǐ period,
it was changed to Tōngshì Shèrén
and belonged to the Zhōngshū Shěng.
The Suí changed the Zhōngshū Shěng to Nèishǐ Shěng.)
4 Yìzhōu Zǒngguǎn, Shǔ Wáng Xiù,
had a magnificent and imposing appearance,
possessed courage,
and was fond of martial arts.
The Emperor often said to Dúgū Hòu:
"Xiù will surely come to a bad end.
While I am alive, there is nothing to worry about,
but when it comes to his brothers,
he will certainly rebel."
When Dà Jiāngjūn Liú Kuài was campaigning against the Xīcuàn,
the Emperor ordered Shàng Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī Yáng Wǔtōng to lead troops as reinforcements.
(This must have been when the Cuàn Wán rebelled again.)
(The character "jiāng" [將]
is pronounced 'jí liàng'.)
The Emperor considered Xiù to be unsuitable for his post,
reprimanded him,
and then said to his assembled ministers:
"Those who will ruin my laws
are my descendants.
It's like a fierce tiger,
which cannot be harmed by other creatures,
but is instead damaged and eaten by insects within its own fur."
Consequently, he divided Xiù's command.
(After Chángshǐ Yuán Yán died,
Xiù gradually became extravagant and presumptuous.
According to the biography of Yuán Yán in the Suí Shū: Yuán Yán died in Kaihuang 13th year.
This was later, in Rénshòu 4th year,
when the Emperor was ill in Rénshòu Gōng,
and there was also Huángmén Shìláng Yuán Yán, who attended the sick Emperor along with Yáng Sù and Liǔ Shù.
This is also true in the biographies of the deposed Crown Prince Yǒng and Liǔ Shù.
If so,
there were two Yuán Yán.)
(The character "cháng" [長]
is pronounced 'zhī liǎng'.)
He captured many mountain tribesmen (Láo) to serve as eunuchs,
and his carriages, horses, and clothing
mimicked those of the imperial entourage.
When Crown Prince Yǒng was deposed due to slander,
and Jìn Wáng Guǎng became Crown Prince,
Xiù was very displeased.
The Crown Prince feared that Xiù would eventually become a future problem,
so he secretly instructed Yáng Sù to find fault with him and slander him.
The Emperor then summoned Xiù,
but Xiù hesitated,
wanting to feign illness and not go.
Zǒngguǎn Sīmǎ Yuán Shī remonstrated.
(Yuán Shī
was the son of Yuán Wénzōng of Northern Qí,
and was probably old at this time.)
"This is my family's affair,
what concern is it of yours!"
Shī replied, shedding tears:
"I, Shī, have the honor of serving in the府幕,
how dare I not be utterly loyal!
The Holy Emperor has issued an edict summoning the King,
but time has passed,
should be "yǐ" [已] according to the biography of Yuán Shī in the Suí Shū.
The Shǔ edition reads "jǐ" [己].)
The common people do not know the King's intentions,
and may perhaps give rise to dissenting opinions.
If there is doubt and alarm internally and externally,
and a thunderous edict is issued,
sending a single envoy,
how will the King clear himself?
I beg the King to consider this carefully!"
The imperial court feared that Xiù might cause trouble.
On the day Wùzǐ,
Yuánzhōu Zǒngguǎn Dúgū Kǎi was appointed Yìzhōu Zǒngguǎn.
(Píngliáng prefecture,
where Yuánzhōu was established.)
When Kǎi arrived,
Xiù still refused to depart;
Kǎi persuaded him for a long time,
and then he set out.
Kǎi observed that Xiù showed signs of regret,
so he deployed his troops as a precaution;
Xiù traveled more than forty *lǐ*,
intending to return and attack Kǎi,
but his scouts learned that preparations had been made,
so he stopped.
5 In the eighth month,
on the day Jiǎzǐ,
Empress Dúgū Shì passed away.
The Crown Prince, in the presence of the Emperor and palace attendants, grieved so intensely that he fainted,
as if unable to bear the loss;
but when in his private chambers,
he ate, drank, spoke, and laughed as usual.
Moreover,
each morning he ordered two *yì* of rice to be brought,
but secretly ordered fatty meat, dried meat (pú), and pickled fish/meat (zhǎ) to be brought.
(Dried meat is *pú*;
fermented fish/meat is *zhǎ*.)
He sealed the containers with wax,
wrapped them in cloth bundles, and brought them in.
Zùozuò Láng Wáng Shào submitted a memorial, saying:
"The Buddha says: 'When a person is about to be born in heaven or in the Land of Amitābha,
the heavenly Buddhas emit great brilliant light,
and come to greet them with fragrant flowers, dancers, and music.'
I humbly believe that the late Empress's blessings, virtues, and auspicious signs
are recorded in various secret texts,
all stating that she is Miàoshàn Púsà.
(In Buddhist scriptures: *pú* [菩]
means 'universal';
*sà* [薩]
means 'to save'.
*Púsà* [菩薩]
means one who can universally save sentient beings.
*Pú* [菩]
is pronounced 'bó hū'.
*Sà* [薩]
is pronounced 'sāng gé'.)
In Rénshòu Gōng, golden and silver flowers rained twice;
on the twenty-third day, at night behind the Dàbǎo Diàn, there was divine light;
(Dàbǎo Diàn
was the sleeping palace within Rénshòu Gōng.)
North of Yǒng'ān Gōng, various natural musical sounds
filled the empty sky;
until the fifth watch of the night,
suddenly, as if asleep,
she ascended to the heavens.
These events all align and correspond
with what is described in the Buddhist scriptures."
The Emperor viewed this with both sorrow and joy.
6 In the ninth month,
on the day Bǐngxū,
the Emperor returned from Rénshòu Gōng.
7 In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the day Guǐchǒu,
Gōngbù Shàngshū Yáng Dá was appointed Nàyán.
(Dá
was Xiúng's younger brother.
Xiúng was originally designated as Guǎngpíng Wáng, then redesignated as Qīngzhāng,
and at this time was again redesignated as Āndé.)
8 In the intercalary month,
on the day Jiǎshēn,
an imperial edict ordered Yáng Sù, Sū Wēi, and Lìbù Shàngshū Niú Hóng, among others, to revise and establish the Wǔlǐ.
(The Wǔlǐ
are rites of auspiciousness, misfortune, military, guests, and festivity.)
9 The Emperor ordered the Senior Ceremonial Official of the Third Rank, Xiāo Jí, to select a burial site for the Empress.
He found an auspicious location,
saying:
"It divines two thousand years for the reign,
and two hundred generations for the lineage."
The Emperor said:
"Auspiciousness and inauspiciousness come from people,
not from the land.
When Gāo Wěi buried his father,
did he not perform divination?
Soon after, his state perished.
Just like my family's ancestral graveyard,
if it were said to be inauspicious,
I would not be the Son of Heaven;
if it were said to be not inauspicious,
my brother would not have died in battle."
The Emperor's brother, Zhěng, followed Emperor Wǔ of Zhōu to attack Qí,
and reached Bìngzhōu,
where he died fighting bravely.
Xiāo Jí withdrew,
and told his clansman Xiāo Píngzhòng:
"The Crown Prince sent the Left Commander Yǔwén Shēn to thank me deeply, saying:
(Yǔwén Shù was then the Left Guard Commander.)
(Shuài,
pronounced suǒ lǜ.)
'It truly had its verification,
I will never forget it.
Now that the imperial tomb is being divined,
make sure I am established early.
After I am established,
I will repay you with wealth and honor.'
I told him, 'In four years,
the Crown Prince will rule the world.'
If the Crown Prince gains power,
will Suí then perish?
What I previously deluded him with, saying
'It divines two thousand years for the reign,'
was a thirty-character statement;
'It divines two hundred generations for the lineage,'
meant taking two transmissions of generations.
You should remember this!"
On the day Rén Yín,
Empress Wénxiàn was buried at Tàilíng.
An edict stated:
"Yáng Sù managed the burial affairs,
diligently seeking an auspicious location.
Considering Yáng Sù's intent in this matter,
his actions demonstrated extreme sincerity and filial piety.
How can this be compared
to his achievements in pacifying barbarians and quelling bandits?
He may be separately enfeoffed with one son as the Duke of Yìkāng,
with a ten-thousand-household邑.
(Yìkāng County Duke.)
The Suí Zhì states: Duýuán County of Gāoliáng Commandery originally had Sòngkāng Commandery.
After conquering Chén, it was renamed Yìkāng Commandery.
Ten thousand bolts of silk,
ten thousand shi of rice,
and gold, pearls, damask, and brocade to match."
10 The Prince of Shǔ, Yáng Xiù, arrived in Cháng'ān.
The Emperor saw him,
but did not speak to him.
The next day, he sent an envoy to severely admonish him.
Yáng Xiù confessed his crimes,
and the Crown Prince and other princes wept as they offered apologies in the courtyard.
The Emperor said:
"Previously, the Prince of Qín squandered wealth and goods,
and I disciplined him with the way of a father.
Now Yáng Xiù harms the common people,
and I must restrain him with the way of a ruler."
Thereupon, he handed him over to the enforcers of the law.
Qìng Zhěng, Grand Master of the Palace with Expanded Authority, remonstrated:
(Qìng is a surname,
originating from the Qìng clan, a grandee of Qí.)
"The commoner Yǒng has already been deposed,
and the Prince of Qín has already died.
Your Majesty does not have many sons remaining;
why go to such an extent?
The Prince of Shǔ has a very forthright and unyielding nature;
now that he is being severely punished,
I fear he may not preserve himself."
The Emperor was greatly enraged,
wanting to cut out his tongue.
He then said to his close ministers:
"Yáng Xiù must be executed in the marketplace to apologize to the people."
He then ordered Yáng Sù and others to investigate and prosecute him.
The Crown Prince secretly made effigies,
with hands tied and hearts nailed,
wearing cangues, chains, and manacles.
He wrote the names of the Emperor and the Prince of Hàn,
and further said:
"Please, the Benevolent Father and Holy Mother of the Western Peak,
take the souls of Yáng Jiān and Yáng Liàng,
in this form,
and do not let them dissipate."
He secretly buried them beneath Mount Huà.
Yáng Sù unearthed them.
He also claimed:
"Yáng Xiù falsely propagated prophecies,
proclaiming strange omens in the capital,
and fabricating auspicious signs in Shǔ."
He also created a proclamation,
saying
"designating a date to inquire about crimes,"
and placed it within Yáng Xiù's collected works.
(Jí refers to collected literary works.)
The Suí Zhì states: Separate collections were
probably first created in the Eastern Capital of Hàn.
Since Língqū,
there have been many writers,
but their aspirations differed,
and their styles varied.
Later gentlemen,
wishing to observe their forms and perceive their inner spirits,
therefore gathered them separately,
naming them "collections."
Literati admired and
recorded them themselves,
thus forming a category of books.
The Emperor said:
"How can such a thing exist in the world!"
In the twelfth month,
on the day Guǐ Sì,
Yáng Xiù was deposed as a commoner,
confined to the Inner Palace Directorate,
and not allowed to see his wife and children.
Only two aboriginal maids served him.
Over a hundred people were implicated.
Yáng Xiù submitted a memorial of confession and apology, saying:
"I humbly wish for Your Majesty's merciful grace,
to bestow pity and compassion.
While my lingering breath has not yet ceased,
I hope to see my young children.
Please grant me a single burial plot,
so that my bones may have a resting place."
(Guāzǐ refers to his beloved children.)
The Emperor then issued an edict enumerating his ten crimes,
and further said:
"I don't know what relation Yáng Jiān and Yáng Liàng are to you?"
Later, he was allowed to live with his son.
Previously,
Yáng Sù had once been mildly rebuked and sent to Nántái.
(Nántái refers to the Censorate.)
After the state was established and faced the market,
all bureaus and ministries were in the south,
hence the Department of State Affairs was called Nánshěng,
and the Censorate was called Nántái.
(Shǎo,
pronounced shī zhǎo.)
Yáng Sù, relying on his noble status,
sat on Yù's bed.
Yù came in from outside,
and from the steps below, holding his tablet solemnly and adjusting his demeanor, said to Yáng Sù:
"I have received an imperial edict to deal with your crime!"
Yáng Sù hastily descended.
Yù sat at the desk,
made Yáng Sù stand in the courtyard,
and debated and questioned him about the facts of the case.
Yáng Sù harbored resentment because of this.
The Prince of Shǔ, Yáng Xiù, once asked Yù for Lǐ Wénbó's collected works on governance.
(Lǐ Wénbó,
a native of Bólíng,
served in Suí but was not appointed.
His nature was pure, upright, and unyielding;
he loved learning tirelessly.
As for doctrines, principles of names, and reason,
he paid special attention;
when reading about the success and failure of governance,
and loyal ministers and valiant scholars,
he never failed to ponder and recite repeatedly.
He was skilled in argumentation
and also good at writing,
having authored ten volumes of Zhìdào Jí,
which were widely circulated in the world.
Why was his writing widely circulated but he was not recognized in his career?
(Zhì,
pronounced zhí lì.))
Yáng Xiù sent Yù ten male and female slaves.
When Yáng Xiù fell into disfavor,
Yáng Sù reported Yù for internal officials associating with feudal lords,
stripped him of his rank and made him a commoner,
and assigned him to garrison duty at Huáiyuǎn Town.
(The New Táng Zhì states that
Yíngzhōu had Huáiyuǎn City.)
The Emperor sent Minister of Agriculture Zhào Zhòngqīng to Yìzhōu to thoroughly investigate Yáng Xiù's case.
Wherever Yáng Xiù's retainers had passed through,
Zhào Zhòngqīng would apply severe laws,
leading to more than half of the commandery and county chief officials being implicated.

Péi Sù

Even if
(Shū Lì fān.)
the emperor

When the memorial was presented,

Lì Dīng fān.)
The emperor above then conveyed the meaning that Yǒng could not be reinstated and dismissed him.
Sù
was Xiá’s son.

(Fú Yòu fān.)
Yáng Sù’s younger brother Yuē, his paternal cousins Wénsī and Wénjì,

His various sons, without any effort in battle,

They extensively managed their assets;
from the capital and various metropolitan areas,

There were thousands of household servants,

The only ones who dared to resist Sù without yielding

Initially, Pí served as the Cìshǐ of Xīníngzhōu.

Pí’s appointment as Cìshǐ of Xīníng

The chieftains of the barbarians all considered those with much gold to be heroic and outstanding,

Pí was troubled by this.

He accepted nothing.

The emperor heard of this and praised him,

Pí saw Yáng Sù monopolizing power,

Zhī Yù fān.)

Zǐ Xù fān.)

When the memorial was presented,

Yáng Yuē was sent out as Cìshǐ of Yīzhōu.

The Crown Prince asked Hèruò Bì:

Bì replied:

The Crown Prince said:

Bì bowed and said:

Bì's intention was to commend himself.
The Lǐ chieftain Lǐ Fózǐ of Jiāozhōu rebelled.
Jiāozhǐ Commandery,
Jiāozhōu.

Jiāozhōu,

Róng was severe and cruel by nature,

If someone pleaded innocent,

Subsequently, if someone committed an offense,

Yuán Hóngsì, the Chief Clerk of Guānzhōu,

Guān,

feared being humiliated by Róng,

He asked about stopping resentment.

"In a country without amnesties,

We request to posthumously name him Wénzhōngzǐ."

On the day Dīngwèi,

He was sixty-four years old.
Gāozǔ was naturally grave and serious,
his commands were enforced and prohibitions observed.
Every
morning he held court,
forgetting fatigue until evening.
Though frugal with wealth,
when it came to rewarding the meritorious,
he spared nothing;
if generals and soldiers died in battle,
he would certainly bestow generous rewards,
and moreover dispatched envoys to visit and console their families.
He cared for and nourished the common people,
encouraged farming and sericulture,
lightened corvée and reduced taxes.
In his personal upkeep,
he always practiced frugality and simplicity.
His imperial carriage and personal items,
if old and worn, were patched up and reused as appropriate;
except for banquets,
his meals never exceeded one meat dish;
the ladies of the rear palace all wore washed and mended clothes.
The entire empire was transformed by him.
During the Kāihuáng and Rénshòu eras,
men generally wore silk or hemp cloth,
not damask or brocade;
their belts and ornaments were merely of copper, iron, bone, or horn,
without gold or jade decorations.
Thus, food and clothing prospered,
and granaries overflowed.
At the beginning of his ascension to the throne,

In his later years,

This is comparing the number of households in the first year of Kāihuáng
with the number at the end of Rénshòu and the beginning of Dàyè.

Línyì (林邑) was at the mouth of the sea.
6 Second month,
on the day of wùchén (戊辰),
an imperial edict commanded officials to display great amounts of gold, treasures, utensils, brocades, carriages, and horses.
Yáng Sù (楊素) and the various generals who had rendered meritorious service in subduing Hànwáng Liàng (漢王諒) were made to stand in front.
Qízhānggōng Niú Hóng (奇章公牛弘) was ordered to proclaim the imperial edict,
extolling their achievements.
The Suízhì (隋志) states: Bázhōu (巴州) had Qízhāng (其章) county,
established by Liáng (梁).
Also Fúyáng (符陽) county,
which previously had Qízhāngjùn (其章郡).
"Qí" (其)
is sometimes written as
Niú Hóng's (牛弘) biography states: He was enfeoffed as Qízhāngjùn Gōng (奇章郡公).
Accumulated merits are called fá (伐).
The Zuǒzhuàn (左傳) states: Dàfū (大夫) speak of fá (伐).
The Hàngjì (漢紀) states: "Unless there are merits or fá (伐)."
Yáng Sù (楊素) and others bowed twice and danced before departing.
On the day of jǐmǎo (己卯),
Yáng Sù (楊素) was appointed Shàngshūlìng (尚書令).
The Táng Liùdiǎn (唐六典) states: Qín (秦) changed the Zhōu (周) system,
all affairs of the empire
were decided by the Prime Minister's office.
The Shàngshū (尚書) were placed within the imperial palace,
with a Lìng (令) and Chéng (丞),
whose duty was merely to transmit memorials.
The early Hàn (漢) followed this.
After Emperors Wǔ (武) and Xuān (宣),
more responsibilities were gradually entrusted to them.
When Emperor Guāngwǔ (光武) personally took charge of official duties,
all imperial affairs were submitted to the Shàngshū (尚書),
who jointly decided with the ruler,
and then passed down to the three supreme ministries.
The Shàngshūlìng (尚書令) became a chief minister.
Since Wèi (魏) and Jìn (晉),
their responsibility became even heavier.
7 An imperial edict ordered a general public mourning,
but the emperor himself wore a light yellow shirt and an iron-mounted belt.
8 In the third month,
on the dìngwèi day,
an imperial edict commanded Yáng Sù, together with Nàyán Yáng Dá and Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng Yǔwén Kǎi, to supervise the construction of the Eastern Capital.
After the Northern Zhōu and Northern Qí were unified,
Luòyáng was designated as the Eastern Capital.
Tens of thousands of households of residents from within Luòzhōu’s city walls and wealthy merchants and great traders from various prefectures were relocated to populate it.
The Èrxiáo Road was abolished,
and the Zōngcè Road was opened.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states: Jìn repelled the Qín army at Xiáo.
There are two hills at Xiáo:
the southern hill
is the tomb of Xià Hòu Gāo;
the northern hill
is where Wén Wáng sought shelter from wind and rain.
Lì Dàoyuán said: This means the mountain paths are deep and winding,
with peaks and mounds casting shadows,
hence it can provide shelter from wind and rain.
The Shuǐ Jīng mentions the mountains of Pánxiáo, Shíxiáo, and Qiānxiáo.
The mountain of Pánxiáo
is the source of the Xiáo River.
The mountain of Shíxiáo
is the source of the Shíxiáo River.
The so-called “two hills at Xiáo”
refer to the mountain of Shíxiáo.
The mountain of Qiānxiáo
is the source of the Qiānxiáo River,
which flows north into the Chán and Luò rivers.
In the Jiàn’ān period of the Hàn dynasty,
Cáo Gōng campaigned westwards,
disliking the treacherous southern route,
and instead opened a northern route,
which most travelers followed thereafter.
Attached to the mountain side of the road,
there is a stone inscription that reads:
“In the third year of Tàikāng of Jìn,
Hóngnóng Tàishǒu Liáng Liǔ repaired the old road.”
East of Tàixiáo and
west of Dōng Xiáo and Xī Xiáo,
it is clear that there was not just one Xiáo.
The Wèi Shū: Dìxíng Zhì states that
Hèngnóng Jùn had Xiáo Xiàn,
established in the eleventh year of Tàihé,
and the county contained the Sānxiáo Mountain.
The Zhì also mentions Xī Hèngnóng Jùn,
whose seat was in Hèngnóng Xiàn,
and which contained Táolín.
The Suí Zhì states: Hénán Jùn’s Táolín Xiàn
was established in the sixteenth year of Kāihuáng,
and contained the Shàngyáng Gōng.
Shǎn Xiàn:
The Later Wèi established Shǎn Zhōu, Hèngnóng Jùn;
the Later Zhōu again established Xiáo Jùn;
in early Kāihuáng,
the commandery was abolished;
in early Dàyè,
the prefecture was abolished,
and Hèngnóng Gōng was established.
Also, Xióng’ěr Xiàn,
established by the Later Zhōu,
contained the Later Wèi’s Xiáo Xiàn;
it was abolished in early Dàyè,
and contained Èrxiáo and Xiáshí Shān.
The Xīn Táng Zhì states: Shǎn Zhōu’s Xiáshí Xiàn,
originally Xiáo,
was moved to Xiáshí Wù,
and contained the Xiùlǐng Gōng.
Língbǎo Xiàn
was originally Táolín;
the ancient Hángǔ Guān was west of the county;
it contained the Táoyuán Gōng.
Luòzhōu’s Yǒngníng Xiàn
was originally Xióng’ěr;
five lǐ to its west was Qíxiù Gōng;
thirty-three lǐ to its south was Lánfēng Gōng.
These were all detached palaces along the route between the Eastern and Western Capitals,
variously established during the Suí and Táng dynasties.
The so-called Zōngcè Road is not recorded,
so it is unknown where this road began
and where it ended.
The Shānhǎi Jīng states: Kuāfù Shān,
nine lǐ west of Hú Xiàn,
has many zōngnán trees;
its northern part is called Táolín.
Perhaps
the character for "zōngnán"
was later corrupted to
"zōngcè",
thus becoming Zōngcè Road?
Without evidence, this cannot be believed,
and further extensive research is needed.
Dù Yòu said: In the seventh year of Dàyè of Suí,
the Tóngguān Road was moved between the northern and southern fortress cities,
and a [AS-FBEF]土[AS-FBED]([AS-FEF4] [AS-FBEC]舟)[AS-FBF0] shòujiàn valley was established,
over four lǐ from the old pass.
Jiǎ
is pronounced gǔ.
[AS-FBEF]土[AS-FBED]([AS-FEF4] [AS-FBEC]舟)[AS-FBF0] has a missing pronunciation.
Zōng
is pronounced zǐ hóng fān.
(Note:
"[AS-FBEF]土[AS-FBED]([AS-FEF4] [AS-FBEC]舟)[AS-FBF0]"
in the modern edition of Dù Yòu’s Tōng Diǎn is written as
"kēng".)
9 On the wùshēn day,
an imperial edict stated:
"Listening to public praise and consulting with the common people
enables one to judge the successes and failures of governance;
now I will tour Huái and Hǎi,
to observe the customs."
112 An imperial command ordered Yǔwén Kǎi and Nèishǐ Shèrén Fēng Déyí and others to construct Xiǎnrén Gōng,
bordering Zàojiàn to the south
and spanning Luòbīn to the north.
The Suí Zhì states: Hénán Jùn’s Shòu’ān Xiàn has Xiǎnrén Gōng.
Shuǐ Jīng Zhù: The Luò River flows past the south of the old city of Yíyáng Xiàn,
then eastwards to merge with the Hēijiàn River,
which originates from the western mountains of Lùhún,
passes through the northwest of Hēijiàn, and enters the Luò.
Zào
is pronounced cái zǎo fān.
[It was] transported to Luòyáng;
also, rare trees and exotic plants,
precious birds and strange beasts were sought from all under heaven
to fill the imperial gardens.
On the xīnhài day,
Shàngshū Yòuchéng Huángfǔ Yì was ordered to mobilize over a million people,
both before and after, from Hénán and the northern Huái prefectures
to open the Tōngjì Qú.
Dù Yòu said: There is the Tōngjì Qú west of Chénliú Jùn’s city;
Emperor Yáng opened it to connect the Jiāng and Huái for grain transport,
and also to draw in the Biàn River,
which is the same as the Làngdàng Qú.
Kǎoyì states: Zájì records it as
"Huángfǔ Gōngyí",
and also says,
"mobilized over 500,000 soldiers and laborers."
We follow the abbreviated record here.
In this year, the Eastern Capital was constructed.
It was eighteen lǐ east of the old capital,
directly south of the mouth of Yīquè,
north of the barrier of Mángshān,
east of the eastern bank of the Chán River,
and west of the western bank of the Jiàn River;
its western city wall adjoined the imperial park,
seven lǐ from Shàngyáng Gōng.
The imperial park wall had a circumference of one hundred twenty-six lǐ,
reaching Mángshān to the north,
Xiàoshuǐ to the west,
and the tributary of the Luò River to the south;
the Gǔ and Luò rivers converged within it,
so water was drawn from the imperial park as a canal
to reach the Hé.
Bǎnjǔ was east of Hǔláo.
Shuǐ Jīng: The Hé River flows east to merge with the Sì River,
then further east past Bǎn Chéng;
to its north is a ford called Bǎnchéng Zhǔkǒu.
Further east, it passes Yíngyáng Xiàn,
where the Làngdàng Qú emerges.
This canal flows south to become the Biàn River,
and Hàn’s Yíngyáng Shímén was located there.
The Suí Zhì states: Yíngyáng Jùn’s Yíngzé Xiàn
was established in the fourth year of Kāihuáng,
named Guǎngwǔ,
and renamed in the first year of Rénshòu.
[It reached] Huái;
Dàliáng
is Jùnyí.
Drawing the Hé into the Biàn,
and the Biàn into the Sì,
these were all old routes.
From Shānyáng to Yángzǐ, it entered the Jiāng.
The Chūnqiū states that Wú built the Hángōu to connect the Jiāng and Huái;
this also followed an old route.
Hángōu
now runs through the city of Yángzhōu.
Shānyáng is now Huái’ān Zhōu.
Yángzǐ is now Zhēn Zhōu.
Hán
is pronounced hán.
Along the canal, imperial roads were built
and planted with willows;
from Cháng’ān to Jiāngdū,
Jiāngdū Jùn is Yángzhōu.
On the gēngshēn day,
Huángmén Shìláng Wáng Hóng and others were dispatched to Jiāngnán to build dragon boats and tens of thousands of other vessels.
The officials supervising the construction of the Eastern Capital were severe and urgent,
and four or five out of ten laborers died;
the authorities transported the dead laborers by cart,
all the way east to Chénggāo,
The Suí Zhì states: Zhèngzhōu’s Yíngyáng Xiàn formerly had Chénggāo Jùn.
They were visible along the road.
Also, Tiānjīng Gōng was built in the Eastern Capital,
where sacrifices were offered to Gāozǔ four times a year.
The Jīng says: Filial piety
is the constant principle of Heaven.
Thus, the palace was named after it.
11 Lín Yì (林邑) King Fàn Zhì (梵志)
sent troops to guard the perilous passes.
Liú Fāng (劉方) attacked and drove them away.
The army crossed the Shé Lí (闍黎) River,
and Lín Yì (林邑) soldiers, mounted on giant elephants,
approached from all four sides.
Fāng (方) was at a disadvantage in battle,
so he dug many small pits,
covered them with grass,
and provoked the enemy with his troops.
When the battle began,
he feigned retreat;
the Lín Yì (林邑) pursued him,
but many elephants fell into the pits and stumbled,
causing mutual panic,
and the army was thrown into chaos.
Fāng (方) shot the elephants with crossbows,
and the elephants ran backward,
trampling their own formation.
Fāng (方) then followed up with his elite troops,
and the Lín Yì (林邑) were utterly defeated,
capturing and beheading tens of thousands.
Fāng (方) led his troops in pursuit,
winning every battle repeatedly.
They passed south of Mǎ Yuán’s (馬援) Bronze Pillars.
The *Xīn Táng Shū* (新唐書) says: "Lín Yì (林邑) fled to Làng Tuó Zhōu (浪陀州).
South of it, in a large bay, are the Five Bronze Pillar Mountains,
shaped like leaning canopies.
To the west are steep cliffs,
and to the east, the sea.
These were erected by Mǎ Yuán (馬援) of the Hàn (漢) dynasty."
Dù Yòu (杜佑) says: "Two thousand *yǔ* (餘) *lǐ* (里) by land and water south of Lín Yì (林邑)
are the Xī Tú Yí (西屠夷),
where Mǎ Yuán (馬援) erected two bronze pillars to mark the border."
"The Bronze Pillar Mountains are ten *lǐ* (里) in circumference,
shaped like leaning canopies,
straddling steep cliffs to the west,
and overlooking the vast sea to the east."
Sòng Bái (宋白) says: "Mǎ Yuán (馬援) campaigned against Jiāozhǐ (交趾).
From Rì Nán (日南), he traveled south over four hundred *lǐ* (里) to Lín Yì (林邑).
Then he traveled south another two thousand *yǔ* (餘) *lǐ* (里)
to the kingdom of Xī Tú Yí (西屠夷).
Yuán (援) reached their country
and cast two bronze pillars at the southern border of Xiàng Lín (象林),
demarcating the territory with the Xī Tú Yí (西屠夷)."
It is estimated that from Jiāozhōu (交州) to the Bronze Pillars is five thousand *lǐ* (里).
According to the accounts of Sòng (宋) and Dù (杜),
the Bronze Pillars are south of Lín Yì (林邑).
What is recorded here,
however, places Lín Yì (林邑) south of the Bronze Pillars.
In summer,
fourth month,
Fàn Zhì (梵志) abandoned his city and fled into the sea.
Fāng (方) entered the city
and captured eighteen temple statues,
all cast in gold;
he carved a stone monument to record his achievements and then returned.
The soldiers suffered from swollen feet,
and four or five tenths died.
Fāng (方) also contracted an illness
and died on the way.
Originally,
the Right Minister (尚書右丞) Lǐ Gāng (李綱) had frequently disagreed with Yáng Sù (楊素) and Sū Wēi (蘇威), offending them.
Sù (素) recommended Gāng (綱) to Gāozǔ (高祖),
making him Fāng’s (方) military marshal (行軍司馬).
Fāng (方), acting on Sù’s (素) intention,
humiliated him,
nearly killing him.
When the army returned,
he was not given a new appointment for a long time.
Wēi (威) again sent Gāng (綱) to Nánhǎi (南海) to coordinate with Lín Yì (林邑),
and did not recall him for a long time.
Gāng (綱) returned on his own to report on affairs.
Wēi (威) impeached Gāng (綱) for abandoning his post,
and he was handed over to the officials for interrogation;
a general amnesty was granted,
he was dismissed from office,
and retired to Hù (鄠).
Hù (鄠) County
belonged to Jīngzhào (京兆) Commandery.
This was Lǐ Gāng (李綱) being forced by Hé Pān Rén (何潘仁), leading to the current situation.
屏,
*bì* (必郢) *fān* (翻).
鄠,
sound *hù* (戶).
12 In the fifth month,
the Western Park (西苑) was built,
with a circumference of two hundred *lǐ* (里);
slightly different from what is recorded in the *Liù Diǎn* (六典).
It was over ten *lǐ* (里) in circumference;
with mountains like Pénglái (蓬萊), Fāngzhàng (方丈), and Yíngzhōu (瀛洲),
resembling the three divine mountains in the sea.
Terraces, towers, palaces, and pavilions
were scattered across the mountains,
appearing and disappearing like spirits.
To the north was the Lóng Lín Qú (龍鱗渠) (Dragon Scale Canal),
winding and flowing into the inner sea.
Along the canal, sixteen courtyards were built,
their gates all facing the canal.
Each courtyard was presided over by a fourth-rank lady,
and the ranks of the inner court ladies were equivalent to those of officials.
It was built with extreme luxury and beauty.
When the palace trees shed their leaves in autumn and winter,
silk flowers and leaves were cut out
and attached to the branches,
and when their color faded, they were replaced with new ones,
always appearing as if in early spring.
In the ponds, silk was also cut into shapes of lotus, water caltrop, and foxnut.
When the imperial carriage went on an outing,
the ice was removed and these were spread out.
The sixteen courtyards competed in the exquisite beauty of their dishes and delicacies to gain favor.
The emperor enjoyed touring the Western Park (西苑) on moonlit nights with several thousand palace women on horseback,
performing the song "Qīng Yè Yóu Qǔ" (清夜遊曲) (Melody of a Clear Night Excursion)
while riding on horseback.
It used Cáo Zhí's (曹植)
poem
"Qīng Yè Yóu Xī Yuán" (清夜遊西園) (Clear Night Excursion to the Western Garden)
to name the song.
好,
*hào* (呼到) *fān* (翻).
騎,
*qí* (奇計) *fān* (翻).
13 The emperor treated his various princes with little kindness
and was very suspicious of them;
Téng Wáng Lún (滕王綸) and Wèi Wáng Jí (衞王集) worried internally,
consulting sorcerers about their fortunes and performing rituals for blessings.
Someone reported that they harbored resentment and practiced curses.
The relevant authorities memorialized for their execution;
In autumn,
seventh month,
on the day *bǐng wǔ* (丙午),
an edict stripped them of their titles and reduced them to commoners,
exiling them to border prefectures.
Lún (綸)
was Zàn’s (瓚) son;
Jí (集)
was Shuǎng’s (爽) son.
Zàn (瓚)
was Gāozǔ’s (高祖) maternal younger brother;
Shuǎng (爽)
was his half-brother.
瓚,
*zàn* (藏旱) *fān* (翻).
14 In the eighth month,
on the day *rén yín* (壬寅),
the emperor journeyed to Jiāngdū (江都).
The *Kǎo Yì* (考異) states: "Miscellaneous records say ninth month,
but we follow the *Suí Dì Jì* (隋帝紀) and *Luè Jì* (略記)."
Wáng Hóng (王弘) sent a dragon boat to welcome him.
On the day *yǐ sì* (乙巳),
the emperor boarded the Xiǎo Zhū Háng (小朱航),
exiting the漕渠 (Cáoqú) (Grand Canal) at Luòkǒu (洛口),
the mouth where the Luò (洛) River enters the Yellow River.
The *Kǎo Yì* (考異) states: "The *Luè Jì* (略記) says,
'On the day *jiǎ zǐ* (甲子),
the dragon boat advanced.'
According to the perpetual calendar,
the first day of this month was *wù zǐ* (戊子),
so there was no *jiǎ zǐ* (甲子)."
It was forty-five *chǐ* (尺) high and two hundred *zhàng* (丈) long.
On the upper deck were the main hall, inner hall, and East and West Audience Halls.
In the middle two decks were one hundred and twenty rooms,
all adorned with gold and jade.
The lower deck was for the palace attendants.
The empress rode the Xiáng Chī Zhōu (翔螭舟) (Soaring Dragon Boat),
which was slightly smaller in design
but had identical decorations.
There were also nine Fú Jǐng (浮景) (Floating Scenery) boats,
three stories high,
all water palaces.

Additionally, there were thousands of boats such as Yàng Cǎi (漾彩), Zhū Niǎo (朱鳥), Cāng Chī (蒼螭), Bái Hǔ (白虎), Xuán Wǔ (玄武), Fēi Yǔ (飛羽), Qīng Fú (青鳧), Líng Bō (陵波), Wǔ Lóu (五樓), Dàochǎng (道場), Xuántán (玄壇), bǎn
*hū* (舟翕), and huáng miè (黃篾), etc.
舟翕,
*tuō hé* (託盍) *fān* (翻).
A large boat is called 舟翕.
篾,
sound *miè* (蔑).
Together with those carrying the supplies for the inner and outer hundred offices,
a total of over eighty thousand boat-pullers were used.
Over nine thousand of those pulling the Yàng Cǎi (漾彩) and larger boats
were called Diàn Jiǎo (殿腳) (Palace Footmen),
all wearing brocade robes.
There were also thousands of boats such as Píng Chéng (平乘), Qīng Lóng (青龍), Méng Chóng (艨艟), cáo chuán (艚舟爰), Bā Dào (八櫂), and Tǐng Gě (艇舸).
These were manned by soldiers from the twelve guards,
who also carried weapons and tents.
The soldiers pulled their own boats
and were not assigned laborers.
The sterns and bows connected for over two hundred *lǐ* (里),
illuminating the rivers and land.
Cavalry flanked both banks,
and flags obscured the fields.
The prefectures and counties they passed through,
within five hundred *lǐ* (里), were ordered to offer food.
For some, one prefecture offered up to a hundred carts,
filled with rare delicacies from land and sea.
When the imperial concubines grew tired of them
and were about to depart,
many were discarded and buried.
15 The Qìdān
raided Yíngzhōu,
Liáoxī Jùn, and established Yíngzhōu.
契,
is pronounced Qī Qǐ,
or Chī.
According to the Suí Zhì: Upon the Emperor’s accession,
he increased the number of Yèzhě Tái officials,
and changed the Tōngshì Shèrén of the Nèishǐ Shěng to Yèzhě Tái officials.
There were twenty Tōngshì Yèzhě,
ranked sixth-grade.
Qǐmín Kèhán dispatched two myriad cavalry,
to receive his orders.
Yúnqǐ divided them into twenty camps,
advancing simultaneously on four routes.
Camps were one lǐ apart,
and were not to intermingle.
They marched when they heard the drum,
and halted when they heard the horn.
Unless on official mission,
they were not to gallop their horses.
Gōngshǐ
refers to an envoy on public business.
They set off with a drum beat.
A Gēgàn
violated the agreement, and was beheaded.
Gēgàn
was a minor official of the Tūjué.
紇,
is pronounced Xiámò.
Thereupon, the Tūjué generals and commanders came to pay their respects,
all crawling on their knees and trembling,
none daring to look up.
The Qìdān had originally been subject to the Tūjué,
and there was no suspicion between them.
As soon as Yúnqǐ entered their territory,
he had the Tūjué falsely claim to be heading towards Liǔchéng.
This was the ancient Liǔchéng.
According to the Suí Zhì,
Liáoxī Jùn and Yíngzhōu
were both administered from Liǔchéng Xiàn,
which was then Lóngchéng Xiàn.
Lóngchéng was originally Hélóngchéng.
Since the Later Wèi,
Yíngzhōu had been administered there.
In the first year of Kāihuáng,
it was renamed Lóngshān Xiàn.
In the eighteenth year,
it was renamed Liǔchéng.
Anyone who leaked the truth would be beheaded.
The Qìdān made no preparations.
Fifty lǐ from their camp,
Yúnqǐ led a swift assault,
capturing all forty thousand of their men and women.
He killed their men,
and gave half of the women and livestock to the Tūjué.
The rest he took back.
The Emperor was greatly pleased,
and gathered his officials, saying:
“Yúnqǐ used the Tūjué to pacify the Qìdān,
his talent encompassing both civil and military arts.
I shall now promote him myself.”
He was promoted to Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ.
16 Initially,
Ābō Kèhán of the Western Tūjué was captured by Yèhù Kèhán.
(See Volume 176, Zhēnmíng First Year of Chén Chángchéng Gōng.)
This was Níyì Kèhán.
Níyì died,
and his son Dámàn succeeded,
titled Chǔluó Kèhán.
His mother, Lady Xiàng,
was originally Chinese,
and remarried Níyì’s younger brother, Póshítèlè.
Towards the end of Kāihuáng,
Póshí and Lady Xiàng came to court.
They encountered Dátóu’s rebellion,
and thus remained in Cháng’ān,
lodging at the Hónglú Sì.
The Hónglú Sì
was in charge of foreign guests.
臚,
is pronounced Lǘ.
His administration was misguided,
and many of his people rebelled.
He was again besieged by the Tiělè.
The Tiělè were
descendants of the Xiōngnú,
with the largest number of clans,
including the Púgǔ, Tóngluó, Qìbì, Xuēyántuó, and other tribes.
Their chieftains were all titled Sījīn.
Although their surnames differed,
they were collectively called Tiělè.
Generally, they shared customs with the Tūjué,
living by raiding and plundering.
They had no great monarch,
and were divided, belonging to both the Eastern and Western Tūjué.
That year,
Chǔluó led troops to attack the Tiělè tribes,
heavily taxing their goods.
He also suspected the Xuēyántuó,
fearing they would revolt.
He gathered several hundred of their chieftains
and killed them all.
Thereupon, all the Tiělè rebelled.
They established Sīlìfā Sījīn Qìbì Gēléng as Mòhé Kèhán,
and also established Xuēyántuó Sījīn Zìyědié as Xiǎo Kèhán.
They fought Chǔluó,
defeating him repeatedly.
Mòhé was exceptionally brave and resolute,
and greatly won the hearts of the people.
He was feared by neighboring states.
Yīwú, Gāochāng, and Yānqí all submitted to him.

"The sun, moon, stars, constellations, mountains, dragons, and 'glorious insects' constitute the imperial emblem."
The Zhōu Dynasty elevated the sun and moon onto flags but omitted the three constellations;
now the ancient system is restored.

The yellow-banner guard

The Empress's imperial procession,

Orders were issued to prefectures and counties to submit feathers,

In Wūchéng there was a tall tree;

There were no branches attached to its sides,

Fearing that her young would be killed, the crane

People at the time sometimes hailed this as an auspicious sign,

"The Son of Heaven creates feather ornaments,

The number of laborers employed exceeded one hundred thousand,

6 Yuándé Crown Prince Zhāo came from Cháng'ān to pay respects to the court.
The Emperor ordered Zhāo to remain in Cháng'ān as acting defender.
朝 (*cháo*),
pronounced *zhíyáo* reversed.
When he was about to return,

He bowed countless times,

On *jiǎxū*,

*Kǎo Yì* (Critical Distinctions) states: Miscellaneous records say:
"Initially,
when the Crown Prince fell ill,
he was at a banquet with Yáng Sù.
The Emperor, deeply wary of Sù,
brought out two cups simultaneously,
but the server, not realizing one was poisoned wine,
mistakenly offered it to the Crown Prince.
After drinking, the poison took effect three days later,
causing him to pass more than two *dòu* of blood.
When the palace servants heard that Sù was fine,
they first realized that the poisoned wine had been mistakenly given to the Crown Prince,
but kept the secret and dared not speak.
The Crown Prince, knowing this,
sighed, saying: 'How could I have imagined dying in place of Yáng Sù?
It is fate!'
He died a few days later.
Later, Sù also eventually perished from poison."
However, other books do not contain this account.
This is probably just a baseless rumor circulated by people at the time
seeing the Crown Prince and Sù die in succession.
After a few cries, he stopped,

7 Chǔ Jǐngwǔ Gōng Yáng Sù,

Outwardly, he was shown special courtesy,

The Grand Astrologer said that the Sui astrological division portended a great funeral,
so Yáng Sù was transferred to become the Duke of Chǔ.
The intention was that Chǔ shared the same astrological division as Suí,
hoping to avert the disaster with this.
Yáng Sù became gravely ill.
The Emperor repeatedly ordered famous physicians to examine him
and bestowed excellent medicines,
yet secretly asked the doctors
and constantly feared he would not die.
Yáng Sù also knew his position and rank had reached their peak,
so he would not take medicine
nor did he take care of himself.
He said to his younger brother, Yáng Yuē:
"Why should I wish to live any longer!"
On the *yǐhài* day,
Yáng Sù died.
He was posthumously granted the title of Tàiwèi Gōng and Administrator of ten commanderies including Hóngnóng.
His funeral was very grand.

Water was agitated to fill the streets;

He said to Bái Míngdá:

(*Suí Shū*: Qí Hòuzhǔ enjoyed foreign music,
indulging endlessly.
Thus, complex techniques and decadent sounds
competed in new sorrow and plaintiveness.
Therefore, people like Cáo Miàodá and Ān Mǎjū
were even enfeoffed as kings and opened residences.)
Emperor Yáng, indulging in decadent music,
likened himself to a ruler of a doomed state.
His licentiousness and confusion were extreme.
I am about to promote you.
You should conduct yourself carefully!"

The emperor was about to undertake campaigns against the Four Barbarians

Shù said to Dìngxīng,

Dìngxīng said,

"The sons of Fánglíng,

but if we keep them in one place,
that also seems inappropriate.

The emperor agreed,
and thereupon poisoned King Chángníng Yǎn.

6 Niú Hóng and others completed the new legal code,
totaling eighteen chapters,
called the Dàyè Lǜ.
On the day Jiǎshēn,
it was first promulgated and put into effect.
The people, long weary of severe strictness,
rejoiced at the lenient policy.
Later, as military conscriptions became frequent,
the people could not endure the burden.
Officials coerced them on the spot to get things done,
no longer adhering to the laws and ordinances.
Liú Xuàn, an officer of the Lǚqí Wèi, participated in the revision of the laws.
Hóng once casually asked Xuàn,
"In the Rites of Zhōu, there were many scholars but few clerks and scribes.
Today, the number of clerks is a hundred times greater than before.
If we reduce them, affairs cannot be managed.
What is the reason for this?"
Xuàn replied,
"Ancient people entrusted responsibility and required results.
At the end of the year, their performance was evaluated as superior or inferior.
Cases were not double-checked,
and documents were not overly detailed.
The role of clerks and scribes
was merely to manage key items.
Today's documents
are always drafted with the fear of subsequent review.
If the drafting is not meticulous,
then a century-old case might be pursued and re-examined thousands of miles away.
Hence the proverb: 'Old clerks die clutching their documents.'
The complexity of affairs and the corruption of governance
stem from this."
Hóng said,
"During the Wèi and Qí eras,
clerks were quite relaxed.
Now, they have no leisure to rest.
Why is this?"
Xuàn replied,
"In the past, a prefecture only established 'gāngjì' (綱紀).
These 'gāngjì'
referred to the Chángshǐ and Sīmǎ.
A county only established a magistrate.
Other subordinate officials were personally appointed by the chief official,
who received edicts to take up their posts,
and there were no more than a few dozen in each prefecture.
Today, it is not so.
All officials, great and small,
are appointed by the Lìbù.
Even the slightest detail of their conduct
falls under the Kǎogōng.
The Kǎogōng Shìláng
is in charge of evaluating the merits and demerits of all civil and military officials, both internal and external,
recording all their achievements, faults, and abilities for the current year and assessing them.
If official business is not simplified, how can one expect leisure?
Is that even possible!"
Hóng praised his words but could not implement them.
7 On the day Rénchén,

measures, weights, and balances were revised
to conform to ancient standards.
Officials from Shàngzhùguó downwards were renamed as Dàfū.
Formerly, from Shàngzhùguó down to Dūdū, there were eleven ranks.
Now, they were changed to Jiǔ Dàfū: Guānglù, Zuǒ/Yòu Guānglù, Jīnzǐ/Yínqīng Guānglù, Zhèngyì, Tōngyì, Cháoqǐng, and Cháosàn.
The Diànnèi Shěng
was in charge of various imperial provisions.
The Yèzhě and Sīlì Tái were added.
The Yèzhě Tái
was in charge of receiving edicts to offer condolences, dispatching envoys for comfort and pacification, carrying credentials for inspection and investigation, and receiving and reporting grievances.
The Sīlì Tái
was in charge of various inspections.
The Tàifǔ Sì was divided to establish the Shàofǔ Jiān.
The Tàifǔ Sì
thenceforth only managed the Zuǒ/Yòu Cáng and Huáng Cáng.
Its Shàngfāng, Sīzhī, Sīrǎn, Kǎijiǎ, Gōngnǔ, and Zhǎngyě were all subordinate to the Shàofǔ Jiān.
Shào,

the Zuǒ/Yòu Bèishēn were renamed Zuǒ/Yòu Xiāowèi;
the Zuǒ/Yòu Wǔwèi retained their old names;
the Lǐngjūn were renamed Zuǒ/Yòu Túnwèi;
the Zuǒ/Yòu Yùwèi were added;
the Zuǒ/Yòu Wǔhóu were renamed Zuǒ/Yòu Hóuwèi. These constituted the Twelve Guards.
The Lǐng Zuǒ/Yòu Fǔ were renamed Zuǒ/Yòu Bèishēnfǔ;
