Chǔluó (處羅) rose startled,
shedding tears and bowing twice,
knelt and received the imperial edict,
and then sent envoys to accompany Jūnshù (君肅) to present sweat-blood horses.
4. In the third month,
on the day Rénxū (壬戌),
Wō Wáng Duōlìsībǐgū (倭王多利思比孤)
The Suíshū (隋書) says: The kingdom of Wō (倭) is southeast of Bǎijì (百濟) and Xīnluó (新羅),
three thousand *lǐ* (里) by water and land,
in the midst of the great sea,
dwelling on mountains and islands;
its capital is in Yé Míduī (邪靡堆),
which is what the Wèizhì (魏志) called Yémǎtái (邪馬臺),
east of Kuàijī (會稽),
near Dān'ěr (儋耳).
Dù Yòu (杜佑) says: Wō (倭) is in the great sea southeast of Dàifāng (帶方),
twelve thousand *lǐ* (里) from Liáodōng (遼東),
roughly east of Mǐnchuān (閩川) and Kuàijī (會稽),
also near Zhūyá (朱崖) and Dān'ěr (儋耳).
They claim to be descendants of Tàibó (太伯).
Also named Rìběn (日本),
they say their country is by the side of the sun,
and so took that name.
Wō (倭),
read Wū-Hé (烏禾) fan.
presented a letter to the Emperor saying:
"From the Son of Heaven in the land where the sun rises, a letter to the Son of Heaven in the land where the sun sets. We trust you are well."
The Emperor read it,
and was displeased,
saying to Hónglú Qīng (鴻臚卿):
"Do not again report letters from barbarians that are disrespectful."
5. On the day Yǐchǒu (乙丑),
the imperial carriage proceeded to Wǔyuán (五原).
The Emperor changed Fēngzhōu (豐州) to Wǔyuán Jùn (五原郡).
This refers to what was built last year.
The Suízhì (隋志) says: The Emperor toured north beyond the frontier,
and the temporary palace was set up as the Liùhé Chéng (六合城),
one hundred twenty paces square,
forty-two feet high.
The Liùhé (六合)
was made of wood,
one foot square,
with a board on one outer side,
made to be assembled and disassembled,
painted blue.
Six boards were stacked to form a wall,
thirty-six feet high,
with a parapet added on top,
the boards six feet high,
opening north and south gates.
Also, at the four corners of the city, two watchtowers were erected,
and the gate towers, gatehouses, and door frames were all decorated with vermilion, blue, and intricate paintings.
They also built the Liùhédian (六合殿) and a thousand-person tent,
carried on spear carts.
Each cart carried three boards of the Liùhé (六合).
The cart shafts could be disassembled and interlocked to form horse spears.
All carts had awnings spread over them,
and beneath the awnings, a flat, single-arrow-firing repeating crossbow was set up,
guarded by five men in shifts.
Between two carts,
cart shafts and horse spears were set up,
with their shafts facing outwards,
forming an outer perimeter.
Next inside, iron caltrops were spread,
and further inside, hidden quivers were placed.
In the middle, crossbow beds were set up,
six feet long and
three feet wide;
steel spikes,
each five inches long,
were inserted into the crossbow bed slats,
called "shrimp whiskers."
All were equipped with mechanisms,
and when activated, the spikes all pointed outwards.
On these beds, rotating trigger crossbows were installed,
with ropes connected to the crossbow mechanisms.
When a person approached from outside,
touching the rope would cause the crossbow mechanism to rotate
and fire towards the point of contact.
Outside this, a fence (zēng, 矰) surrounded the temporary palace for two *zhàng* (丈),
with one bell and one post,
the post raising the fence
two feet five inches off the ground.
At the north and south gates of the temporary palace, hammers and chimes were placed,
connected to the fence,
activated by a mechanism.
If someone touched the fence,
all the bells would sound,
and the hammers would strike the two chimes,
to signal an alarm.
This was called "striking the chimes."
The Kǎoyì (考異) says: Miscellaneous records state,
"When the Emperor visited Qǐmín's (啟民) tent, a mobile city was built,
two thousand paces in circumference,
over twenty *zhàng* (丈) high."
We now follow the Suí Lǐyízhì (隋禮儀志).
Each time they halted,
the cart shafts were turned outwards to form an outer perimeter,
and iron caltrops were spread inside;
The Éryǎ Yì (爾雅翼) says: Today, in military camps, iron thorns are made
to cover enemy paths,
called "iron蒺蔾" (iron caltrops).
Some say: "iron蒺蔾" (iron caltrops) and "菱角" (water caltrops) originated when Emperor Yáng (煬帝) made them during his campaign against Liáo (遼).
However, such items already existed in the Liùtāo (六韜),
and the Zhāocuò Chuán (朝錯傳) referred to them as "渠答" (qúdá).
Steel spikes were all inserted,
pointing outwards;
rotating trigger crossbows were installed above,
with ropes connected to the mechanisms.
When a person touched a rope,
the crossbow mechanism would rotate
and fire towards the point of contact.
Outside this, a fence (zēng, 矰) was erected all around,
with bell posts and hammers and chimes to signal an alarm.
6 The Emperor sought those capable of traversing distant lands.
The屯田主事 Túntián Zhǔshì Cháng Jùn and others requested to be envoys to Chìtǔ.
The屯田曹 Túntián Cáo
was subordinate to the工部尚書 Gōngbù Shàngshū.
Each department (諸曹 zhū cáo) under the尚書 Shàngshū had a主事 zhǔshì,
which was an unofficial civil post (流外吏職 liúwài lìzhí).
The Suí Shū states: The kingdom of Chìtǔ,
a branch of Fúnán,
is in the South Sea.
It takes over a hundred days to reach by water.
The color of the soil where its capital is located is mostly red,
hence its name.
Dù Yòu said: Sailing directly south from Yázhōu,
with favorable winds, one reaches the kingdom of Chìtǔ in just over ten days.
In that country, at noon in May,
all object shadows fall to the south.
They eat three meals a day,
and all rice is cooked freshly for each meal.
Otherwise,
it quickly passes its time,
and immediately spoils and stinks,
as the heat is exceptionally intense.
使 Shǐ is pronounced Sūlì (疏利).
On the day Bǐngyín,
Cháng Jùn was ordered to carry five thousand bolts of goods,
to be bestowed upon its king.
Chìtǔ was a distant country in the South Sea.
7 The Emperor spent no day without constructing palaces and residences.
Although there were many imperial gardens, pavilions, and halls in the two capitals and Jiāngdū,
he grew increasingly tired of them over time.
Whenever he went on an imperial tour,
he would look around
but find nothing to his liking,
not knowing where to go.
So,
he gathered maps of all the mountains and rivers in the realm,
personally reviewed them,
to find scenic spots suitable for establishing palaces and gardens.
In summer,
in the fourth month,
an edict was issued to construct the Fényánggōng
at the source of the Fénshuǐ, north of Fénzhōu.
The Suí Zhì states: Fényuán Xiàn in Lóufán Jùn,
formerly Kělán,
was renamed Jìnglè
in the fourth year of Dàyè.
It has the Fényánggōng, Guǎncén Shān, Tiānchí, and Fénshuǐ.
The Shísānzhōu Zhì states: The Fénshuǐ originates from Yànjīng Shān in Wǔzhōu,
which is another name for Guǎncén.
The Shuǐ Jīng Zhù mentions
a large pond on Yànjīng Shān,
commonly known as Tiānchí.
According to records, Emperor Yáng constructed the Fényánggōng encircling Tiānchí;
details can be found in the later commentary on Wǔtái.
8 Initially,
Yuándé Tàizǐ (元德太子) died.
See year two in the scroll above.
Yuándé's (元德) civil and military personnel, numbering over twenty thousand,
were all assigned to Yǎn (暕).
The Emperor carefully selected his officials for him,
appointing Liǔ Jiǎnzhī (柳謇之), a junior minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, as the Chief Clerk of Qí Wáng (齊王).
He also warned him, saying:
“Qí Wáng's (齊王) virtue and achievements are well-cultivated and complete;
wealth and honor will naturally gather upon your household.
Zhōng (鍾)
means 'to gather'.
Crimes will also affect you.”
Jiǎnzhī (謇之)
was a cousin of Qìngzhī (慶之).
Liǔ Qìng (柳慶) served Yǔwén Tài (宇文泰).
Cóng (從)
is read as cái yòng (才用).
Hundreds of officials flocked to pay their respects,
filling the roads.
Yǎn (暕) became arrogant and indulgent because of this,
associating with petty individuals,
and many of his actions were unlawful.
He dispatched his attendants Qiáo Lìngzé (喬令則) and Kùdí Zhòngqí (庫狄仲錡).
Kùdí (庫狄)
is a double-surname.
Qí (錡)
is read as yú qǐ (魚豈).
Lìngzé (令則) and others took advantage of this freedom,
inquiring about beautiful women in people's homes.
They would falsely claim Yǎn's (暕) order to summon them,
take them into Yǎn's (暕) residence,
rape them, and then send them away.
Zhòngqí (仲錡) and Zhìwěi (智偉) went to Lǒngxī (隴西),
flogging and roasting various Hú (胡) people,
demanding their fine horses.
The Emperor changed Wèizhōu (渭州) to Lǒngxī Jùn (隴西郡).
Zhuā (撾)
is read as cè guā (側瓜).
Yǎn (暕) ordered them to return the horses to their owners,
but Zhòngqí (仲錡) and others falsely claimed they were gifts from the King,
taking them back to their own homes.
Yǎn (暕) did not know this.
Lèpíng Gōngzhǔ (樂平公主) once reported to the Emperor,
saying that a Liǔ (柳) family woman was beautiful.
Lèpíng Gōngzhǔ (樂平公主)
was the Empress of Zhou Tiānyuán (周天元).
Lè (樂)
is pronounced Luò (洛).
After some time,
the princess again presented the Liǔ (柳) woman to Yǎn (暕),
and Yǎn (暕) took her in.
Later,
the Emperor asked the princess:
“Where is the Liǔ (柳) woman?”
The princess replied:
“She is with Qí Wáng (齊王).”
The Emperor was displeased.
Yǎn (暕) accompanied the Emperor on a visit to Fényáng Gōng (汾陽宮)
for a great hunt.
The Emperor ordered Yǎn (暕) to enter the enclosure with a thousand cavalry.
Yǎn (暕) caught many elk and deer and presented them;
but the Emperor had not caught any.
He then became angry at his accompanying officials,
who all said they were obstructed by Yǎn's (暕) attendants,
preventing the beasts from approaching.
The Emperor then grew furious,
seeking Yǎn's (暕) faults and transgressions.
At that time, there was a regulation: county magistrates were not allowed to leave their jurisdiction without cause.
There was an official, Huángfǔ Xǔ (皇甫詡), the magistrate of Yīquē (伊闕),
who was favored by Yǎn (暕).
He violated the prohibition
and brought Xǔ (詡) to Fényáng Gōng (汾陽宮).
The Imperial Censor Wéi Déyù (韋德裕), anticipating the Emperor's wishes, impeached Yǎn (暕).
The Emperor ordered over a thousand armored soldiers to thoroughly search Yǎn's (暕) residence,
and then fully investigated the matter.
Yǎn's (暕) wife, Wéi Shì (韋氏), had died early.
Yǎn (暕) had an illicit relationship with his sister, Yuán Shì (元氏),
and they had a daughter.
Yǎn (暕) summoned a physiognomist
and had him examine everyone in the rear palace.
The physiognomist pointed to his sister and said:
“The one who gave birth to this child will become Empress.”
Yǎn (暕), knowing that Yuándé Tàizǐ (元德太子) had three sons –
the three sons were Yòu (侑), Tán (倓), Dòng (侗) –
secretly engaged in heterodox practices for "evil suppression."
Now, all these were revealed.
The Emperor was greatly angered,
executing Lìngzé (令則) and several others,
and ordering his sister to commit suicide.
All of Yǎn's (暕) officials were banished to distant borders.
Liǔ Jiǎnzhī (柳謇之) was dismissed from office
for failing to provide proper guidance.
At that time, Zhào Wáng Gǎo (趙王杲) was still young.
The Emperor said to his attending ministers:
“I only have Yǎn (暕) as a son.
Otherwise,
I would have displayed him in the market and court to clarify the national law.”
From then on, Yǎn's (暕) favor and affection waned daily.
Although he was the Metropolitan Prefect,
he no longer concerned himself with current affairs.
The Emperor always ordered one Hǔbēn Lángjiàng (虎賁郎將) to supervise his household affairs.
The Emperor established twelve guards,
with four Hùjūn (護軍) in each guard,
responsible for assisting the generals.
If there were no generals, one Hùjūn (護軍) would temporarily assume the role.
Later, Hùjūn (護軍) was changed to Hǔbēn Lángjiàng (虎賁郎將),
a fourth-rank official.
Cháo (朝)
is read as zhí yáo (直遙).
Fù (復)
is read as fú yòu (扶又).
Héng (恆)
is read as hù dēng (戶登).
Lìng (令)
is read as lì dīng (力丁).
Bēn (賁)
is pronounced bēn.
Jiàng (將)
is read as jí liàng (即亮).
Jiān (監)
is read as gǔ xián (古銜).
The Hǔbēn (虎賁) would report everything.
The Emperor also constantly worried that Yǎn (暕) might cause trouble,
so the attendants provided to him
were all old and weak,
merely to fill the positions.
Yǔ Zhì (庾質), the Grand Astrologer,
son of Jìcái (季才),
had a son who was an official under Qí Wáng (齊王).
The suí wáng (隋王) residence had both Yuán (掾) and Shǔ (屬) officials.
“You cannot serve me wholeheartedly,
yet you let your son serve Qí Wáng (齊王).
How can you be so contradictory?”
He replied:
“Your servant serves Your Majesty,
and my son serves Qí Wáng (齊王).
In reality, it is one heart,
I dare not have two.”
The Emperor was still angry
and demoted him to magistrate of Héshuǐ (合水).
In the 16th year of Kāihuáng (開皇),
Héshuǐ Xiàn (合水縣) was established,
serving as the administrative seat of Qìngzhōu (慶州).
The Emperor changed Qìngzhōu (慶州) to Hónghuà Jùn (弘化郡).
The Táng (唐) dynasty changed Héshuǐ Xiàn (合水縣) to Ānhuà (安化).
9 On the day Yǐmǎo (乙卯),
an imperial edict stated that because Tujue Qǐmín Kèhán (突厥啟民可汗)
adhered to the court's civilization
and wished to reform barbarian customs,
a city and houses should be built at Wànshòu Shù (萬壽戍).
His tents, bedding, and all other items
should be of the finest quality.
10In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the day Xīnsì (辛巳),
over two hundred thousand able-bodied men were dispatched to build the Great Wall,
starting from Yúgǔ (榆谷) and extending eastward.
This Yúgǔ (榆谷) should be west of Yúlín (榆林).
11 Péi Jù persuaded the Tīelè,
to attack the Tǔyùhún,
thoroughly defeating them.
Fúyǔn, the Khagan of Tǔyùhún, fled eastward,
entering Xīpíng territory.
The Emperor changed Shànzhōu to Xīpíng Jùn.
吐,
read tūn rùshēng.
谷,
sounds like yù.
可,
from kān rùshēng.
汗,
sounds like hán.
The Emperor sent Āndé Wáng Xióng out to Jiāohé.
Previously, Wáng Xióng was mentioned in writing;
why is Āndé Wáng Xióng mentioned again here?
According to Xióng's biography,
after Xióng returned from campaigning against Tǔyùhún with the Emperor,
he was then enfeoffed as Guān Wáng.
At the time of Gāo Jǐng's execution,
Xióng was still Āndé Wáng.
The Zīzhì Tōngjiàn merely followed the old historical texts.
The Emperor changed Kuòzhōu to Jiāohé Jùn.
使,
shū lì fān.
降,
hù jiāng fān.
澆,
gǔ yáo fān.
Yǔwén Shù was enfeoffed as Xǔguó Gōng.
This was the city of Línqiāng Xiàn in the Hàn dynasty.
He dared not surrender,
but led his troops to flee westward;
Shù led his army in pursuit,
capturing the two cities of Màntóu and Chìshuǐ.
According to the Suí Zhì: When the Emperor pacified Tǔyùhún,
he established Héyuán Jùn at the old Chìshuǐ city,
and Màntóu city was under its jurisdiction.
曼,
sounds like wàn.
They captured two hundred people, from the king and dukes downwards,
and returned with four thousand male and female captives.
Fúyǔn fled south to Xuěshān.
This is the Western Snow Mountain to the west of the mountains of Shǔ.
Four thousand lǐ from east to west,
and two thousand lǐ from north to south,
all became territory of the Suí dynasty.
Zhōu,
Xiàn, Zhèn, and Shù were established.
Shànshàn, Qiěmò, Xīhǎi, and Héyuán four commanderies were established,
along with counties such as Xiǎnwǔ, Jìyuǎn, Sùníng, Fúrōng, Xuāndé, Wēidìng, Yuǎnhuà, and Chìshuǐ.
The Zhì states
that they were established in the fifth year.
12 In the eighth month,
on the day Xīnyǒu,
the Emperor personally offered sacrifices at Héngyuè.
Héngyuè is
the Northern Peak, Héngshān.
恆,
hù dēng fān.
The commandery governors of Héběi Dào all gathered,
and more than ten countries from the Western Regions, brought by Péi Jù, all came to assist in the sacrifice.
The Kǎoyì states: Péi Jù's biography says
"the third year,"
which is an error.
We now follow the Emperor's Annals.
13 In the ninth month,
on the day Xīnwèi,
an edict ordered all falconers in the realm to assemble in Dōngjīng.
Yīngshī refers to
those skilled in training eagles and falcons.
14 In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day Yǐmǎo,
new regulations were promulgated.
In the fourth month of last year, on the day Rénchén,
weights and measures were reformed,
all in accordance with ancient patterns,
and now they were promulgated throughout the realm.
15 Cháng Jùn and others arrived at the border of Chìtǔ.
Lìfùduōsāi, the King of Chìtǔ, sent an envoy with thirty ships to welcome them,
presenting a golden chain to moor Jùn's ship.
After sailing for over a hundred days,
and being in the territory for over a month,
they finally reached its capital.
The capital of Chìtǔ was called Sēngzhī Chéng.
The utensils
were extremely precious and beautiful,
and the envoys were treated with great courtesy.
The king sent his son Náyéjiā to accompany Jùn to pay tribute.
16 The Emperor appointed Xuē Shìxióng of Hédōng, the Right Protector-General of the Palace Guard, as the Grand General of the Marching Army for the Yùmén Dao.
The Emperor changed Púzhōu to Hédōng Jùn.
According to the Suí Zhì: Yùmén Xiàn belonged to Dūnhuáng Jùn.
The title Xíngjūn Zǒngguǎn was changed to Xíngjūn Dàjiàng.
將,
jí liàng fān.
The army marched out from Yùmén,
but Qǐmín did not arrive.
Shìxióng's isolated army crossed the desert.
Yīwú initially thought the Suí army could not reach them,
so they made no preparations;
upon hearing that Shìxióng's army had already crossed the desert,
they were greatly afraid,
and requested to surrender.
Liúshā is also called Qì.
磧,
qī jì fān.
降,
hù jiāng fān.
He left Wáng Wēi, a Silver-Green Guanglù Dàfū, with over a thousand armored soldiers to guard it, and then returned.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the day Bǐngzǐ,
Dōngjīng was renamed Dōngdū.
2 The Khagan Qǐmín of the Tujue came to pay respects at court,
and the gifts bestowed were even more generous.
3 On the day Guǐwèi,
an edict ordered the equalization of land throughout the realm.
4 On the day Wùzǐ,
the Emperor returned west from Dōngdū.
5 On the day Jǐchǒu,
an edict prohibited all private iron forks, grappling hooks, and bladed tools.
6 In the second month,
on the day Wùshēn,
the imperial carriage arrived at Xīkīng.
7 In the third month,
on the day Jǐsì,
he made a western tour to Héyòu;
on the day Yǐhài,
he visited his old residence in Fúfēng.
Héyòu refers to
the area of Wǔwēi and other commanderies west of the river.
The Emperor changed Qízhōu to Fúfēng Jùn.
In the fourth month,
on the day Guǐhài,
he departed through Línjīn Guān.
Línjīn Guān should be in the Fāohǎn area,
by a ford on the river.
The Shuǐ Jīng Zhù states: The Héshǔi flows eastward from Jiāohé,
passing south of Hánchuān Chéng,
then eastward passing north of Línjīn Chéng,
and south of Báitǔ Chéng,
serving as a crossing point along the river.
Upon reaching Xīpíng,
he deployed troops and practiced military drills,
intending to attack Tǔyùhún.
In the fifth month,
on the day Yǐhài,
the Emperor went on a great hunt in Báiyán Shān.
According to the Suí Zhì: In Huàlóng Xiàn of Xīpíng Jùn, there is Báiyán Shān.
Dù Yòu states: Báiyán Shān is in Guǎngwēi Xiàn of Kuòzhōu,
Emperor Yáng of Suí passed this mountain when campaigning against Tǔhún.
吐,
from tūn rùshēng.
谷,
sounds like yù.
The Kǎoyì states: The Suí Dì Jì says:
"two thousand lǐ,"
suspected to be a mistake for "twenty lǐ."
On the day Gēngchén,
he entered Chángníng Gǔ.
Chángníng Gǔ is in the area of the ancient Jìnchāng Jùn.
The Shuǐ Jīng Zhù states: The Huángshuǐ flows past the old city of Línqiāng Xiàn to the south,
then eastward,
where Chángníng Chuānshuǐ flows into it.
Chángníng Shuǐ flows southeast past Jìnchāng Chuān,
and there is also Chángníng Tíng.
North of the pavilion is Yǎngnǚ Lǐng,
which is the northern mountain of Hào-Wěi and Xīpíng.
On the day Bǐngxū,
he reached Hào-Wěi Chuān.
The Shuǐ Jīng Zhù states: Hào-Wěi Hé flows out from beyond the frontier,
passes through Xiān Gǔ Sài of Xīpíng,
then eastward passing southeast of Yǎngnǚ Běishān.
According to the Suí Zhì: In Huángshuǐ Xiàn of Xīpíng Jùn, there is the old Hào-Wěi Xiàn.
浩亹,
sounds like gào mén.
浩,
also sounds like gé.
He executed Huáng Gèn, the Dūshuǐ Shǐzhě, and nine supervisors.
The Emperor changed Dūshuǐ Jiān to Dūshuǐ Shǐzhě.
The Kǎoyì states: The Suí Dì Jì says:
"At Liáng Hào-Wěi,
imperial horses crossed, and the bridge collapsed."
We now follow the concise record.
Only when the bridge was completed
did they proceed.
Yùyùnhún Kèhán Fúyǔn (吐谷渾可汗伏允) led his host to secure Fùyuánchuān (覆袁川).
可,
from kān (刊) in the entering tone.
汗,
read hán (寒).
帥,
read shuài (率).
The Minister of War, Duàn Wénzhèn (段文振), camped in the north at Xuěshān (雪山).
The Grand Minister of the Imperial Stud, Yáng Yìchén (楊義臣), camped in the east at Pípáxiá (琵琶峽).
General Zhāng Shòu (張壽) camped in the west at Nílíng (泥嶺).
They surrounded him on all four sides.
Fúyǔn (伏允) escaped with several tens of horsemen.
He sent his distinguished prince to falsely claim to be Fúyǔn (伏允),
and secure Chēwǒzhēnshān (車我真山).
On the day Rénchén (壬辰),
an imperial edict ordered the Grand General of the Right Palace Guard, Zhāng Dìnghé (張定和), to go and capture him.
Zhāng Dìnghé (張定和) underestimated the small number of their troops,

The Yùyùnhún (吐谷渾) ambushers shot and killed him.
His deputy general, Liǔ Wǔjiàn (柳武建), attacked the Yùyùnhún (吐谷渾)
and defeated them.
On the day Jiǎwǔ (甲午),
the Yùyùnhún (吐谷渾) Xiāntóu Wáng Qióngcu (仙頭王窮䠞),
䠞,

In the sixth month,
on the day Dīngyǒu (丁酉),
Liáng Mò (梁默) and others, Left Grand Master of Glorious Happiness, were sent to pursue and attack Fúyǔn (伏允).
Their army was defeated
and they were killed by Fúyǔn (伏允).
The Minister of the Imperial Guard, Liú Quán (劉權),
set out through the Yīwú (伊吾) pass,

The Suí Zhì (隋志) states: Xīhǎi Jùn (西海郡) has Qīnghǎi (青海).
The Yùyùnhún Zhuàn (吐谷渾傳) states: Qīnghǎi (青海) is east of Fúsì Chéng (伏俟城),

Taking advantage of their victory, they pursued the fleeing enemy

The Yùyùnhún (吐谷渾) capital, Fúsì Chéng (伏俟城),
is fifteen *lǐ* west of Qīnghǎi (青海).
On the day Xīnchǒu (辛丑),
the Emperor said to the Attendant Gentleman Cài Zhēng (蔡徵):
"Since ancient times, emperors have had the ritual of inspection tours.
However, many emperors south of the Yangtze River would apply makeup,
sit in their deep palaces,
and not meet the common people.
What is the reason for this?"
He replied:
"This is why they could not maintain their reigns for long."
On the day Bǐngwǔ (丙午),
he arrived at Zhāngyè (張掖).
The Emperor renamed Gānzhōu (甘州) to Zhāngyè Jùn (張掖郡).
He ordered Péi Jǔ (裴矩) to persuade the King of Gāochāng (高昌), Qū Bóyǎ (麴伯雅),

說,

and the Tǔtún Shè (吐屯設),

On the day Rénzǐ (壬子),
the Emperor arrived at Yānzhīshān (燕支山).
The Suí Zhì (隋志) states: Wǔwēi Jùn (武威郡) Fānhé Xiàn (番禾縣) has Yānzhīshān (燕支山).
啗,

朝,

He ordered everyone to wear gold and jade,
don brocade and felt,

The Emperor further ordered the men and women of Wǔwēi (武威) and Zhāngyè (張掖) to dress splendidly and watch freely.
For those whose clothes, carriages, and horses were not fresh,

The cavalry and mounts were so numerous they blocked the way,
stretching for dozens of *lǐ*,
to show the prosperity of China.
The Tǔtún Shè (吐屯設) offered thousands of *lǐ* of land in the Western Regions.
The Emperor was greatly pleased.
On the day Guǐchǒu (癸丑),
the commanderies of Xīhǎi (西海), Héyuán (河源), Shànshàn (鄯善), and Qiěmò (且末) were established.
Xīhǎi Jùn (西海郡) was established at Fúsì Chéng (伏俟城).
Héyuán Jùn (河源郡) was established at Chǐshuǐ Chéng (赤水城).
Shànshàn Jùn (鄯善郡) was established at the old Lóulán Chéng (樓蘭城).
Qiěmò Jùn (且末郡) was established at the old Qiěmò Chéng (且末城).

鄯,

且,

He ordered Liú Quán (劉權) to guard the Jīshí Zhèn (積石鎮) in Héyuán Jùn (河源郡).
The Zhì (志) states: Héyuán Jùn (河源郡) has Jīshíshān (積石山),
where the river originates.
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: Jīshíshān (積石山) is south of Lóngzhī Xiàn (龍支縣) in Xīpíng Jùn (西平郡).
He was to defend against the Yùyùnhún (吐谷渾)
and keep the road to the Western Regions open.
At this time, there were a total of one hundred and ninety commanderies
and one thousand two hundred and fifty-five counties in the empire,
with over eight million nine hundred thousand households.
It stretched nine thousand three hundred *lǐ* from east to west,
and fourteen thousand eight hundred and fifteen *lǐ* from north to south.
The prosperity of the Suí (隋) dynasty
reached its peak here.
The Emperor considered Péi Jǔ (裴矩) to have a strategy for conciliation and pacification,
and promoted him to the rank of Yínqīng Guānglù Dàfū (銀青光祿大夫).
From the various counties in Xījīng (西京) and the various commanderies in the northwest,
all tribute was transported beyond the frontier,
amounting to hundreds of millions annually.
For those who died due to dangerous and distant routes or encounters with bandits and raiders,
or whose livestock died and failed to arrive,
the commanderies and counties would confiscate their families' property.
Because of this, the common people lost their livelihoods,
and the western regions suffered first.
Initially,
Yùyùnhún (吐谷渾) Fúyǔn (伏允) sent his son Shùn (順) to pay respects at court.
吐,

谷,

When Fúyǔn (伏允) was defeated and fled,
having no means to support himself,
he led several thousand horsemen to seek refuge with the Dǎngxiàng (党項).
The Suí Shū (隋書) states: The Dǎngxiàng Qiāng (党項羌) are descendants of Sānmiáo (三苗).
Their tribes include Dàngchāng (宕昌) and Báiláng (白狼),
all claiming to be descendants of macaques.
They bordered Líntáo (臨洮) and Xīpíng (西平) to the east,
and resisted Yèhù (葉護) to the west.
They stretched for thousands of *lǐ* from north to south,
residing in mountain valleys.
Each surname formed a separate tribe.
帥,
read shuài (率).
党,

可,
from kān (刊) in the entering tone.
汗,

He ordered him to take command of the remaining troops,
and appointed his Grand King, Níluòzhōu (尼洛周), as his assistant.
When they reached Xīpíng (西平),
his subordinates killed Níluòzhōu (尼洛周),
and Shùn (順) was unable to enter and returned.
On the day Bǐngchén (丙辰),
the Emperor presided at Guānfēng Diàn (觀風殿),
which was also the Guānfēng Xíngdiàn (觀風行殿).
He invited Qū Bóyǎ (麴伯雅), King of Gāochāng (高昌), and the Yīwú (伊吾) Tǔtún Shè (吐屯設) to ascend the hall for a banquet.
The Kǎoyì (考異) states: The brief record is on the day Rén Yín (壬寅) in the sixth month.
We now follow the Suí Dìjì (隋帝紀).
The Nine-Part Music was performed.
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: Emperor Yáng (煬帝) established the Qīngyuè (清樂), Gūcí (龜茲), Xīliáng (西涼), Tiānzhú (天竺), Kāngguó (康國), Shūlè (疏勒), Ānguó (安國), Gāolí (高麗), and Lǐbì (禮畢) as the nine parts.
使,
read shū lì (疏吏).
Gifts were bestowed according to their ranks.
On the day Wùwǔ (戊午),
a general amnesty was proclaimed.
The Yùyùnhún (吐谷渾) had Qīnghǎi (青海).
It was popularly believed that if mares were placed there,
they would obtain dragon offspring.
The Yùyùnhún Zhuàn (吐谷渾傳) states: There is a small mountain in Qīnghǎi (青海).
It was customary for their people to release mares there every winter,
saying they would obtain dragon offspring.
The Yùyùnhún (吐谷渾) once obtained Persian grass horses
and released them into Qīnghǎi (青海).
As a result, a dappled colt was born
that could travel a thousand *lǐ* a day.
It was then called Qīnghǎi Cōng (青海驄).
種,
read zhāng yǒng (章勇).
In the seventh month,
a horse pasture was established at Qīnghǎi (青海).
Two thousand mares were released into the valleys to seek dragon offspring,
but without effect, so it was stopped.
The imperial carriage returned east.
It passed through Dàdǒubágǔ.
The mountain path was narrow and dangerous;
they advanced in a single file, like fish on a string,
one after another,
just like strung fish.
The civil and military officials were hungry, cold, and wet.
Late at night, they couldn't reach the front camp.
Dài (逮)
means jí (及, to reach).
Kǎoyì (考異) says: "The Dìjì (帝紀) records this in the guǐmǎo (癸卯) month of the sixth month.
However, although the western regions are cold,
it is not possible for there to be heavy snow in the sixth month,
freezing people and livestock to death.
Therefore, we follow the Lǜejì (略記) here."
The Lǜejì (略記) writes Dádí Bágǔ (達十拔谷);
we follow the Dìjì (帝紀) now.
The imperial concubines and princesses sometimes became lost in disarray,
sleeping mixed with the soldiers in the mountains.
In the ninth month,
on the yǐ
wèi (乙未) day,
the imperial carriage entered Xījīng (西京).
In winter,
the eleventh month,
on the bǐng zǐ (丙子) day,
the emperor again visited Dōngdū (東都).
Pèi Yùn (裴蘊), Assistant Minister of the Mínbù (民部), reported that there were still many unregistered households and fraudulently recorded old and young individuals in the public registers.
He proposed a visual inspection (màoyue 貌閱),
stating that if even one person was found to be incorrectly registered,
the official in charge would be dismissed.
He also allowed commoners to report unregistered able-bodied men (dīng 丁),
in which case the family reported would be forced to pay the taxes and provide the labor service on behalf of the informer.
That year,
the registers submitted by all commanderies showed an increase of two hundred
three thousand able-bodied men,
and six hundred forty-one thousand five hundred newly registered individuals.
The emperor, examining the reports at court,
said to his officials:
"Previous dynasties lacked talented individuals,
which led to such deception and fraud.
Now, the household registration is accurate,
entirely due to Pèi Yùn."
From this, Pèi Yùn (裴蘊) gradually gained trust and favor.
Before long,
he was promoted to Yùshǐ Dàfū (御史大夫),
and, along with Pèi Jǔ (裴矩) and Yú Shìjī (虞世基), he participated in handling confidential matters.
Yùn (蘊) was skilled at observing the subtle intentions of the ruler.
If the emperor desired to condemn someone,
he would bend the law to fabricate their guilt.
If the emperor wished to pardon someone,
he would follow lesser statutes
and release them accordingly.
Thereafter, all major and minor cases
were entrusted to Yùn (蘊).
The Xíngbù (刑部) and Dàlǐ (大理) dared not contend with him;
they had to report to him for instructions and decisions
before they could make a final judgment.
Yùn (蘊) possessed astute eloquence;
his words flowed like a cascading river.
Whether a case was made severe or lenient
all depended on his words.
His analysis was clear and sharp,
and people of his time could not challenge him.
The Shū (書) says:
"He who knows men is wise,
and he can appoint officials."
The historian is referring to the difficulty of knowing men and being good at appointing them.
The Qǐmín Kèhán (啟民可汗) of the Tūjué (突厥) died.
The emperor suspended court for three days on his behalf.
He established his son Duōjí (咄吉),
who became Shǐbì Kèhán (始畢可汗).
He sent a memorial requesting to marry a princess,
and an imperial edict permitted it according to their custom.
Initially, Xuē Dàohéng (薛道衡), Assistant Minister of the Nèishǐ (內史), was renowned for his talent and scholarship.
He had long held important positions.
At the end of Gāozǔ's (高祖) reign,
he was sent out as the Zǒngguǎn (總管) of Xiāngzhōu (襄州).
The emperor changed Xiāngzhōu (襄zhou) to Xiāngyáng Jùn (襄陽郡).
He was summoned from his post as the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Fānzhōu (番州).
The Suí Zhì (隋志) states: "Guǎngzhōu (廣州) was renamed Fānzhōu (番州) in the first year of Rénshòu (仁壽).
It was probably named after Pānyú (番禺) as a prefecture.
The emperor changed it to Nánhǎi Jùn (南海郡)."
Fān (番)
is pronounced pān (潘) according to the Hànshū Yīnyì (漢書音義).
Upon Dàohéng's (道衡) arrival,
he presented a eulogy to Emperor Gāozǔ Wén (高祖文).
The emperor, upon reading it,
was displeased.
He turned to Sū Wēi (蘇威) and said,
"Dàohéng (道衡) greatly praises the former court."
Zhì (致)
means jí (極, extremely).
The Shī Xiǎoxù (詩小序) says: "Yú Zǎo (魚藻) criticizes King Yōu (幽王).
It says that all things have lost their nature,
and the king resides in Hàojīng (鎬京),
unable to find joy.
Therefore, the gentleman thinks of the ancient King Wǔ (武王)."
"I will have him punished."
Fáng Yànqiān (房彥謙), the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Sīlì (司隸), advised Dàohéng (道衡) to cut off contact with guests
and adopt a humble and submissive demeanor.
The emperor appointed one Sīlì Dàfū (司隸大夫)
to be the head of the Sīlì Tái (司隸臺).
He also appointed fourteen Sīlì Cìshǐ (司隸刺史),
of Zheng Liùpǐn (正六品) rank,
to inspect the commanderies outside the capital region.
When discussing the new regulations,
a decision was long delayed.
Dàohéng (道衡) said to the court officials,
"If Gāo Jǐng (高熲) had not died,
these regulations would have been implemented long ago."
Someone reported this to the emperor.
The emperor angrily said,
"You remember Gāo Jǐng (高熲)?!"
He handed him over to the law enforcement officials for investigation.
Tuī (推)
means xúnyì (尋繹, to investigate thoroughly);
to investigate and examine the matter.
"Dàohéng (道衡) relies on his talent and old connections,
harboring disloyal intentions towards the sovereign.
He attributes evil to the state,
wantonly creating trouble.
Discussing his crime by name
seems obscure,
but examining his true intentions,
it is deeply rebellious."
The emperor said,
"Indeed.
When I was young and campaigned with him,"
referring to the time when Chén (陳) was conquered,
Shào (少)
is read zhào (照) in Pīnyīn.
"he and Gāo Jǐng (高熲), Hè Ruòbì (賀若弼) and others wielded outward authority.
When I ascended the throne,
he felt uneasy.
Fortunately, the empire was peaceful,
and he had no opportunity to rebel.
Your assessment of his rebellion
perfectly captures his true heart."
Dàohéng (道衡), believing that his offense was not a major one,
urged the Xìansī (憲司, Censorate) to quickly pass judgment.
He hoped that when the report was submitted, the emperor would pardon him.
He instructed his family to prepare a feast
for guests who would come to congratulate him.
When the report was submitted,
the emperor ordered him to commit suicide.
Dàohéng (道衡) was utterly surprised
and unable to bring himself to do it.
The Xìansī (憲司) submitted another memorial,
and he was strangled to death.
His wife and children were exiled to Qiěmò (且末).
The people of the empire felt injustice for him.
The emperor conducted a grand review of military equipment,
praising the beauty of the weapons and armor.
Yǔwén Shù (宇文述) then remarked,
"These are all the achievements of Yún Dìngxīng (雲定興)."
The emperor immediately promoted Dìngxīng (定興) to Tàifǔ Chéng (太府丞).
In spring,
the first month,
on the guǐ hài (癸亥) day, the first day of the month,
three *kè* (刻) before dawn,
several dozen bandits,
wearing plain caps and white clothes,
burning incense and holding flowers,
proclaimed themselves to be the Maitreya Buddha.
They entered through the Jiànguó Mén (建國門).
Buddhist teachings
hold that when the Śākyamuni Buddha declines,
the Maitreya Buddha will appear in the world.
Therefore, the bandits used this name to commit their crimes.
Jiànguó Mén (建國門) was probably the Duānmén (端門) of the imperial city in Dōngdū (東都).
The Táng Liùdiǎn (唐六典) states: "In the fifth year of Wǔdé (武德), Wáng Shìchōng (王世充) was pacified.
Disliking its grandeur,
the Gānyáng Diàn (乾陽殿) and Jiànguó Mén (建國門) were burned."
Huá (華)
is read huā (花).
Kǎoyì (考異) says: "Zájì (雜記) places this in the first month of the fifth year,
and also says
'three hundred people'."
We follow the Suí Shū (隋書) here.
Subsequently, they seized weapons from the guards
and were about to cause chaos,
but Qí Wáng (齊王) Lián (暕) encountered and executed them.
Consequently, a major search was conducted throughout the capital,
and over a thousand families were implicated.
2 Since the chieftains of various foreign tribes had all gathered in Luòyáng,
on the dìngchǒu day,
in the street outside Duānmén Gate
(the street outside the Duānmén Gate of the imperial city of Luòyáng),
a theater area measuring five thousand paces in circumference
hosted eighteen thousand musicians playing string and wind instruments.
Their sound was heard for dozens of *lǐ*,
from dusk till dawn,
with lanterns and torches illuminating the heavens and earth.
The festivities lasted for a full month before ceasing,
costing enormous sums.
From then on, it became an annual custom.
(The dìngchǒu day
was the fifteenth day of the first month.
The enjoyment of the Yuánxiāo Lantern Festival by people today
likely began to flourish from this time.)
The various foreign tribes requested to enter the Fēngdū Market to trade.
(The eastern market of Dōngdū was called Fēngdū,
the southern market was called Dàtóng,
and the northern market was called Tōngyuǎn.)
An order was first given to tidy up the shops and stalls;
their eaves and structures were made uniform.
Lavish canopies and curtains were set up,
and precious goods were piled high.
People and objects presented a splendid sight.
Even vegetable sellers were provided with *lóngxū* mats.
(*Lóngxū* mats are woven from *lóngxū* grass.
Today, many residents of Ānqìng Prefecture along the Huái River are skilled at weaving *lóngxū* mats.)
All foreign guests were invited to sit,
and after eating and drinking to their fill, they departed.
No payment was taken,
and they were deceived by saying:
"China is abundant and prosperous;
food and drink are customarily free."
The foreign guests were all astonished and praised it.
However, the clever ones somewhat perceived the truth.
Seeing trees wrapped with silk,
they said:
"China also has poor people
whose clothes do not cover their bodies.
Why not give these materials to them?
What is the point of wrapping them around trees?"
The market people were ashamed and could not answer.
The Emperor praised Péi Jù's ability,
saying to his attendants:
"Péi Jù deeply understands my intentions.
Whatever he presents and advises on
are all my preconceived plans;
before I even express them,
Jù immediately brings them to my attention.
If not for his devoted service to the country,
who could be like this!"

At this time, Jù, along with Yǔwén Shù, the Grand General of the Right Yìwèi, Yú Shìjī, the Aide in the Bureau of Internal Affairs, Péi Yùn, the Grand Censor, and Guō Yǎn, the Grand Master of Guanglù, were all favored for their flattery.
Shù was good at serving the Emperor,
his demeanor and conduct were obsequious,
and all the attendants guarding the Emperor took him as an example.
Guō Yǎn once advised the Emperor to hold court every five days,
saying:
"There is no need to emulate Gāozǔ
and toil oneself unnecessarily."
The Emperor considered him even more loyal,
saying:
"Only Guō Yǎn shares the same heart as me."
When the Emperor held court, he was solemn and grave;
his pronouncements and edicts
were admirable in their words and meaning.
However, inwardly he indulged in sensual pleasures.
When he was in the two capitals or on tours,
he always had monks, nuns, Taoist priests, and female officials accompanying him.
(Female officials
were female Taoist priests.)
Xiāo Jù, Duke of Liáng (who was
a nephew of Cóng),
and Yǔwén Xiǎo, the Right Grand Master of the Thousand Oxen (who was
a grandson of Qìng),
(according to the Suí system,
there were twelve Left and Right Guards of the Thousand Oxen,
in charge of imperial bows and arrows.
Yǔwén Qìng is mentioned in volume 173, in the eleventh year of Tàijiàn of Chén Gāozōng.
Xiǎo's
pronunciation is *hù liǎo*.)
The Emperor daily lavishly laid out wine and food in the pavilions and groves of the imperial park.
He ordered Yàn Wáng Tán, Jù, Xiǎo, and Gāozǔ's concubines to sit at one table;
monks, nuns, Taoist priests, and female officials at another;
and the Emperor himself with his favorite concubines at a third.
The tables were loosely connected.
As soon as court adjourned, they would join these banquets.
During the feasts, they would urge each other to drink and eat,
and when drunk and amidst the disorderly dishes,
no impropriety was left undone.
This became the norm.
Beautiful women from the Yáng clan
were often brought into his presence.
Xiǎo entered and exited the palace at will,
unrestrained by palace restrictions.
Even the imperial concubines and princesses suffered scandalous reputations,
yet the Emperor did not punish him for it.
3 The Emperor again dispatched Zhū Kuān to persuade Liúqiú to submit.
Liúqiú refused to comply.
The Emperor then sent Chén Líng of Lújiāng, a Tiger-Wolf General, and Zhāng Zhènzhōu of Tóng'ān, an Aide in the Bureau of Court Review, to lead over ten thousand soldiers from Dōngyáng.
They sailed from Yì'ān to attack it.
After sailing for over a month,
they reached its country,
with Zhènzhōu as the vanguard.
Kělàdōu, the King of Liúqiú,
dispatched troops to meet them in battle.
They were repeatedly defeated,
and thus the expedition reached their capital.
The residence of the King of Liúqiú was called the Póluódàn Cave.
It had three layers of moats and palisades,
surrounded by flowing water,
and thorn bushes as a fence.
Again defeated,
they retreated into the palisades.
Líng and others, taking advantage of their victory, attacked and captured it,
beheading Kělàdōu and
capturing over ten thousand of its people before returning.
In the second month,
on the yǐsì day,
Líng and others presented the Liúqiú captives.
The hundred officials were given rewards,
Líng was promoted to Right Grand Master of Guānglù,
and Zhènzhōu to Gold-Purple Grand Master of Guānglù.
4 On the yǐmǎo day,
an edict was issued stating:
"In recent times, the granting of feudal lands has been arbitrary,
with names and reality diverging.
From now on, only those with meritorious achievements may be granted enfeoffments,
and their descendants may inherit them."
Consequently, the previously granted five ranks of nobility
for those without merit were all abolished.
5 On the gēngshēn day,

6 In the third month,

7 Previously,

"In recent years, labor has been excessive,

Later, he looked at Héng and said to his attendants:

He then compiled a record of Qí Wáng Jiǎn taking Huángfǔ Xǔ with him on the imperial retinue, and when the Emperor previously visited Zhuōjùn to offer sacrifices at Héngyuè, many of the elders who came to pay respects had disheveled clothing and caps.
He reproached Héng for the Censorate's inability to correct such matters.
(Zhāng Héng was the Grand Censor,
hence he was reprimanded for the duties of the Censorate.)
After a long time,
Héng supervised the construction of the Lóufán city.

Lóufán Commandery was established,
which was the former Lán Prefecture of the Latter Wèi.

At that time, Fényáng Palace was built there,
hence the city was constructed.)
(*Shǒu* is pronounced *shì yòu*.)
Héng was able to have an audience with the Emperor.
The Emperor disliked that Héng had not lost weight,
believing he was not contemplating his faults.
He said to Héng:
"You are very robust and healthy.
You should return to your commandery for now."
He then dispatched him to Yúlín.
Not long after,
an edict ordered Héng to supervise the construction of the Jiāngdū Palace.
When Yáng Xuángǎn, Minister of Rites, sent an envoy to Jiāngdū,
Héng said to Xuángǎn:
"Xuē Dàohéng truly died unjustly."
Xuángǎn reported this to the Emperor.
Wáng Shìchōng, the Administrator of Jiāngdū Commandery, also reported that Héng frequently reduced the provisions.
The Emperor then became enraged.
He was shackled and brought to the Jiāngdū market,
intending to execute him.
After a long time, he was released,

Wáng Shìchōng was appointed to oversee the Jiāngdū Palace.
Wang Shìchōng 王世充 was originally a Hú 胡 (non-Han people) from the Western Regions.
His surname was Zhī 支.
His father was Shōu 收.
When he was young, his mother married into the Wáng 王 family,
so he took their surname.
Shìchōng 世充 was cunning and deceitful,
possessed rhetorical skill,
was well-versed in books and historical records,
fond of military strategy,
and practiced law.
The Emperor frequently visited Jiāngdū 江都.
Shìchōng 世充 was skilled at observing facial expressions and flattering,
ornamenting ponds and terraces,
and presenting rare treasures.
Because of this, he gained favor.
This laid the foundation for Wáng Shìchōng 王世充 to usurp power when the time was ripe.
Sī 伺 (to observe),
read as xiāng lì fān 相吏翻 (the pronunciation of 相 and 吏 combined).
8. In the summer,
sixth month,
on the jiǎyín 甲寅 day,
an imperial decree was issued that the Administrator of Jiāngdū 江都 would hold a rank equivalent to the Metropolitan Prefect.
According to the Suí 隋 system,
the Metropolitan Prefect was of the third rank, senior grade.
9. In the winter,
twelfth month,
on the jǐwèi 己未 day,
Niú Hóng 牛弘, the Xiàn Hóu 憲侯 of Wén'ān 文安, passed away.

Zú 卒 (to pass away),

His scholarship was profound and extensive.
Among the old officials of the Suí 隋 dynasty,
he was the only one
who was trusted from beginning to end,
and never caused any regret or blame.
His younger brother Bì 弼
was fond of wine and boorish.
Once, in a drunken state, he shot and killed the ox pulling Hóng's 弘 carriage.
When Hóng 弘 returned home,
his wife met him and said:
"Your younger brother shot and killed the ox."
Hóng 弘 showed no surprise or questioned it,
merely replied:
"Make jerky."
After he was seated,
his wife again said:
"Your younger brother suddenly shot and killed the ox,
this is a very strange matter!"
Hóng 弘 said:
"I already know."
His expression remained unchanged,
and he continued to read without interruption.
10. An imperial edict ordered the digging of the Jiāngnán Hé 江南河 (Southern River),

Kuài 會 (Kuàijī 會稽),
read as gǔ wài fān 古外翻 (the pronunciation of 古 and 外 combined).
11. The Emperor, seeing that all officials accompanying the imperial procession wore *kùzhě* 袴褶 (trousers and tunic)

in this year,

Those of the fifth rank and above

Those of the sixth rank and below
shall wear both crimson and green.

Zhù 著 (to wear),
read as zé lüè fān 則略翻 (the pronunciation of 則 and 略 combined).
Fēi 緋 (crimson),

Commoners wore white,

12. When the Emperor visited Qǐmín's 啟民 tent,
see volume three of the previous scroll.
Qǐmín 啟民 dared not conceal it,
and brought him to see the Emperor.
The Grand Guardian, Péi Jù 裴矩, persuaded the Emperor, saying:
"Gāolì 高麗 was originally the land enfeoffed to Jīzǐ 箕子.

and his state was passed down to his grandson Yòuqú 右渠.
Emperor Wǔ 武 of Hàn 漢 destroyed it
and established four commanderies.
At the end of Hàn 漢, Gōngsūn Dù 公孫度 occupied it,
and his state was passed down to his grandson Yuān 淵.
Wèi 魏 destroyed it,
and until Jìn 晉, it remained commanderies and counties.
The ancestors of Gāolì 高麗
originated from Fúyú 夫餘.
Zhūméng 朱蒙 established the state,
calling it Gāogōulí 高句驪,
and took Gāo 高 as their clan name.
Since Wèi 魏 and Jìn 晉,
with China embroiled in military chaos,
Gāolì 高麗 invaded
and seized the territory of Liáodōng 遼東.
Shuō 說 (to persuade),

How can we not take it,
and allow a land of robes and caps
to become a barbarian region!"
Now that their envoy has personally witnessed Qǐmín 啟民 and his entire nation submitting to our influence,
we can leverage their fear

The Emperor agreed.
He commanded Niú Hóng 牛弘 to convey the imperial decree, saying:
"Because I see Qǐmín's 啟民 sincere devotion to the state,

Next year, I will proceed to Zhuójùn 涿郡.
When you return, tell the King of Gāolì 高麗:
Do not
be suspicious or fearful.
The rites of preservation and nurturing
will be as they are for Qǐmín 啟民.
If, however, you do not pay homage,
I will lead Qǐmín 啟民 to tour your land."
The King of Gāolì 高麗 became fearful.
His vassal courtesies were quite lacking,
and the Emperor was preparing to punish him.
He assessed the wealthy people of the empire to buy warhorses,
with each horse costing up to one hundred thousand cash.
He inspected weapons and armor,
ensuring they were fine and new,
and if any were substandard or faulty,
the inspector would be immediately beheaded.
1. In the spring,
first month,
on the rén'yín 壬寅 day,
Guō Yǎn 郭衍, the Xiāng Hóu 襄侯 of Zhēndìng 真定, passed away.

Héngshān Jùn 恆山郡 was governed from Zhēndìng Xiàn 真定縣.

the Emperor journeyed from Jiāngdū 江都 to Zhuójùn 涿郡.

crossed the Yellow River and entered the Yǒngjì Qú 永濟渠.

He then commanded the officials of the four departments—Xuǎnbù 選部 (Personnel Department), Ménxià 門下 (Chancellery), Nèishǐ 內史 (Palace Secretariat), and Yùshǐ 御史 (Censorate)—to select and appoint new officials in front of the boats.
Over three thousand people were subjected to selection.
Some followed the boats on foot for over three thousand *lǐ* (li),
without receiving appointments.
They suffered from cold, hunger, and exhaustion,
and consequently, one or two out of ten died.

an imperial edict was issued to subjugate Gāolì.
An imperial command was given to Yuán Hóngsì, the Grand Administrator of Yōuzhōu.

Officials supervised the laborers,
who stood in the water day and night,
barely daring to rest.
From the waist down, maggots grew on all of them.
Three or four tenths of them died.

in the fourth month,
on the day of Gēngwǔ,
the imperial carriage arrived at Línshuò Gōng in Zhuójùn.

All were ordered to be provided with housing and settled.

regardless of distance,

is Zhuójùn.
Xiān,
rhymes with Xī.

belonged to Héjiān Jùn.
Chéng,
rhymes with Shéng Zhèng.
Soldiers were ordered to pull them themselves,

in the seventh month,
commoners from south of Jiāng and Huái, along with ships, were mobilized to transport rice from Líyáng and Luòkǒu granaries to Zhuójùn.
The prows and sterns of ships followed one another for over a thousand *lǐ*.
Carrying armor and tools for assault,
there were constantly several hundred thousand people on the road, going and coming,
clogging the roads,
day and night without cease.
The dead lay piled upon each other,
and the stench filled the roads.
The entire empire was in turmoil.

when the Emperor made his western tour,

Meaning that Shèkuì and Chǔluó would both submit to Suí.
"Your words are correct."

and said to him:

Yú (鄃)
was a Hàn (漢) dynasty county,
previously abolished.
In the sixteenth year of Kāihuáng (開皇), it was re-established,
and belonged to Qīnghé Jùn (清河郡).
Héqu (河曲)
refers to the bend of the Qīnghé (清河).
The *Xīn Táng Shū* (新唐書) writes
"Hézhǔ" (河渚).
Yú (鄃),
pronounced *shū* (輸).
Tiáo (蓨),
formerly called Xiū (脩).
In the fifth year of Kāihuáng (開皇), it was changed to belong to Xìndū Jùn (信都郡).
Tiáo (蓨),
pronounced *tiáo* (條).
He collected all of their family members
and killed them.
The *Xīn Shū* (新書) says: At that time, bandits moved through Zhāngnán (漳南),
plundering and killing people,
and burning villages.
However, they alone did not enter Jiàndé's (建德) village,
for which reason the commandery and county suspected him of colluding with the bandits.
Shì Dá (士達) proclaimed himself Dōnghǎi Gōng (東海公),
and made Jiàndé (建德) his Commander of Troops (司兵).
Soon after,
Sūn Ānzǔ (孫安祖) was killed by Zhāng Jīnchēng (張金稱).
All his followers went over to Jiàndé (建德),
and his army grew to over ten thousand men.
Jiàndé (建德) was able to humble himself and connect with people,
sharing their hardships and comforts with his soldiers.
Because of this, people vied to join him,
and were willing to die for him.
From then on, bandits sprang up like a swarm of bees everywhere,
too numerous to count.
Those with many followers reached over ten thousand,
attacking and capturing cities.
On the *jiǎzǐ* (甲子) day,
an imperial edict ordered the *Dūwèi* (都尉) and *Yīngyáng* (鷹揚) officials to cooperate with the commanderies and counties to pursue and arrest them.
The Suí (隋) dynasty established *Fèngchē* (奉車) and *Fùmǎ Dūwèi* (駙馬都尉),
belonging to the Three Guards (三衞).
The Emperor abolished them all.
This was probably setting up *Dūwèi* (都尉) to suppress the bandits.
The Emperor also changed *Piàojì* (驃騎) to *Yīngyáng Lángjiàng* (鷹揚郎將).
They were to be executed on the spot upon capture.
1. In spring,
the first month,
*Kǎo Yì* (考異) says: The *Luè Jì* (略記) states:
"On the *guǐchǒu* (癸丑) day,
the Emperor presided over the front hall."
According to the long calendar,
the first day of this month was *xīnsì* (辛巳).
There was no *guǐchǒu* (癸丑).
The *Luè Jì* (略記) often has errors in its *jiǎzǐ* (甲子) dating.
We do not use it here,
but follow the *Suí Shū* (隋書) in all cases.

A Tūjué (突厥) official,

In Míngshā Xiàn (鳴沙縣) of Líng Zhōu (靈州),
the Later Zhōu (後周) dynasty established Huì Zhōu (會州) and Huìníng Jùn (會寧郡),
which were soon abolished.
The Táng (唐) dynasty re-established them.
*Jiāng* (將),
pronounced *jí liàng* (即亮) fan (反);

*Léi* (羸),

"Dádù Què Shè" (達度闕設).
Here we follow the *Péi Jù Zhuàn* (裴矩傳).
Among Tūjué (突厥) officials,
princes and sons were *Tèlè* (特勒).
He was bestowed the title Hébō
Nà Kèhán (那可汗),
and given generous rewards.
2. Previously,
the Sōnggāo (嵩高) Daoist Pān Dàn (潘誕)
*Suí Zhì* (隋志): In Sōngyáng Xiàn (嵩陽縣) of Hénán Jùn (河南郡) there is Sōnggāo Shān (嵩高山).
was refining elixirs of immortality for the Emperor.
The Emperor built the Sōngyáng Guàn (嵩陽觀) for him,
with hundreds of magnificent rooms,
and assigned one hundred and twenty virgin boys and one hundred and twenty virgin girls to serve him,
their rank equivalent to a third-grade official.
Several thousand laborers were regularly employed,
and the expenses were enormous.
Pān Dàn (潘誕) claimed that the elixir required realgar and stalactite essence.
He had stonecutters excavate dozens of places in the large stones of Sōnggāo (嵩高) to a depth of one hundred *chǐ* (尺).
After six years,
the elixir was not completed.
The Emperor questioned him,
and Dàn (誕) replied:
"Without realgar and stalactite essence,
if I can obtain three *hú* (斛) and six *dǒu* (斗) each of the gall and marrow of virgin boys and girls,
they can substitute for it."
The Emperor was enraged,
arrested him and brought him to Zhuō Jùn (涿郡),
where he was executed.
Just before his death,
he told people:
"This is because the Son of Heaven has no fortune,
and the time for my 'military release' (兵解) has arrived.
I am to be reborn in Brahmaloka (梵摩天)."
3 Soldiers from all directions all assembled at Zhuójùn,
the Emperor summoned Yǔ Zhì, the Magistrate of Héshuǐ.
Yǔ Zhì came from Héshuǐ,
and had an audience with the Emperor in the fourth year.
"The forces of Gāolì cannot withstand a single commandery of mine.
Now, I will use these forces to attack them.
Do you think they can be conquered?"
He replied, saying:
"They can be conquered by attacking them.
However, your servant presumptuously has a humble opinion,
and does not wish for Your Majesty to go in person."
The Emperor showed displeasure and said:
"Now that I have gathered the troops here,
how can I retreat without even seeing the enemy first?"
He replied:
"If we fight but do not conquer,
I fear it will damage your imperial prestige.
If Your Majesty remains here,
and orders fierce generals and strong soldiers,
instructing them in strategy,
to travel at double speed,
taking them by surprise,
they will surely conquer them.
The opportunity lies in speed;
if slow, there will be no achievement."
The Emperor was displeased,
and said:
"Since you shrink from going,
you may stay here yourself."
Gěng Xún, Supervisor of the Right Imperial Manufactory Bureau, submitted a strongly-worded remonstrance.
The Jiānshì [Supervisor]
supervises the artisans,
with a rank of ninth grade.
The Emperor ordered his attendants to execute him,
but Hé Chóu earnestly pleaded for him,
and he was pardoned.
On the Rénwǔ day,
an imperial edict commanded the twelve armies of the left to proceed via the routes of Lòufāng, Chángcén, Mínghǎi, Gàimǎ, Jiàn'ān, Nánsū, Liáodōng, Xuántú, Fúyú, Cháoxiǎn, Wòjǔ, Lè Làng, and others.
The Emperor personally indicated the routes the various armies were to take,
mostly using old names of Hàn counties.
The Monograph on Geography of the Hàn Dynasty records: Lòufāng, Chángcén, and Cháoxiǎn
belonged to Lè Làng Commandery.
Gàimǎ
belonged to Xuántú Commandery;
there was Gàimǎ Mountain there.
Liáodōng
was a Hàn commandery name.
Mínghǎi
was probably Hǎimíng County of Hàn's Lè Làng Commandery.
Jiàn'ān, Nánsū, and Fúyú
were all places defended by cities of the Gāolì kingdom.
Wòjǔ
was also an ancient place name;
at that time its territory had already entered the borders of Xīnlúo.
The Monograph on Geography of the Hàn Dynasty records: Niánchán, Hánzī, Húnmí, Tíxī, Dōngyí, Dàifāng, and other counties
belonged to Lè Làng Commandery.
Hòuchéng and Xiāngpíng
belonged to Liáodōng Commandery.
Líntún
was also a commandery name established by Emperor Wǔ of Hàn.
Tàdùn
was where Tàdùn of the Wūwán from Liáoxī resided at the end of the Hàn Dynasty.
Sùshèn
was the country of the ancient Sùshèn people;
its land was at that time inhabited by the Mòhé.
Jiéshí
was the Jiéshí of Yǔ Gòng.
Dù Yòu believed this Jiéshí was within Gāolì.
Dù Yòu said: Mount Jiéshí
was in Suìchéng County of Hàn's Lè Làng Commandery;
the Qín Great Wall started from this mountain.
Now it is verified that the Great Wall extended east, cutting across the Liáo River and entering Gāolì;
its remains still exist.
Píngrǎng City
was the capital of the Gāolì kingdom,
also called Cháng'ān City.
It was six *lǐ* from east to west,
winding along the mountains,
and on its south bordered the Pèi River.
Dù Yòu said: The King of Gāolì had resided in Píngrǎng City since the Eastern Jìn Dynasty,
which was Wángxiǎn City of Hàn's Lè Làng Commandery.
Proclaimed to be two million,
those who supplied provisions were twice that number.
Sacrifices were made to the God of Earth on the southern Sānggān River,
and to the Lord on High south of Línshuò Palace.
The 'Wángzhì' records: When the Son of Heaven is about to set out,
he sacrifices to the Lord on High
and sacrifices to the God of Earth.
Zhèng's Commentary states: *Lèi* and *Yí*
are both names of sacrifices.
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: The way of Heaven is distant,
so one makes offerings and reports to it by means of corresponding rites.
The God of Earth governs killing,
therefore, one seeks convenience.
The God of Earth governs *yin*;
all things are here cut off and killed,
therefore it is called *yí*.
The Sānggān River
passes south of Jìchéng.
The Classic of Waters records: The Shī River originates from Yīnguǎn County of Yànmén,
flows northeast through Sānggān County of Dàijùn,
where it is called Sānggān River,
then east past the north of Jì County of Guǎngyáng.
Now it is south of Jìchéng;
the cities and towns have undergone changes.
The Rites of Zhōu records sacrifices to Mǎzǔ.
Zhèng's Commentary says: Mǎzǔ
are the Heavenly Steeds.
There were forty cavalry units,
each unit one hundred men;
ten units formed a regiment.
Eighty infantry units
were divided into four regiments;
each regiment had one deputy general.
Their armor, helmet plumes, and banners
were of different colors for each regiment.
There was one envoy for receiving surrender,
who received imperial edicts to console and pacify,
and was not subject to the control of the supreme commander.
Their baggage trains, dispersed soldiers, etc., were also formed into four regiments,
making infantry escort them as they marched.
Advancing, stopping, and establishing camps
all had ordered procedures and regulations.
On the Guǐwèi day,
the first army departed;
one army was dispatched each day,
forty *lǐ* apart from each other,
continuously establishing camps as they gradually advanced.
After forty days,
all had departed.
Head to tail, they followed one another;
drums and horns were heard from one to the next,
and banners and flags stretched for nine hundred sixty *lǐ*.
The imperial camp comprised the Twelve Guards, Three Bureaus, Five Departments, and Nine Courts,
divided and assigned to the Inner, Outer, Front, Rear, Left, and Right Six Armies,
which departed next,
stretching for another eighty *lǐ*.
The grandeur of this recent ancient military expedition
had never been seen before.
4 On the Jiǎchén day,
Yuán Shòu, the Director of the Palace Secretariat, passed away.

on the Rénxū day,
Guāndé King Xióng passed away.
Guān King Xióng
was posthumously named Dé.
6 Běipíng Xiānghóu Duàn Wénzhèn was appointed Minister of War.
He submitted a memorial,
believing that the Emperor
"treats the Tujue with excessive favor,
placing them within the frontier,
supplying them with soldiers and provisions.
The nature of the Rong and Di is to be
without kinship and greedy.
In the future, they will certainly become a national menace.
It is fitting to admonish and dispatch them in due course,
ordering them to go outside the frontier.
Thereafter, clearly establish beacon towers,
guard and defend along the borders,
ensuring strictness and seriousness.
This is a long-term strategy for ten thousand years."
Hú Sīzhèng, a secretary in the Ministry of War (Bīngcáo Láng),
was the grandson of Hú Sīchūn.
The Emperor changed the title of the various departmental secretaries (Zhūcáo Shìláng) in the ministries to Láng.
The Bīngcáo Láng
was the Bīngbù Shìláng of the Kāihuáng era.
Hú Sīchūn
was the one who sowed discord between Emperor Xiàowǔ of Later Wèi and Gāo Huān.
Hú Sīzhèng was favored and trusted by the Emperor,
who assigned him sole charge of military affairs.
Wénzhèn knew that Zhèng was treacherous and unreliable,
and should not be entrusted with crucial matters.
He repeatedly spoke to the Emperor about this,
but the Emperor did not listen.
When Gāolì was to be campaigned against,
Wénzhèn was made Zuǒ Hòuwèi Dàjiāngjūn,
advancing along the Nánsū Road.
Wénzhèn fell gravely ill on the way,
and submitted a memorial saying:
"I have observed that the petty savages of Liáodōng
have not yet submitted to severe punishment.
Our six armies have traveled afar,
and Your Majesty has personally toiled.
However, the barbarians are often deceitful,
and great caution is required in preparation.
If they express surrender orally,
it should not be accepted hastily.
The rainy season is approaching,
and we cannot delay too long.
I only wish that all armies be sternly ordered
to advance swiftly like shooting stars.
Both land and naval forces should proceed together,
taking them by surprise.
Then Píngrǎng, an isolated city,
can likely be captured.
If its roots are overturned,
the remaining cities will be conquered themselves.
If it is not settled in time,
and we encounter autumn rains,
it will become extremely difficult.
With military provisions exhausted
and a strong enemy in front,
and the Mòhé emerging from behind,
hesitation and indecision
would not be the best strategy."
In the third month,
on the Xīnmǎo day,
Wénzhèn died.
The Emperor deeply lamented his passing.
7 On the Guǐsì day,

All the armies gathered

The Gāolì soldiers blocked the water and defended,

Zuǒtúnwèi Dàjiāngjūn Mài Tiězhàng said to others:
"A man's life has its proper end.
How can one burn moxa on the bridge of one's nose,

and die in the hands of one's children!"
黃 (Huáng)
refers to a hot illness.
Heat causes headaches,
so moxa is burned to cauterize the bridge of the nose.
Heat causes upper congestion,
and melon pedicels are bitter and cold,
so they are sprayed into the nose to clear the diaphragm.
差 (Chà)
means to heal.
然 (Rán)
is the same as 燃 (rán).
灸 (Jiǔ),
pronounced jū yòu.
頞 (È),
pronounced wū gé;
鼻頞 (bí'è).

蔕 (Dì),

He said to his three sons:
"I have received the nation's grace,
and today is my day to die!
If I die a good death,

The Emperor ordered Minister of Works Yǔwén Kǎi to build three floating bridges on the west bank of the Liáo River.
When completed,
the bridges were moved towards the east bank.
The bridges were short, failing to reach the bank by more than a丈 (zhàng).
A large number of Gāolì soldiers arrived,
and the valiant Suí soldiers eagerly jumped into the water to engage in battle.
The Gāolì soldiers attacked from higher ground,
and the Suí soldiers could not land,
with many dying.
Mài Tiězhàng leaped onto the bank and,
along with Hǔbēn Lángjiàng Qián Shìxíong and Mèng Chā, died in battle.
The Kǎoyì states: miscellaneous records say
"Qián Yīng, Mèng Jīnchā."
We follow the Suí Dìjì here.
The bridges were pulled back to the west bank.
An edict posthumously granted Tiězhàng the title of Sùgōng.
Sù
was the name of an ancient state.
His second son, Zhòngcái, and youngest son, Jìcái, were both appointed Zhèngyì Dàfū.
The Emperor further ordered 少府監 Shàofǔ Jiān Hé Chóu to connect the bridges.
It was completed in two days.
The various armies then advanced one after another,
engaging in a major battle on the east bank.
The Gāolì army was greatly defeated,
with casualties numbering in the tens of thousands.
The armies, emboldened by victory, advanced to besiege Liáodōng City,
which was Xiāngpíng City in the Hàn dynasty.
The imperial carriage crossed the Liáo River.
The Kǎoyì states: the Suí Dìjì:
"On the Guǐsì day,
the Emperor led the army;
on the Jiǎzǐ day,
he reached the Liáo River bridge;
on the Wùxū day,
Mài Tiězhàng died;
on the Jiǎwǔ day,
the imperial carriage crossed the Liáo River;
on the Yǐwèi day,
a large encampment was made;
on the Bǐngshēn day,
a general amnesty was granted."
According to the Chánglì,
the first day of that month was Gēngchén.
It is impossible for there to be a Jiǎzǐ.
Furthermore, after Wùxū,
it is impossible for there to be Jiǎwǔ, Yǐwèi, and Bǐngshēn.
This must be an error.
We now remove them all.
An imperial edict was then issued, granting amnesty to the empire.
Minister of Justice Wèi Wénshēng and Department Director of the Right Liú Shìlóng were ordered to pacify the people of Liáozuǒ,
granting them ten years of tax exemption and corvée labor remission,
and establishing commanderies and counties
to govern them.
8 In the summer,
fifth month,
on the Rénwǔ day,
Nàyán Yáng Dá passed away.
9 When the various generals went eastwards,
the Emperor personally warned them, saying:
"This time, we are bringing comfort to the people and punishing the guilty;
it is not for personal glory.
Some generals may not understand my intention
and wish to use light forces for a surprise attack,
fighting alone with isolated troops,
to establish personal fame and obtain rewards and honors.
This is not the proper way for a large army to enforce the law.
This means it is not the proper method for a large army's expedition.
Jiāng,
which is read as 'liàng'.
When divided into three routes,
whenever an attack is launched,
all three routes must be aware of each other.
No light force should advance alone,
lest it suffer losses.
Furthermore,
for all military movements and halts,
reports must be submitted, and approval awaited.
None should act on their own initiative."
As Liáodōng had repeatedly suffered defeats in battle,
it then entrenched itself within the city and held it firmly.
The Emperor ordered all armies to attack it.
He also commanded the generals,
"If Gāolì surrenders,
they should be pacified and accepted immediately;
no troops should be allowed to run wild."
When Liáodōng City was about to fall,
the people inside the city repeatedly spoke of surrendering.
The generals, obeying the imperial decree, dared not seize the opportunity.
They first sent urgent reports.
By the time the reply arrived,
the city's defenses were also prepared,
and they immediately came out to resist the battle.
This happened repeatedly,
but the Emperor remained unaware.
Eventually, the city had not been taken for a long time.
In the sixth month,
on the day Jǐwèi,
the Emperor went to the south of Liáodōng City
to observe the layout of its walls and moats.
He then summoned the generals and reprimanded them, saying:
"You all consider yourselves high-ranking officials
and rely on your family heritage,
intending to treat me with your dullness and cowardice!
When we were in the capital,
none of you wished for me to come,
fearing that you would be implicated in defeat.
I have come here now
precisely to observe your actions
and to behead you!
You are now afraid of death
and none are willing to exert their full strength.
Do you think I cannot kill you?!"
All the generals were terrified and turned pale.
The Emperor then stayed a few *lǐ* west of the city
and commanded from Liùhé City.
This Liùhé City was somewhat similar to the system of the mobile city from the third year of the reign.
Its circumference was eight *lǐ*,
and the city wall and parapet were ten *rèn* high.
The Right Yìwèi Great General Lái Hùér led the Jiāng and Huái naval forces,
with hundreds of *lǐ* of ships prow to stern,
advancing first by sea.
They entered via the Pèishuǐ.
The 'Bān Zhì' states: The Pèishuǐ flows west to Zēngdì County and enters the sea,
all within the territory of Lèlàng.
Shuài,
read as 'shuài'.
Zhú Lú,
pronounced 'zhú lú'.
Pèi,
read as 'pǔ dà'.
They met with Gāolì,
attacked,
and greatly defeated them.
Hùér wanted to take advantage of the victory to press on to their city,
but the Vice Commander Zhōu Fǎshàng stopped him,
asking to wait for the other armies to arrive before advancing together.
Hùér did not listen.
He selected forty thousand elite armored soldiers
and advanced directly to the foot of the city.
Gāolì had ambushed troops in an empty temple within the outer city wall.
They sent out troops to fight Hùér and feigned defeat.
Hùér pursued them into the city,
allowing his troops to plunder and take captives,
thus losing their formations.
The ambush troops were unleashed,
and Hùér suffered a great defeat,
barely escaping with his life.
No more than a few thousand of his soldiers returned.
Gāolì pursued them to their ships.
Zhōu Fǎshàng arrayed his formation to await them,
and Gāolì then retreated.
Hùér led his troops back to camp at Hǎipǔ,
not daring to remain to meet the other armies.
The Left Yìwèi Great General Yǔwén Shù went out via the Fúyú Road.
The Right Yìwèi Great General Yú Zhòngwén went out via the Lèlàng Road.
According to the Suí system: each of the twelve guards had one Great General.
Lái Hùér and Yú Zhòngwén are both listed as Right Yìwèi Great Generals,
why is this?
After examining their biographies,
Yú Zhòngwén
was Right Yìwèi Great General at the beginning of the Emperor's reign.
When the Tǔhún were campaigned against,
Lái Hùér was already Right Yìwèi Great General.
The Zīzhì Tōngjiàn presumably recorded Zhòngwén's office retrospectively.
The Right Yìwèi General Xuē Shìxióng went out via the Wòjǔ Road.
The Left Túnwèi General Xīn Shìxióng went out via the Xuántú Road.
The Right Yùwèi General Zhāng Jǐn went out via the Xiāngpíng Road.
The Right Wǔhóu General Zhào Xiàocái went out via the Jiéshí Road.
The Prefect of Zhuōjùn, Acting Left Wǔwèi General Cuī Hóngshēng went out via the Suìchéng Road.
The Acting Right Yùwèi Hǔbēn Lángjiàng Wèi Wénshēng went out via the Zēngdì Road.
All were to rendezvous west of the Yālùshuǐ.
The 'Bān Zhì' states: In Xīgàimǎ County of Xuántú Commandery, there is the Mǎzīshuǐ.
The 'New Book of Táng' states: The Mǎzīshuǐ originates from the Bái Shān of Mòhé,
its color is like a duck's head,
hence it is called Yālùshuǐ.
Píngyǎng City is southeast of the Yālù.
The Jīn people called the Yālùshuǐ the Hùntóngjiāng.
Dù Yòu said: The Yālùshuǐ is three hundred *bù* wide,
four hundred fifty *lǐ* northwest of Píngyǎng,
and four hundred eighty *lǐ* southeast of the Liáoshuǐ.
Horses and men were all given 100 days' rations,
as well as breastplates, spears,
along with clothing, military equipment, and tents.
Each person carried over three *shí*,
so heavy that none could carry it.
An order was issued to the army:
"Any soldier who
abandons rice or grain shall be executed!"
The soldiers all dug pits under their tents and buried it.
When they had only traveled halfway,
their rations were already nearly exhausted.
Gāolì sent its grand minister, Yǐzhī Wéndé, to their camp to feign surrender.
Yǐzhī
is a compound surname of the Eastern Barbarians.
支
is pronounced lì zhī.
降
is pronounced hù jiāng;
similarly below.
Kǎoyì says: The Gémìngjì records it as
"Wèi zhī Wéndé,"
but we now follow the Suíshū and Běishǐ.
Yú Zhòngwén had previously received secret instructions:
"If Gāo Yuán or Wéndé come,
you must capture them."
Zhòngwén was about to seize him,
but Liú Shìlóng, the Shàngshū Yòuchéng and Grand Commissioner for Pacification,
firmly stopped him.

The Emperor changed Qízhōu (岐州) to Fúfēng Jùn (扶風郡).

bestowed extremely generous rewards,

He rewarded them for their achievements in resisting and suppressing Yáng Xuángǎn (楊玄感),

*Láo* (勞),

25 Liú Yuánjìn (劉元進) attacked Dānyáng (丹陽).
The *Suíshū* (隋書) biography of Tǔwàn Xù (吐萬緒) states: At that time, Yuánjìn (元進) attacked Rùnzhōu (潤州) with his troops.
According to the Táng (唐) gazetteer,
in the third year of Wǔdé (武德) [620 CE],
Rùnzhōu (潤zhōu) was first established on the land of Yánlíng Xiàn (延陵縣),
and Dānyáng Xiàn (丹陽縣) under the jurisdiction of Rùnzhōu (潤zhōu),
originally Qú’ā (曲阿),
was also a name changed by the Táng (唐).
The Dānyáng (丹陽) attacked by Yuánjìn (元進)
was probably this Dānyáng (丹陽) and not the Dānyáng Jùn (丹陽郡) of the Suí (隋) gazetteer;
the Dānyáng Jùn (丹陽郡) of the Suí (隋) dynasty
had its seat at Shítóu Chéng (石頭城).
The *Suíshū* (隋書) was compiled after Wǔdé (武德),
so when it mentions Rùnzhōu (潤zhōu)
and Dānyáng (丹陽),
it uses the Táng (唐) prefecture and county names.
Yuánjìn (元進) lifted the siege and departed,
and Xù (緒) advanced to garrison Qú’ā (曲阿).
Observing this and verifying it with the *Suíshū* (隋書),
then what Yuánjìn (元進) attacked was indeed Rùnzhōu (潤zhōu).
They held their ground for over a hundred days;
Xù (緒) attacked them,
and the rebel forces were utterly routed,
with tens of thousands killed.
Yuánjìn (元進) escaped alone in the night,
and secured his stronghold.
Zhū Xiè (朱燮), Guǎn Chóng (管崇) and others were encamped at Pílíng (毗陵),
with their camps stretching for over a hundred *lǐ*.
Xù (緒) pressed on with his victory and attacked,
defeating them again.
The rebels retreated to secure Huángshān (黃山).
The *Suízhì* (隋志) states that
Wúxiàn (吳縣) has Huángshān (黃山).
Yuánjìn (元進) and Xiè (燮) barely escaped with their lives.
In the battle, Chóng (崇) and his generals and soldiers, over five thousand men, were beheaded,
and their thirty thousand or more women and children were captured.
Xù (緒) then lifted the siege of Kuàijī (會稽).
Yú Jùluó (魚俱羅) and Xù (緒) marched together,
winning every battle,
yet the common people who joined the rebellion were as numerous as those flocking to a market,
and the rebels, though defeated, regrouped,
their power growing even stronger.
Yuánjìn (元進) retreated and occupied Jiàn'ān (建安).
The Emperor ordered Xù (緒) to advance and suppress them,
but Xù (緒), whose soldiers were exhausted,
requested to rest his forces until the next spring.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The *Dìjì* (帝紀) says:
"Xù (緒) and Jùluó (俱羅) were unable to achieve victory for successive years."
According to Xù's (緒) request to wait until next spring,
and Wáng Shìchōng (王世充) attacking Mèng Ràng (孟讓) ten years later,
then Yuánjìn's (元進) defeat must have been precisely at the turn of this winter and spring.
Yuánjìn (元進) retreated and occupied Jiàn'ān (建安),
and was able to resist Shìchōng (世充) on the river,
probably after regrouping.
Jùluó (俱羅) also believed that the rebels could not be pacified in a short time.
His sons were in Luòjīng (洛京).
Luòyáng (洛陽) was the eastern capital,
hence it was called Luòjīng (洛京).
The Emperor was enraged.
Officials, anticipating the Emperor's wishes,
reported that Xù (緒) was cowardly,
and Jùluó (俱羅) was defeated.
Jùluó (俱羅) was executed,
and Xù (緒) was summoned to the imperial traveling palace.
Xù (緒) died on the way
from grief and indignation.
The Emperor then dispatched Jiāngdū Chéng (江都丞) Wáng Shìchōng (王世充).
Wáng Shìchōng (王世充) was Jiāngdū Jùnchéng (江都郡丞).

We follow the *Suíshū* (隋書) here.

The Emperor considered Shìchōng (世充) to have the talent of a general and commander,

Chapter 27. Dù Fúwēi of Zhāngqiū and Fǔ Gōngshí of Línjì were sworn brothers,
The two counties of Zhāngqiū and Línjì,
according to the Suí Zhì, both belonged to Qí Jùn.
Zhāngqiū
was Hán Yángqiū Xiàn.
During the Sòng and Wèi dynasties, it was Gāotáng.
In the sixteenth year of Kāihuáng,
it was changed to Zhāngqiū.
Sòng Bái said: In the seventh year of Tiānbǎo of the Gāo Qí dynasty,
the county seat of Gāotáng was moved to Gǔ Huángjīn Chéng.
The Suí dynasty changed it to Zhāngqiū Xiàn,
named after Zhāngqiū Hill southeast of the county.
Línjì
was Gūan Xiàn during the Hàn dynasty.
It had long been abandoned.
In the sixth year of Kāihuáng, Cháoyáng Xiàn was established.
In the sixteenth year, its name was changed to Línjì.
The Fǔ surname
originated from Fǔ Lì, a grand master of the Jìn dynasty.

Zhìguǒ's separate clan was the Fǔ family.
Yán Shīgǔ said: Wěn
means to sever.

Jì,
pronounced zǐ lǐ.
Shí,

Wěn,

The Dù Fúwēi biography in the Táng Shū states: Gōngshí often stole his aunt's sheep to feed Fúwēi.

"Now I and you suffer together under the Suí government.
