Tàishǐ Lìng Yǔ Zhì (太史令庾質) remonstrated, saying:
"For years now, we have been campaigning against Liáo (遼),
and the people are truly weary and worn out.
Your Majesty should pacify and govern within the passes,
so that the common people can devote their full strength to agriculture and sericulture.
In three to five years,
when the four seas are somewhat prosperous and full,
then it would be appropriate to undertake a tour of inspection. "
The emperor was displeased.
Yǔ Zhì (庾質) feigned illness and did not follow.
The emperor was enraged
and had Yǔ Zhì (庾質) imprisoned.
He eventually died in prison.
In the twelfth month,
on the day Rénshēn (壬申),
the emperor went to the Eastern Capital
and issued a general amnesty.
On the day Wùzǐ (戊子),
he entered the Eastern Capital.
Dōnghǎi (東海) bandit leader Péng Xiàocái (彭孝才) plundered Yíshuǐ (沂水).
Liú Xù (劉昫) said: Yíshuǐ (沂水)
was Dōngguǎn (東莞) County in the Hàn (漢) Dynasty.
The Suí (隋) Dynasty changed it to Dōng'ān (東安) County,
then soon changed it back to Yíshuǐ (沂水),
which belonged to Lángyá Jùn (琅邪郡).
Although Chún (純) was repeatedly victorious in battle,
the bandits grew in number daily.
Some slandered Chún (純), saying he was cowardly.
The emperor was angered,
had Chún (純) chained and brought to the Eastern Capital,
and executed him.
Mèng Ràng (孟讓) led raids from Chángbái Shān (長白山) against various commanderies,
reaching Xūyí (盱眙).
His forces numbered over a hundred thousand,
and they occupied Dūliáng Gōng (都梁宮).
The Suí Zhì (隋志) states: Xūyí (盱眙) County belonged to Jiāngdū Jùn (江都郡),
and had Dūliáng Shān (都梁山),
where Dūliáng Gōng (都梁宮) was located.
The mountain produced Dūliáng (都梁) incense,
hence its name.
Xūyí (盱眙)
is pronounced "xūyí".
Jiāngdū Chéng Wáng Shìchōng (江都丞王世充) led troops to resist him,
constructing five palisades to block the strategic pass
and feigning weakness.
Mèng Ràng (孟讓) laughed, saying:
"Wáng Shìchōng (王世充) is a petty scribe of law and order,
how can he lead troops!
I will capture him alive today,
and march triumphantly into Jiāngdū (江都)! "
At that time, the people had all built fortified strongholds for self-defense,
and there was nothing to plunder in the countryside.
The bandit forces gradually became hungry and disheartened.
So, they left a small force
to besiege the five palisades,
and sent people to plunder the south.
Wáng Shìchōng (王世充) waited for them to become lax,
then unleashed his troops to attack.
He thoroughly defeated them.
Mèng Ràng (孟讓) fled with a few dozen cavalry,
and over ten thousand heads were cut off.
Qíjùn (齊郡) bandit leader Zuǒ Xiàoyǒu (左孝友) with a force of one hundred thousand was encamped on Zūngǒu Shān (蹲狗山).
Zūngǒu (蹲狗) was named for its shape.
Zūn (蹲)
is pronounced "cú zūn".
Zuǒ Xiàoyǒu (左孝友), in dire straits, surrendered.
Xūtúo (須陀) gained great prestige in Dōngxià (東夏).
For his merits, he was promoted to Qíjùn Tōngshǒu (齊郡通守).
The emperor abolished the prefectures and established commanderies,
placing a Tàishǒu (太守) in each commandery.
Afterwards, each commandery additionally appointed one Tōngshǒu (通守),
whose rank was second to the Tàishǒu (太守).
Shǒu (守)
is pronounced "shì yòu".
Zhuójùn (涿郡) bandit leader Lú Míngyuè (盧明月) with a force of over one hundred thousand was encamped at Zhù'ā (祝阿).
The Suí Zhì (隋志) states: Zhù'ā (祝阿) County
belonged to Qíjùn (齊郡).
The Táng (唐) Dynasty changed it to Yǔchéng (禹城) County.
Kǎoyì (考異) says: The Biography of Qín Shúbǎo (秦叔寶) in the Táng (唐) records it as
"Xiàpī (下邳)".
Now we follow the Suí Shū (隋書).
They held their ground for over ten days.
Running out of provisions, they were about to retreat.
He said to his officers and soldiers:
"The enemy, seeing our retreat,
will surely pursue us with all their forces.
If we use a thousand men to assault and occupy their camp,
there will be great advantage.
This is indeed a dangerous task.
Who can go?"
No one answered,
except Luó Shìxìn (羅士信) and Qín Shúbǎo (秦叔寶) of Lìchéng (歷城) who volunteered.
The Suí Zhì (隋志) states: Lìchéng (歷城) County was part of Qíjùn (齊郡).
He sent the two of them to lead a thousand soldiers to lie in ambush among the reeds.
Lú Míngyuè (盧明月) pursued them with all his forces.
Luó Shìxìn (羅士信) and Qín Shúbǎo (秦叔寶) galloped to his palisade.
The palisade gate was closed.
The two climbed onto the watchtower,
each killing several people,
causing great chaos within the camp.
The two cut open the gate to let in the outside troops,
and then set fire to over thirty of his palisades.
Smoke and flames billowed into the sky.
Lú Míngyuè (盧明月) rushed back.
Xūtúo (須陀) turned his army and attacked vigorously,
utterly defeating him.
Lú Míngyuè (盧明月) fled with several hundred cavalry,
and countless were captured or killed.
Qín Shúbǎo (秦叔寶)'s given name was Qióng (瓊),
but he was known by his courtesy name.
In spring,
the first month,
the number of officials in the Mìshū Shěng (祕書省) was increased by 120.
The Suí (隋) system stated: In the Mìshū Shěng (祕書省),
there was one Jiān (監) and one Chéng (丞),
four Láng (郎),
twelve Jiàoshū Láng (校書郎),
four Zhèngzì (正字),
two Zhùzuò Láng (著作郎),
eight Zuǒláng (佐郎),
and two each of Jiàoshū Láng (校書郎) and Zhèngzì (正字).
The emperor added one Shàojiān (少監),
reduced the Jiàoshū Láng (校書郎) to ten,
and added four Zuǒláng (佐郎).
He also established ten Rúlín Láng (儒林郎),
twenty Wénlín Láng (文林郎),
increased the Jiàoshū Láng (校書郎) by forty,
and added twenty Kǎishū Láng (楷書郎),
totaling 117 people.
The emperor enjoyed reading and writing.
Since he was Yángzhōu Zǒngguǎn (揚州總管),
in the tenth year of Kāihuáng (開皇),
the emperor was Yángzhōu Zǒngguǎn (揚州總管).
Hǎo (好)
is pronounced "hū dào".
He often ordered revisions and compilations.
Until he became emperor,
for nearly twenty years before and after,
revisions and compilations never paused.
From classics, literature, military, agriculture, geography, medicine, divination, Buddhism, Daoism, and even to board games, falconry, and dog-keeping,
all were made into new books,
none lacking in thoroughness and mastery,
totaling thirty-one works
and over seventeen thousand volumes.
Initially,
there were 370,000 volumes in the Jiāzé Diàn (嘉則殿) in the Western Capital.
The emperor ordered Mìshū Jiān Liǔ Gùyán (祕書監柳顧言) and others to arrange and categorize them.
After removing duplicates and miscellaneous items,
he obtained over 37,000 authoritative imperial volumes,
which were stored in the Xiūwén Diàn (修文殿) in the Eastern Capital.
He also had fifty duplicate copies made,
classified into three grades,
and distributed to the palaces, ministries, and government offices of the Western Capital and Eastern Capital.
The original
books were all splendidly bound and trimmed,
with precious rollers and brocade covers.
Fourteen book rooms were built in front of the Guānwén Diàn (觀文殿).
Their windows, beds, cushions, and curtains
were all extremely precious and beautiful.
Every three rooms had a square opening,
with brocade curtains hanging over the doors.
Above were two flying immortals.
Outside the doors, mechanisms were installed in the ground.
When the emperor visited a book room,
and a palace woman held an incense burner,
(incense burners originated in the Hàn (漢) Dynasty.
The Hàn Guān Diǎnzí (漢官典職) states: Shàngshū Láng (尚書郎) were given two female scribes,
dressed in clean clothes,
holding incense burners to burn incense.)
the flying immortals would descend,
draw up the curtains and ascend.
The doors and cupboard doors would all open automatically.
When the emperor left,
they would close again to their original state.
Due to widespread household abandonment
and the proliferation of bandits,
in the second month,
on the day Gēngwǔ (庚午),
the emperor issued an edict commanding all people to live in cities,
with fields provided nearby.
All commanderies, counties, post stations, villages, and fortified settlements were to build walls.
The leader of the bandits in Shànggǔ (上谷), Wáng Xúbá (王須拔), proclaimed himself Màntiān Wáng (漫天王)
and named his state Yàn (燕).
The bandit leader Wèi Dāor (魏刀兒) proclaimed himself Lìshān Fēi (歷山飛). Their forces each numbered over one hundred thousand.
They were allied with the Tūjué (突厥) in the north and plundered Yàn (燕) and Zhào (趙) in the south.
4 Initially,
Gāo Zǔ dreamt that a flood submerged the capital city.
He found this unsettling,
so he relocated the capital to Dàxīng.
In the third year of Kāihuáng,
the capital was moved to the new city.
Mù’s death is recorded in volume 176 of Chén Chángchéng Gōng’s Zhìdé fourth year.
His uncle Hún resented his stinginess,
and had his nephew Shàn Héng murder him by stealth,
then implicated his cousin Qú Tán,
forcing him to pay with his life.
Hún said to his wife’s elder brother, Zuǒwèi Shuài Yǔwén Shù:
"If I obtain the inherited fief,
I will present half of the state's tribute annually."
Shù spoke on his behalf to the Crown Prince,
and memorialized Gāo Zǔ,
who appointed Hún as Mù’s successor.
Two years later,
Hún no longer gave the state's tribute to Shù,
and Shù resented this deeply.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
Hún rose through official ranks to Yòuxiāowèi Dàjiāngjūn,
and was re-enfeoffed as Chéng Gōng.
The Emperor, seeing his clan's power and influence grow,
became wary of him.
It so happened that the fangshi Ān Gētuó
said,
"The Lǐ clan will become the Son of Heaven,"
and advised the Emperor to exterminate all those named Lǐ within the realm.
Hún’s nephew, Jiàngzuò Jiān Mǐn,
whose childhood name was Hóng’ér,
aroused the Emperor's suspicion that his name corresponded to the prophecy.
The Emperor frequently hinted at this to him directly,
hoping he would take his own life.
Mǐn was greatly frightened,
and frequently conversed privately with Hún and Shàn Héng, dismissing others.
Shù slandered him to the Emperor,
and then dispatched Hǔbēnláng Jiàng Héjiāng Péi Rénjī to submit a memorial accusing Hún of rebellion.
The Emperor changed Púzhōu to Hédōng Jùn.
Bēn,
read Bēn.
Jiàng,
read Jìliàng;
same below.
The Emperor sent Shàngshū Zuǒchéng Yuán Wéndū and Yùshǐ Dàfū Péi Yùn to jointly investigate the case.
After several days of interrogation,
no evidence of rebellion was found,
and this was reported truthfully to the throne.
The Emperor then sent Shù to conduct a thorough investigation.
Shù enticed and instructed Mǐn’s wife, Yǔwén Shì, to submit a memorial,
falsely accusing Hún of planning, under the pretext of crossing Liáo,
to lead his family's sons and younger brothers who were generals to jointly attack and seize the imperial camp,
and establish Mǐn as the Son of Heaven.
Shù brought it in,
and presented it.
The Emperor wept, saying:
"Our imperial house was almost overturned;
it is thanks to you, my lord, that we are saved."
In the third month,
on the day Dīngyǒu,
Hún, Mǐn, Shàn Héng, and thirty-two members of their clan were executed.
All from the third degree of kinship upwards were exiled to the border regions.
A few months later,
Mǐn’s wife also died by poisoning.
Mǐn’s wife, Yǔwén Shì,
was the daughter of Zhōu Tiānyuán and
the Emperor's sister's son.
5 Two peacocks flew from the Western Garden and gathered in front of the court hall in Bǎochéng.
The Western Garden was west of Luòchéng,
built in the first year.
Later, when the Táng army attacked Wáng Shìchōng,
Shìchōng ordered his brother Shìwěi to guard Bǎochéng.
Thus, Bǎochéng was within the outer city of Luòchéng,
forming a city in itself.
Since the court hall was there,
then all the offices of the various departments were also there,
forming a city in itself,
attached to the southeast of the palace city.
Táng followed the Suí system,
also making Luòyáng the Eastern Capital (Dōngjīng).
The Liùdiǎn states: The Eastern City is east of the Imperial City (Huángchéng),
the Imperial City is within the Eastern City,
the offices of the hundred officials are arranged according to the system of the capital city,
and the Imperial Palace is north of the Imperial City.
From this, I deduce that
the Imperial City was likely the Suí’s Bǎochéng,
located southeast of the palace city.
Cháo,
read Zhíyáo;
same below.
A memorial declared them to be luán,
and the Emperor established the Qīnshì Yīngyáng Fǔ,
commanding the three guards: Qīnshì, Xūnshì, and Wǔshì.
The Three Guards
were the Sānwèi,
each with a Yuèqí Xiàowèi and a Bùbīng Xiàowèi.
Kǎoyì states: Zájì says:
"In the second month of the fifth year,
Mǎ Dérú memorialized that peacocks were luán."
The year, month, and surname here follow Lüèjì and Wēn Dàyǎ’s Chuàngyè Qǐjūzhù.
With no means to verify,
all the officials offered congratulations.
An imperial edict declared that Dérú's sincere heart had mysteriously coincided,
being the first to witness the auspicious sign.
He was promoted to Cháosàn Dàfū,
and awarded one hundred bolts of silk;
others were all given bundles of silk.
Furthermore, the Yíluán Diàn was constructed on that site.
6 On the day Jǐyǒu,
the Emperor traveled to Tàiyuán;
in summer,
the fourth month,
he visited Fényáng Gōng to escape the summer heat.
The palace city was cramped,
and officials and soldiers were scattered among the mountain valleys,
building grass huts as their dwellings.
7 Lǐ Yuān, the Wèiwèi Shǎoqīng, was appointed Shānxī Hédōng Fǔwèi Dàshǐ,
authorized to dismiss, promote, select, and appoint civil and military officials in commanderies and counties,
and also to dispatch Hédōng troops to suppress bandits.
Yuān marched to Lóngmén,
attacked the bandit leader Mú Duān’ér,
and defeated him.
Liú Xǔ states: Lóngmén,
was Hàn Àishì Xiàn,
later renamed Lóngmén by the Northern Wèi;
Suí Zhì places it under Hédōng Jùn.
Shuài,
read Suǒlèi.
Mú,
read Wú,
a surname.
8 In autumn,
the eighth month,
on the day Yǐchǒu,
the Emperor toured the northern frontier.
Kǎoyì states: Zájì says:
"In the sixth month,
Turkic bandits raided and plundered Lánchéng Zhèn.
Fàn Ānguì was sent to attack them,
but the imperial army was defeated,
Ānguì died,
and all officials were greatly alarmed.
In the seventh month,
the Emperor visited Yànmén,
first arriving at Tiānchí,
where it rained.
The mountain valleys were two feet deep in mud.
The accompanying officials were in disarray,
many tents did not arrive,
and they sat exposed in the rain all night.
By dawn, many had died.
The palace women had no food
and borrowed dried provisions from the guards."
Now following Suí Shū.
Initially,
Péi Jù, seeing the growing power of the Turkic Shǐbì Kèhán's tribe,
presented a strategy to divide their strength,
intending to marry an imperial relative to his younger brother Chìjí Shè,
and appoint him as Nánmiàn Kèhán.
Chìjí did not dare accept,
and Shǐbì, hearing of this, gradually grew resentful.
The Turkic minister Shǐshǔ Húxī was very resourceful
and favored by Shǐbì.
Jù deceitfully arranged a market exchange with him,
lured him to Mǎyì Xià,
and killed him.
The Emperor changed Shuòzhōu to Mǎyì Jùn.
Yòu,
read Yǒu.
(Jù then sent a message to Shǐbì saying,) "Shǐshǔ Húxī rebelled against the Khagan and came to surrender.
We have already beheaded him for you."
Shǐbì understood the situation,
and from then on did not come to court.
On the day Wùchén,
Shǐbì led several hundred thousand cavalry to plan an assault on the imperial chariot.
Princess Yìchéng had previously sent an envoy to report the change.
On the day Rénshēn,
the imperial chariot galloped into Yànmén.
Suí Zhì states: Yànmén Commandery.
The Later Zhōu established Sìzhōu,
and in the fifth year of Kāihuáng, it was changed to Dàizhōu.
The Emperor changed it to Yànmén Commandery.
Guō,
a Hàn county.
The Later Wèi established Shíchéng County,
and in the tenth year of Kāihuáng, it was changed to Píngkòu.
In the early years of Dàyè, it was changed to Guō County,
belonging to Yànmén Commandery.
Jiǎn,
pronounced as Gǔ Hàn.
Guō,
pronounced Guō.
On the day Guǐyǒu,
the Tujue besieged Yànmén.
Everyone was terrified.
They dismantled civilian houses for defensive equipment.
There were 150,000 soldiers and civilians in the city,
with provisions enough for only two ten-day periods.
Of the forty-one cities in Yànmén,
the Tujue captured thirty-nine,
only Yànmén and Guō did not fall.
The Tujue attacked Yànmén fiercely,
arrows reaching before the Emperor.
The Emperor was greatly frightened,
holding Zhào Wáng Gǎo and weeping,
his eyes completely swollen.
Yǔwén Shù, the Grand General of the Left Guard, advised the Emperor to select several thousand elite cavalry to break out of the encirclement.
Nàyán Sū Wēi said:
"If we defend the city, we have ample strength.
Light cavalry is their strength.
Your Majesty is the lord of ten thousand chariots,
how can you move lightly!"
Mínbù Shàngshū Fán Zǐgài said:
"Your Majesty would be taking a dangerous gamble.
If something went wrong,
what would be the use of regret?
It would be better to rely on the strong city to blunt their sharpness,
and dispatch orders to summon troops from all directions for reinforcement.
If Your Majesty personally soothes the officers and soldiers,
announcing that there will be no more campaigns against Liáodōng,
and generously rewards their merits,
everyone will surely exert themselves,
so why worry about failure!"
Nèishǐ Shìláng Xiāo Yǔ believed:
"According to Tujue custom,
the Kèhédūn knows about military plans.
The wife of a Tujue Khagan is called Kèhédūn.
Kè,
pronounced like Cóng Kān Rùshēng.
They must rely on the aid of a great nation.
If an envoy were to inform her,
even if it were useless,
what harm could it do?
Moreover,
the officers and soldiers fear
that once Your Majesty is free from the Tujue threat,
you will again attend to Gāolì.
If an imperial edict were issued,
proclaiming a pardon for Gāolì and focusing solely on suppressing the Tujue,
then the hearts of the multitude would be at ease,
and everyone would fight for themselves."
Yǔ
was the Emperor's brother-in-law.
Yú Shìjī also advised the Emperor to revise the reward system,
and issue an edict to halt the campaign in Liáodōng.
The Emperor followed this advice.
The Emperor personally inspected the officers and soldiers,
and said to them:
"Strive to defeat the rebels!
If you can preserve yourselves,
all those in the ranks,
worry not about wealth and nobility.
I will certainly not allow officials to tamper with documents and negate your merits."
He then issued an order:
"Those who perform meritorious service in defending the city,
if without office, shall be directly appointed to the sixth rank and
bestowed with a hundred bolts of cloth;
those with office shall be promoted accordingly."
Envoys offering comfort and rewards
were seen along the roads,
so everyone rejoiced,
fighting day and night,
with many casualties.
On the day Jiǎshēn,
an edict was issued throughout the empire to recruit soldiers.
Governors and magistrates rushed to respond to the crisis.
Lǐ Yuān's son, Shìmín,
aged sixteen,
answered the call and was assigned to the army of Túnyuè Jiāngjūn Yún Dìngxīng.
He persuaded Dìngxīng to carry many banners and drums as a diversionary tactic,
saying:
"Shǐbì dares to lead an army to besiege the Son of Heaven
because he surely believes we cannot come to the rescue in haste.
It is advisable to extend banners for dozens of li without interruption during the day,
and have gongs and drums respond to each other at night.
The barbarians will surely believe that a large relief army has arrived,
and will flee at the sight.
Otherwise,
they are numerous and we are few;
if they attack with their full force,
we will certainly not be able to withstand them."
Dìngxīng followed his advice.
The Emperor sent a secret envoy to seek help from Princess Yìchéng.
The princess sent an envoy to inform Shǐbì, saying:
"There is an emergency in the north."
Reinforcements from Dōngdū and various commanderies also arrived at Xīnkǒu.
Jiǔyù Zhì states: Xīnzhōu Xiùróng County has Xīnkǒu Zhài.
Suí Zhì states: Xiùróng belonged to Lóufán Commandery.
Dù Yòu said: The Suí established Xīnzhōu,
named after Xīnkǒu.
On the day Jiǎchén,
Shǐbì lifted the siege and departed.
The Emperor sent people out to scout;
the valleys were all empty,
with no barbarian horses.
He then dispatched two thousand cavalry to pursue them.
Upon reaching Mǎyì,
they captured over two thousand Tujue elderly and weak and returned.
On the day Dīngwèi,
the imperial chariot returned to Tàiyuán.
The Emperor changed Bìngzhōu to Tàiyuán Commandery.
Qí,
pronounced Qí Jì fān.
Huán,
pronounced Cóng Xuān fān,
also as it is.
"Now that bandits are not quelled,
and soldiers and horses are exhausted,
I wish Your Majesty would return to Xījīng promptly,
to strengthen the roots and solidify the foundation,
for the sake of the empire."
The Emperor initially agreed.
Yǔwén Shù said:
"Many of the accompanying officials' wives and children are in Dōngdū.
It would be appropriate to proceed to Luòyáng along this route,
entering through Tóngguān."
The Emperor followed his advice.
Winter,
tenth month.
On the day Rénxū,
the Emperor arrived at Dōngdū.
Kǎoyì states: Luèjì says:
"On the ninth month Xīnwèi,
the Emperor entered Dōngdū."
Now following Suí Dì Jì.
He said to his attending officials:
"There are still many people."
His intention was that previously when Yang Xuángǎn was pacified,
relatively few people were killed.
Sū Wēi later argued that the reward system was too generous and
should be reconsidered.
Fán Zǐgài strongly insisted
that it was inappropriate to lose credibility.
The Emperor said:
"You wish to win over the people's sentiments!"
Zǐgài was afraid
and dared not reply.
The Emperor was stingy with official rewards.
When Yang Xuángǎn was first pacified,
many were due for honors.
So he established new military ranks: Jiànjié Wèi was Zheng Liu Pin,
followed by Fènwǔ, Xuānhuì, Suīdé, Huáirén, Bǐngyì, Fèngchéng, Lìxìn, and other Wèi,
each dropping one rank.
Of the seventeen thousand officers and soldiers who defended Yànmén,
only fifteen hundred received honors,
all based on the merits of pacifying Xuángǎn.
Those who achieved first merit in one battle were promoted one rank;
those who previously had no military rank only received Lìxìn Wèi.
Those who achieved first merit in three battles reached Bǐngyì Wèi.
Those in the ranks without merit were promoted one rank after four battles,
and also received no gifts.
It was then still discussed to attack Gāolì,
which caused universal indignation among the officers and soldiers.
Initially,
Xiāo Yǔ, as a maternal relative, possessed talent and good conduct.
He had served the emperor in the Eastern Palace,
and was successively promoted to Nèishǐ Shìláng,
entrusted with important state affairs.
Yǔ was by nature firm and upright;
he frequently spoke out, displeasing the emperor,
who gradually distanced himself from him.
When the siege of Yànmén was lifted,
the emperor said to his attendants:
“The Tūjué are presumptuous and perverse,
how can they possibly achieve anything!
When they had not yet dispersed,
Xiāo Yǔ hastily caused alarm and agitation;
his actions are unforgivable!”
He was dismissed and made Héchí Jùnshǒu.
The "Suí Zhì" states: Héchí Commandery
was originally Nánqí Zhōu, established during the Later Wèi dynasty.
The Later Zhōu changed its name to Fèng Zhōu.

In the first year of Yìníng

In the eleventh month of this year,

and then enthroned and renamed the era for Dài Wáng.
*Tōngjiàn* thus uses this to mark the year.
1. Spring,
first month.

Dù Fúwēi always selected five thousand death-defying warriors,

He treated them with great favor.
In battles,

After battle, he would inspect them,

All acquired wealth and goods

If a soldier died in battle,

Thus, people fought for themselves,
and were invincible wherever they went.

Dū (都),

He was Tǐng's son,

At that time, the people of Dōngdū all regarded Mì as a starving bandit who stole grain,

The scholars of the Guózǐ Sān Guǎn

The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Húguān Lù* states:

Jiǎ Xióng was made to hold the arrows,
and Lǐ Mì swore to Heaven,
then shot precisely into the center of the '王' character.

This account is crude and shallow,
so we do not adopt it.
The *Héluò Jì* states:

We now follow the *Púshān Gōng Zhuàn* and the *Suí Shū* and *Táng Shū*.

The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Lüèjì* states,

Bēn,

Jiàng,

Yí,

Yǎo,
pronounced like the characters 五 and 巧.

Piào,

Jí,

On the day Yǐwèi,

Within the Eastern Capital city, there was a shortage of grain,

This was the rhetoric of Zǔ Jūnyàn.
Yuè Wáng Dòng dispatched the Tàicháng Chéng Yuán Shàndá to travel secretly through the bandit territory
to Jiāngdū to report:
"Lǐ Mì has an army of a million men,
besieging the Eastern Capital,
and occupying Luòkǒu Cāng.
There is no food within the city.
If Your Majesty returns quickly,
the rabble will surely disperse;
otherwise,
the Eastern Capital will certainly fall."
He then sighed and sobbed,
and the Emperor's expression changed for it.
Yú Shìjī stepped forward and said:
"Yuè Wáng is young,
and this sort of person is deceiving him.
If what he says is true,
how could Shàndá have managed to come here?"
The Emperor then became furious and said:
"Shàndá is a petty person;
how dare he insult me in court!"
He then sent him through the bandit territory towards Dōngyáng to hasten transport.
This Dōngyáng
probably refers to Wùzhōu Dōngyáng Jùn.
After this, everyone kept silent,
and no one dared to report about the bandits.
Shìjī's appearance was calm and thoughtful,
and his words often accorded with the Emperor's wishes,
so he was especially favored and loved by the Emperor.
No court official could compare with him.
His relatives and partisans relied on him,
selling official positions and perverting justice,
with bribery openly practiced,
and his gate was like a marketplace.
Because of this, both court and common people detested him.
The Nèishǐ Shèrén Fēng Déyí attached himself to Shìjī.
Since Shìjī was not skilled in official duties—
“閑” (xián) here means skilled—
Déyí would promulgate imperial edicts,
flatter and comply with the Emperor's intentions,
and any memorials or petitions from other officials that displeased the Emperor
were all hidden and not presented.
In judging cases and applying laws,
he often made harsh rulings and severe accusations.
In discussing merits and distributing rewards,
he would suppress and diminish them.
Therefore, while Shìjī's favor grew daily, the Suí government deteriorated further,
all due to Déyí's actions.
13 At first,
Tánggōng Lǐ Yuān married into the family of Shénwǔ Sùgōng Dòu Yì.

is a commandery name.

However, the muddled ruler still lives,
and his auxiliary troops are still numerous.
All those under my command are people from Shāndōng.
Seeing Luòyáng not yet taken,
who among them would be willing to follow me westward?
My generals are all former bandits;
if left behind, they would each compete for supremacy.
If this happens,
then our great enterprise will collapse."
Xiàohé said:
"If the main army cannot yet advance westward,
then I request to travel secretly to observe the situation."
Mì permitted it.
Xiàohé and several dozen cavalry arrived at Shǎn County.
The Suí Zhì states,
Shǎn County belonged to Hénán Commandery.
騎 [Jì],
sound of qí jì fān.
陝 [Shǎn],
sound of shì rǎn fān.
At that time, Mì's army was very sharp,
and whenever they entered the park,
they engaged in continuous battles with Suí forces.
The park refers to the Western Park built at the beginning of the Dàyè reign.
While he was still lying in camp,
on Dīngchǒu,
Yuè Wáng Dòng sent Duàn Dá and Páng Yù to lead troops out at night,
and deploy them northwest of Huíluò Granary.
Mì and Péi Rénjī went out to battle,
but Dá and the others soundly defeated them,
killing and wounding more than half.
Mì then abandoned Huíluò
and fled to Luòkǒu.
The Kǎoyì states: The Luè Jì says:
"On the Wùshēn day of the fourth month,
Duàn Dá and others led Guānnèi troops to array themselves west and south of the granary.
Mì led his troops out to resist,
and severely defeated the ferocious ruffians.
Mì returned to fortify the granary.
On the Dīngchǒu day of the fifth month,
Dá and others again led troops out and arrayed themselves west and north of the granary.
Mì again came to resist
and was soundly defeated.
Mì fled to Luòkǒu."
According to the Suí Shū, Běi Shǐ, Xīn and Jiù Táng Shū,
all state that
"Mì was struck by a stray arrow
and lay in camp.
The Eastern Capital sent out troops to attack him,
Mì's forces were greatly routed,
they abandoned Huíluò Granary
and fled to Luòkǒu."
None of them mention the month and day.
The Hélùo Jì states:
"Mì's army suffered a defeat
and returned to Gǒng County.
The Eastern Capital regained Huíluò Granary."
The Púshān Gōng Zhuàn states:
"On the twenty-eighth day of the fifth month,
Yuè Wáng sent out his army at night,
and Duàn Dá and others fought a great battle west and north of the granary;
Mì's army was defeated
and returned to Gǒng County."
It also does not say that Mì was defeated twice in consecutive months.
Wùshēn
was the twenty-eighth day of the fourth month;
Dīngchǒu
was the twenty-eighth day of the fifth month.
It is probably that Zhào Yì, following the Púshān Gōng Zhuàn,
mistakenly divided Mì's single defeat into two separate events.
Chái Xiàohé's troops heard of Mì's retreat,
and scattered.
Xiàohé returned to Mì with a light cavalry escort.
Yáng Défāng and Zhèng Détāo both died.
The Kǎoyì states: Yáng Défāng
is written as
"Wáng Dérén" in the Húguān Lù.
We now follow the Hélùo Jì.
Zhèng Qiánxiàng of Xíngyáng served as Right Sīmǎ.
The Kǎoyì states: The Suí and Táng Shū both write it as
"Qiánxiàng",
only the Húguān Lù writes it as
"Qiánxiàng" [Gānxiàng],
stating that
"Mì killed his elder brother Gānfù.
Gānfù's son Huìtōng later followed Shèng Yànshī to kill Mì."
We now follow this.
15 Lǐ Jiànchéng and Lǐ Yuánjí abandoned their younger brother Zhìyún in Hédōng and left.
Officials arrested Zhìyún and sent him to Cháng'ān,
where he was killed.
Jiànchéng and Yuánjí met Chái Shào on the road,
and traveled with him.

Yìníng first year

1 In the sixth month,
on Jǐmǎo,
Lǐ Jiànchéng and others arrived in Jìnyáng.
2 Liú Wénjìng advised Lǐ Yuān to ally with the Tujue,
using their soldiers and horses to augment his military strength.
Yuān agreed to this,
and personally drafted a letter,
with humble words and generous gifts,
sending it to Shǐbì Kèhán,
stating:
"I wish to raise a great army of righteousness,
to welcome the Emperor from afar,
and restore peace and kinship with the Tujue,
as it was during the Kāihuáng era.
If you can go south with me,
I ask that you do not plunder the common people;
if you merely desire peace and kinship,
and to receive treasures while remaining idle,
then that is also your choice, Kèhán."
Shǐbì received the letter,
and said to his ministers:
"The character of the Suí emperor
is known to me.
If we welcome him back,
he will surely harm Tánggōng and attack us, without a doubt.
If Tánggōng becomes emperor himself,
I will not avoid the intense heat
and will assist him with soldiers and horses."
He immediately ordered this sentiment to be written in a reply.
The envoy returned in seven days,
and his generals and aides were all delighted,
requesting to follow the Tujue's suggestion.
Yuān refused.
Péi Jì and Liú Wénjìng both said:
"Although our righteous army is gathered, our military horses are extremely scarce.
We do not need foreign soldiers;
what we need
is what we desire.
If we delay again,
we fear they might change their minds."
Yuān said:
"Gentlemen, you should consider the next best option."
Jì and the others then requested to honor the Son of Heaven as Tàishàng Huáng,
and establish the Prince of Dài as emperor,
to stabilize the Suí dynasty;
to send proclamations to the commanderies and counties;
to change the flags and banners,
using a mixture of crimson and white,
to show the Tujue.
The color of Suí was red.
Now using crimson mixed with white
shows a departure from pure loyalty to Suí.
幟 [Zhì],
sound of chāng zhì fān.
厥 [Jué],
sound of jiǔ wù fān.
"This can be called 'covering one's ears to steal a bell,'"
This is a vulgar saying;
it means that one who steals a bell dislikes the sound of the bell and covers his ears to steal it.
This is deceiving oneself, but not others.
We have no choice but to do this."
He then agreed,
and sent an envoy to inform the Tujue of this plan.
Xīhé jùn did not obey Yuān’s command.
On the jiǎshēn day,
Yuān sent Jiànchéng and Shìmín to lead troops to attack Xīhé.
He ordered Tàiyuán lìng Tàiyuán Wēn Dàyǒu to accompany them,
according to Suí Zhì,
Tàiyuán xiàn,
formerly called Jìnyáng,
in the tenth year of Kāihuáng,
Tàiyuán xiàn was established by division,
and the Lóngshān xiàn established by the Latter Qí was renamed Jìnyáng xiàn.
Both counties belonged to Tàiyuán jùn.
Lìng
is pronounced lì-zhèng.
“My sons are young,
so I appoint you as a military advisor.
The success or failure of this undertaking
will be divined by this expedition.”
At that time, the soldiers had just been gathered,
and were all unaccustomed to military life.
Jiànchéng and Shìmín shared their hardships,
and when they encountered the enemy, they personally led the charge.
They did not eat nearby vegetables and fruits
unless they bought them.
If a soldier stole something,
they would seek out the owner to compensate them,
but they would not interrogate the thief.
The soldiers and the people were all grateful and pleased.
When they reached the foot of Xīhé City,
any people who wished to enter the city
were allowed to do so.
The Administrator, Gāo Dérú, closed the gates and resisted.
On the jǐchǒu day,
they attacked and captured it.
Dérú was seized and brought to the army gate.
Shìmín rebuked him, saying:
“You pointed to a wild bird and called it a luán,
deceiving the ruler
to obtain a high office.
This matter is recorded in volume 182, Dàyè eleventh year.”
Shǔ
is pronounced suǒ-jù.
Also suǒ-zhǔ.
“I am here precisely to execute treacherous people!”
Then he beheaded him.
Of the rest, not a single person was killed,
nor was a single hair harmed.
Everyone was pacified and encouraged to resume their livelihoods.
Wèi
is the same as wèi.
When the righteous army first rose,
and the hearts of the people were thus,
it was certainly possible to take over the empire.
The round trip took a total of nine days.
Yuān was delighted and said:
“With such a campaign,
even traversing the whole empire would be possible!”
He meant that Shìmín conducted military campaigns with discipline.
Yuān opened the granaries to relieve the poor,
and the number of those who responded to the call daily increased.
Yuān ordered the formation of three armies,
divided into left and right,
collectively called righteous warriors.
Péi Jì and others proposed that Yuān be titled Great General.
On the guǐsì day,
the Grand General’s Office was established.
Jì was made Zhǎngshǐ,
Liú Wénjìng was Sīmǎ,
Táng Jiǎn and the former Cháng'ān wèi Wēn Dàyǎ were Jìshì.
Dàyǎ, together with his younger brother Dàyǒu, jointly managed confidential matters.
Wǔ Shìhuò was Kǎicáo.
Liú Zhènghuì, Wǔchéng Cuī Shànwéi, and Tàiyuán Zhāng Dàoyuán were Hùcáo.
Jìnyáng zhǎng Shàngguī Jiāng Máo was Sīgōng Cānjūn.
Tàigǔ zhǎng Yīn Kāishān was Fǔyuàn.
This was when Táng Gōng established the Grand General’s Office,
and appointed officials,
adopting the systems of the Suí imperial princes’ offices, grand general’s offices, and prefectural and commandery officials.
Under the Suí system,
only imperial princes had yuàn, shǔ, and jìshì.
The grand general’s office had a kǎicáo.
Prefectures and commanderies had hùcáo,

Emperor Yáng changed zhou to jùn,
and jùn appointed various sīshūzuǒ.
A shūzuǒ was effectively a cānjūn,
and a xíngshūzuǒ was effectively a xíngcānjūn.

Wǔchéng xiàn

Shàngguī xiàn
belonged to Tiānshuǐ jùn.
Tàigǔ xiàn

formerly called Yángyì,

Huò

Máo

Zhǎng

Gāopíng xiàn.

Emperor Yáng changed Qínzhōu to Tiānshuǐ jùn,
named after an ancient commandery.

Jiāng

Qiáoxiàn belonged to Qiáojùn.
Shàn
is pronounced ér-yàn.
Shǒu

3 Lǐ Mì again led his forces towards Dōngdū.
On the bǐngshēn day,
a great battle took place at Pínglè Yuán.

His demeanor was completely respectful.
Kě

I will buy them for you on credit;

the Língshòu bandit leader Xī Shìlíng
According to Suí Zhì,

Yuān appointed him as Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn and Yànjùn Gōng,

Observing the words of the Duke of Táng,

Yuān entered the Quèshǔ Valley.

King of Dài Yòu sent Tiger-Claw Commander Sòng Lǎoshēng to lead twenty thousand elite troops to garrison Huòyì,

Yuān (淵) sent a letter to invite Lǐ Mì (李密).

[Lǐ Mì (李密)] wished to be the convenor of the alliance,

Táng Gōng (唐公) was descended from Lǐ Hǔ (李虎),
and Mì (密) from Lǐ Bì (李弼);

However, Lǐ Bì's (李弼) ancestors
were originally from Xiāngpíng (襄平) in Liáodōng (遼東).
Lǐ Hǔ's (李虎) ancestors were from Xīliáng (西涼),
originally from Chéngjì (成紀) in Lǒngxī (隴西).
What is meant by roots and lineage
is simply having the same surname.
'We are the alliance convenor, jointly supported by heroes from all corners of the land.'
'唯' [wéi],
should be written as
'惟' [wéi].
'惟' [wéi],
means 'to think'.
For details, see the proper verification.
'Unite our efforts and hearts,
capture Zǐyīng (子嬰) in Xiányáng (咸陽),

This means Suí Yángdì (隋煬帝).
Yì (殪),
read as 'yú jì fān'.

Qí (騎),
read as 'qí jì fān'.

I currently have affairs in Guānzhōng (關中),

it is better to use humble words to praise and encourage him to inflate his ambition,
so that he will block the path of Chénggāo (成皋) for me,
and tie up the troops of Dōngdū (東都).
Blocking the path of Chénggāo (成皋)
would cut off communication for the envoys from Jiāngdū (江都);
tying up the troops of Dōngdū (東都)
would prevent them from responding to Cháng'ān (長安) in the west.
Zhé (折),
read as 'zhī shé fān'.
Wéi (為),
read as 'yú wěi fān'.
Sāi (塞),
read as 'xī zé fān'.
After Guānzhōng (關中) is pacified,
we will hold the strategic passes and build up our might,

The Zhànguó Cè (戰國策) states: When Zhào (趙) was about to attack Yān (燕),

"Today, I came across the Yì Shuǐ (易水),

and a snipe pecked at its flesh.
The clam closed and clamped the snipe's beak.
The snipe said: 'If it doesn't rain today,
and doesn't rain tomorrow,
there will be dried clam meat.'
The clam also said to the snipe: 'If I don't come out today,
and don't come out tomorrow,
there will surely be a dead snipe.'
A fisherman saw them and caught both.
Now Yān (燕) and Zhào (趙) are locked in a standoff,
I fear that powerful Qín (秦) will become the fisherman."
Táng Gōng (唐公) wished to make Lǐ Mì (李密) and Dōngdū (東都) standoff against each other, while he reaped the fisherman's profit.
Yù (鷸),
read as 'yú lǜ fān'.
"Although I am incompetent and inferior,

and was sent out as one of the Eight Envoys.

Shǐ (使),
read as 'shū lì fān';

Táng Gōng (唐公) once served as a general,
hence this statement.
This is what the wise are responsible for.
Therefore, I gather righteous armies on a grand scale,

to jointly stabilize the world,
with the aim of honoring Suí (隋).
Heaven gives birth to the common people,

who among us today is fit to rule,
if not you, my son!
I, an old man, have passed the age of knowing fate.
Confucius said:
'At fifty, I knew the decrees of Heaven.'
I joyfully support you, my great younger brother,
and wish to cling to your scales and attach myself to your wings.
I only hope that you, my younger brother, will swiftly accept the mandate and omens,
to bring peace to the myriad people!
To be the head of the clan alliance,
to be included in the family register –
Shǔjí (屬籍) refers to
the register of clan members.
Zhǎng (長),
read as 'zhī liǎng fān'.
This honor is enough.
To slay Shāng Xīn (商辛) at Mùyě (牧野) is something I cannot bear to speak of;
to capture Zǐyīng (子嬰) in Xiányáng (咸陽) is a command I dare not heed yet.
The regions around Fénjìn (汾晉)
still need to be pacified;
the meeting at Méngjīn (盟津)
is not yet scheduled. "
Mì (密) was very pleased upon receiving the letter,
and showed it to his generals and aides, saying:
"Táng Gōng (唐公) has deferred to me;
the world is not difficult to pacify!"
From then on, envoys went back and forth without interruption.
The rain had fallen for a long time without stopping,
and Lǐ Yuān's army was short of provisions.
Liú Wénjìng had not yet returned,
and rumors spread that the Tūjué and Liú Wǔzhōu might take advantage of the emptiness to attack Jìnyáng.
Lǐ Yuān summoned his generals and advisors to deliberate on returning north.
Péi Jì and others all said:
"Sòng Lǎoshēng and Qūtū Tōng have joined forces and occupy strategic positions,
making it difficult to subdue them quickly.
Although Lǐ Mì claims alliance,
his treacherous designs are unfathomable.
The Tūjué are greedy and untrustworthy,
acting solely for profit.
Wǔzhōu
is a vassal of the Hú.
Tàiyuán is a major regional city,
and the families of our righteous army are there.
It is better to return and protect our base,
and then plan for future endeavors."
Lǐ Shìmín said:
"Now that crops cover the fields,
why worry about a shortage of provisions!
Lǎoshēng is impetuous,
and can be captured in one battle.
Lǐ Mì is too attached to his granaries,
and has no time for distant strategies.
Although Wǔzhōu and the Tūjué outwardly appear to be allied,
inwardly they are suspicious of each other.
Even if Wǔzhōu desires Tàiyuán in the long term,
how can he forget Màiyì in the short term!
We originally rose with a great cause,
fearless of personal danger to save the common people.
We should first enter Xiányáng
and issue commands to the world.
If we encounter a small enemy
and immediately withdraw our army,
I fear that those who joined our righteous cause will disintegrate overnight,
and we will only be left to defend the single city of Tàiyuán against bandits,
how then can we preserve ourselves!"
Lǐ Jiànchéng also agreed.
Lǐ Yuān did not listen,
and hastily ordered the army to set out.
Shìmín was about to enter again to remonstrate,
but it was already dusk,
and Lǐ Yuān had gone to bed.
Shìmín could not enter,
and wept loudly outside,
his voice audible inside the tent.
Lǐ Yuān summoned him and asked,
Shìmín said:
"Our army moved with righteousness;
if we advance and fight, we will conquer;
if we retreat, we will disperse.
With the troops dispersed in front,
and the enemy pressing from behind,
death is imminent,
how can I not be sad!"
Lǐ Yuān then understood and said:
"The army has already departed,
what can be done?"
Shìmín said:
"The right army is ready but has not yet departed;
ready
means prepared.
The distance is also not great;
I request to personally pursue them."
Lǐ Yuān smiled and said:
"My success or failure all depends on you;
what more can I say,
you may do as you please."
Shìmín then, with Jiànchéng,
pursued the left army overnight and brought them back.
On the day of Bǐngzǐ,
provisions from Tàiyuán also arrived.
Lǐ Guǐ, the Sīmǎ of the Wǔwēi Yīngyáng Fǔ,
(Emperor Yáng had changed Liángzhōu to Wǔwēi Jùn.

was fond of chivalry.
Xuē Jǔ raised a rebellion in Jīnchéng.

in the fourth month of summer,
Xuē Jǔ rose up.)

Everyone agreed,

Cáo Zhēn said:

On the day of Bǐngchén,

Lǐ Guǐ proclaimed himself the Great King of Liáng in Héxī,

Guān Jǐn and others wished to kill all the Suí officials

Lǐ Guǐ said:
"Since you have pressed me to be your leader,

Now we are raising a righteous army to save the people,

Thereupon, he made Xiè Tǒngshī the Tàipú Qīng

The Xī Tūjué Quēdùshè, who occupied Huìníngchuān,

He summoned all the wealthy people,

Xuē Jǔ often warned him, saying:

Xuē Jǔ dispatched Jìn Wáng Rén Yuè to lead troops to advance towards Jiànkǒu,

Xiāo Yǔ resisted him at Héchí,

將 (jiāng)

the same below.

Xuē Jǔ and Lǐ Guǐ's general Lǐ Yūn fought at Chāngsōng.

belonged to Wǔwēi Jùn.
Lǐ Guǐ wanted to release them,

Lǐ Guǐ said:
"If Heaven blesses me,

Lǐ Guǐ did not kill Suí officials

9 Yángdì issued an edict to Xuē Shìxíong, the Grand General of the Left Guard and Defender of Zhuōjùn, to lead 30,000 elite soldiers from Yāndì to suppress Lǐ Mì.
He commanded Wáng Shìchōng and other generals to all be subject to Xuē Shìxíong's command.
Any bandits encountered along the way
were to be summarily executed.
Xuē Shìxíong marched to Hèjiān
and encamped at Qīlǐjǐng.
Qīlǐjǐng
was named so because the place was seven *lǐ* from Hèjiān.
Dòu Jiàndé evacuated all the cities and fled south,
claiming he was returning to Dòuzǐkàng.
Xuē Shìxíong thought Dòu Jiàndé feared him

Dòu Jiàndé planned to raid him.
The distance from Dòu Jiàndé's position to Xuē Shìxíong's camp was 140 *lǐ*.
Dòu Jiàndé led 280 suicide warriors as the vanguard,
ordering the rest of his troops to follow.
Dòu Jiàndé made a pact with his officers and men:
"If we arrive at night,
we will attack their camp.
If it is already daybreak,
we will surrender."
When they were less than one *lǐ* away,
dawn was breaking.
Dòu Jiàndé, panicked, considered surrendering.
Just then, a heavy fog suddenly arose,
making it impossible for people to distinguish others even at arm's length.
Dòu Jiàndé rejoiced, saying:
"Heaven is helping me!"
贊 (zàn)
means to help.
Xuē Shìxíong's soldiers were in great disarray,
all climbing over the palisades and fleeing.
Xuē Shìxíong could not restrain them
and, with several dozen cavalrymen from his retinue, fled back to Zhuōjùn.
The Kǎoyì states: The Gémìng Jì records:
"The Emperor, seeing Lǐ Mì at Luòkǒu, upon returning from the Liaodong campaign,
ordered Xuē Shìxíong, General of the Right Yì Guard, to select and train elite troops from the garrisoned forces, as well as brave and fierce men from Yōu and Yì, to suppress Lǐ Mì.
In any areas passed through,
if there were small-scale robberies,
they were to be summarily executed.
Furthermore, Wáng Shìchōng and other armies were all to take orders from Xuē Shìxíong.
Xuē Shìxíong then personally led 60,000 elite troops.
In late April,
he set up camp outside Hèjiān Jùn city.
The prefectures and counties all prepared cattle, wine, and military provisions to await General Xuē.
At that time, Dòu Jiàndé lacked provisions,
and his soldiers had already dispersed,
with fewer than a thousand remaining.
They were harvesting wheat in Wǔqiáng Xiàn to eat.
When they heard Xuē Shìxíong's army had reached Hèjiān,

He asked a female shaman: 'If I want to flee and avoid them,
what should I do?'
The shaman replied: 'You won't escape.'
He asked: 'If I want to surrender, what then?'
The shaman replied: 'That is also not auspicious.'
He asked: 'If I want to take advantage of their unpreparedness and attack them,
what then?'
The shaman replied: 'If you arrive tonight before dawn,
it will be very auspicious.'
At the time of the divination,
it was already noon.
The place of divination
was 140 *lǐ* from Hèjiān.
Dòu Jiàndé selected 280 elite soldiers to go first,
ordering the rest to follow.
Dòu Jiàndé resolved with his men, saying: 'If we arrive at night, we attack.
If it's morning, we surrender.
Success or failure
depends on this action.'
So they set off.
When they were two *lǐ* from Xuē Shìxíong's camp,
it was already nearing dawn,
and they also heard horn calls, indicating preparation to depart.
Dòu Jiàndé was panicked and wanted to surrender.
A moment later,
a heavy fog suddenly arose.
Dòu Jiàndé said: 'This is Heaven helping me.'
So he led his troops into the camp and attacked,
and Xuē Shìxíong's army was thrown into great confusion.
Xuē Shìxíong's retinue had already prepared to depart,

The soldiers from Yōu and Yì did not wish to serve as garrison troops

Since they did not know the number of the enemy,
they all abandoned their armor and fled,

Lǐ Mì had earlier recruited and appeased the prefectures and counties in Héběi,
and most of them complied.
Xuē Shìxíong died of shame and indignation."
The Táng Dòu Jiàndé Zhuàn states:

Dòu Jiàndé led a thousand suicide warriors to raid him.
Xuē Shìxíong fled with several hundred cavalry."
Now we follow the Suí Xuē Shìxíong Zhuàn,
referencing Dòu Jiàndé Zhuàn and Gémìng Jì.
Dòu Jiàndé then besieged Hèjiān.
On the 10th of the eighth month,

Lǐ Yuān said:

*Jiǎ*,

Cháng,
pronounced like zhī-liǎng.
Jīn-Zǐ Guāng-Lù,

They were to encamp west of the Hé to await the main army.
He appointed Rèn Huái as Zhāo-Wèi Dà-Shǐ.

Yuān said to Cháng-Xié:
"Qū-Tū Tōng has no small number of elite troops,

which clearly shows that his men are not willing to fight for him.
However, Tōng fears punishment
and dares not not come out.
If he crosses the Hé himself to attack you,
then I will advance to attack Hé-Dōng,
which he will surely not be able to defend.
If he keeps his entire army to defend the city,
then you will cut off his Hé-Liáng.
Hé-Liáng
refers to Pú-Jīn Qiáo.
Afterwards, we will attack his rear,
and if he does not flee, he will surely be captured."
11 Many Xiāo-Guǒ who were with Yáng-Dì in Jiāng-Dū fled.
The emperor was troubled by this and
asked Péi Jù about it.
He replied:
"Human nature is such that without a partner,
it is difficult to stay long.
Please allow the soldiers to marry here."
The emperor agreed.
In the ninth month,
he summoned all widows and virgins in Jiāng-Dū's territory to the palace,
allowing the generals and soldiers to take whomever they wished.
Those who had previously committed adultery were allowed to confess
and were then assigned a partner.

Jiàng,

Initially,
Guìxiāng county magistrate, Wèi Déshēn of Hóngnóng,

He governed without strictness.
During the campaign in Liáodōng,

The people could not endure it,
but only the villages of Guìxiāng were undisturbed.
They shared what they had,
not exhausting their strength,

Yuán Bǎocáng received an imperial edict to capture bandits,

The construction in neighboring cities

where officials successively supervised and pressed each other,
bustling day and night,
yet still unable to succeed.
Déshēn allowed repairs and construction to proceed as convenient,
and the government office was silent,
always as if nothing was happening.
He only cautioned his subordinates not to surpass other counties too much,
so as not to cause hardship to the common people.
Nevertheless, the people themselves exerted their utmost,
always making it the best among all counties,
and the people loved him as their parents.
Bǎocáng was deeply envious of his ability

The soldiers under his command heard that Bǎocáng had surrendered to Mì,
thought of their relatives,
and immediately left the city gate,
facing east, weeping loudly, and then returned.
Some advised them to surrender to Mì,
but they all cried, saying:
"We came with Wèi Míngfǔ,
how can we bear to abandon him and leave!"
Hénán and Shāndōng experienced great floods,

Emperor Yáng decreed the opening of Líyáng Granary to provide relief,

Xú Shìjì said to Lǐ Mì:

On Wùwǔ,
Yuān led all his armies to besiege Hédōng,

The generals and subordinates again pressed Lǐ Yuān to assume the title of Tàiwèi.
He increased and appointed officials and staff,

At this time, Hédōng had not yet been captured,
and the powerful figures from the Sānfǔ region arrived by the thousands daily.
Lǐ Yuān wanted to lead his troops west towards Cháng'ān,
but hesitated and could not decide.
Péi Jì said:
"Qūchū Tōng commands a large army,
relying on a strong fortress.
If we abandon it and leave,
and then fail to capture Cháng'ān,
we will be pursued by Hédōng from the rear,
facing enemies from both front and back.
This is a dangerous path.
It would be better to first conquer Hédōng,
and then proceed west.
Cháng'ān relies on Qūchū Tōng for support;
if Qūchū Tōng is defeated,
Cháng'ān will surely fall."
Lǐ Shìmín said:
"Not so.
In warfare, speed is paramount.
We are riding on the momentum of successive victories,
pacifying the submitting masses,
and marching west with drums beating.
The people of Cháng'ān will be terrified at the mere sight of us,
too bewildered to plan,
too timid to decide.
Taking it will be like shaking withered leaves from a tree.
If we linger and exhaust ourselves beneath a strong fortress,
they will be able to formulate plans and prepare to await us.
Sitting idly will waste days and months,
and the morale of the troops will wane.
Then the great endeavor will be lost.
Moreover, the generals who have risen like swarms of bees in Guānzhōng
have not yet pledged allegiance to anyone;
we must hasten to win them over.
Qūchū Tōng is merely a trapped foe defending himself,
not worthy of concern."
Lǐ Yuān followed both suggestions,
leaving his generals to besiege Hédōng,
and personally leading his army west.

These three accounts contradict each other,

The Emperor sent Sè Jiāngdū Jùnchéng Féng Címíng to Dōngdū.
