he crossed the Wèi River from Línjìn,
Cháoyì was
ancient Línjìn territory.
He opened granaries to relieve the starving populace.
On the day Xīnwèi,
he returned to Chángchūn Palace;
on the day Rénshēn,
he advanced to Fēngyì.
Suí Zhì: Fēngyì County,
was attached to a commandery.
Officials, common people, and bandits flocked to him like a flowing stream.
Shìmín recruited their heroes and outstanding talents to serve as his staff,
encamping at Jīngyáng.
Jīngyáng County belonged to Jīngzhào Commandery.
Lady Lǐ led over ten thousand elite troops to meet Shìmín north of the Wèi River,
and she and Chái Shào each established their own headquarters,
known as
the "Niángzǐ Jūn" (Ladies' Army).
Earlier,
tens of thousands of slave bandits from Píngliáng besieged the Fúfēng Grand Administrator Dòu Jìn.
The Emperor changed Yuán Prefecture to Píngliáng Commandery,
and Qí Prefecture to Fúfēng Commandery.
先,
read as xī jiàn.
守,
read as shì yòu.
璡,
read as jiāng lín.
The bandits' food ran out.
Qiū Shīlì sent his younger brother Xínggōng to lead five hundred men carrying rice, wheat, cattle, and wine to the slave bandits' camp.
The slave leader gave a long bow,
but Xínggōng personally cut him down with his sword,
and said to his followers:
"You are all good people,
why do you serve slaves as your masters,
causing the world to call you 'slave bandits'?"
All bowed down and said:
"We wish to serve you instead."
Xínggōng then led his followers and Shīlì to meet Shìmín north of the Wèi River,
and Shìmín appointed him Guānglù Dàfū.
Jìn was
Cóng's cousin.
Xīchéng Assistant Magistrate Fáng Xuánlíng met Shìmín at the army gate.
Kǎo Yì says: The Old Book of Táng, biography of Xuánlíng, states:
"Wēn Yànbó also recommended him."
However, Yànbó was then with Luó Yì.
Therefore, this is not adopted here.
Shìmín appointed him Jìshì Cānjūn,
and took him as his chief strategist.
Xuánlíng also considered himself to have met a kindred spirit,
pouring out his heart and effort,
doing everything he knew how to do.
Yuān ordered Liú Hóngjī and Yīn Kāishān to divide their forces and sweep west through Fúfēng.
They had 60,000 troops,
crossed the Wèi River southwards,
and encamped at the old city of Cháng'ān.
Kǎoyì says: Chuàngyè Zhù states:
"The Duke of Dūnhuáng proceeded from Jīngyáng towards Sīzhú,
leaving Hóngjī and Kāishān to encamp at the old city of Cháng'ān."
This now follows the biography of Hóngjī in the Táng Shū.
Hóngjī attacked them proactively,
defeating them.
Shìmín led his troops towards Sīzhú,
and Lǐ Zhòngwén, Hé Pānrén, and Xiàng Shànzhì all led their forces to join him.
They encamped at Āchéng,
with 130,000 combat-ready soldiers.
Their military discipline was strict and orderly,
not harming even a single autumn hair.
On the yǐhài day,
Shìmín sent an envoy from Zhōuzhì to inform Yuān,
requesting a date to proceed to Cháng'ān.
Yuān said:
"Qūtū, having gone east, cannot return west;
there is nothing to fear from him!"
He then ordered Jiànchéng to select elite troops from Cāngshàng and proceed from Xīnfēng towards Chánglè Gōng.
Xīnfēng County belonged to Jīngzhào Commandery;
Chánglè Gōng
was the old Han palace.
Lè
is pronounced Luò.
From Zhōuzhì proceeding to Cháng'ān
was therefore called north.
All were to arrive at the appointed place and await orders.
On the bǐngzǐ day,
Yuān led his army west,
from Féngyì going west.
They accepted surrenders,
with households joining in great numbers.
He released palace women to return to their relatives.
In winter,
tenth month,
on the xīnsì day,
Yuān arrived at Cháng'ān,
setting up camp northwest of Chūnmíngmén.
Chūnmíngmén
was the central of the three gates on the east side of Cháng'ān city.
He amassed over 200,000 troops.
Yuān ordered each to stay within their fortifications,
and not to enter villages to pillage.
He repeatedly sent envoys to the city walls to explain to Wèi Wénshēng and others his intention to honor the Suí dynasty,
but received no reply.
On the xīnmǎo day,
he ordered all armies to advance and besiege the city.
On the jiǎwǔ day,
Yuān moved his headquarters to Ānxīng Fāng.
Ānxīng Fāng
was likely outside Ānxīngmén.
Yōng Lù says: The three gates on the east side of Cháng'ān city were
Tōnghuà, Chūnmíng, and Ānxīng.
Shuài
is read as lǜ.

17 Bālíng Colonel Dǒng Jǐngzhēn of Póyáng, Léi Shìměng, military commanders Zhèng Wénxiù, Xǔ Xuánchè, Wàn Zàn, Xú Déjī, Guō Huá, and Zhāng Xiù of Miǎnyáng, etc., conspired to seize the commandery and rebel against the Suí.
Suí Zhì says: Bālíng Commandery,
Liáng established Bā Prefecture;
after pacifying Chén,
it was renamed Yuè Prefecture.
In the early Dàyè era,
it was renamed Luó Prefecture,
and soon after changed to a commandery.
Emperor Yáng changed the Grand Commandant to Colonel,
and the Commandant to Military Commander.
Miǎnyáng Commandery,
later Fù Prefecture was established;
in the early Dàyè era,
it was renamed Miǎn Prefecture,
and soon after changed to a commandery.
Jiào
is pronounced hù jiào fān,
shuài
is pronounced suǒ lèi fān;
similarly below.
Zàn
is pronounced cáng hàn fān.
Miǎn
is pronounced mí yǎn fān.
Jǐngzhēn said:
"I have always been of humble birth,
and am not respected by the multitude.
Xiāo Xiǎn, the magistrate of Luóchuān,
is a descendant of the Liáng imperial house.
According to Suí Shū Dì Jì,
Luóchuān County is Luó County of Bālíng Commandery.
Xiǎn
was a grandson of Yán, who was a great-grandson of Emperor Xuān of Liáng.
Let us enthrone him to meet the popular expectation."
Thereupon, he sent an envoy to inform Xiǎn.
Xiǎn gladly agreed,
declaring that he was suppressing bandits,
and recruited several thousand men.
Xiǎn
was Yán's grandson.
Xiāo Yán fled to Chén, seen in the eighth year of Kāihuáng;
his death is seen in the ninth year.
At that time, the bandit leader Shěn Liǔshēng from Yǐngchuān was attacking Luóchuān.
Emperor Yáng changed Xǔ Prefecture to Yǐngchuān Commandery.
Xiǎn then told his followers:
"Today the whole empire is in rebellion,
and Suí governance has collapsed.
The heroes of Bālíng have raised an army,
wishing to make me their lord.
If I accept their plea and issue orders throughout Jiāngnán,
I can restore the fortunes of Liáng.
By this, when I summon Liǔshēng,
he will also surely follow me."
All the followers were pleased and
obeyed.
Thereupon, he declared himself Duke of Liáng,
changing the Suí dress and banner colors to be entirely as of old Liáng.
Liǔshēng then led his followers to submit to him,
and Xiǎn appointed Liǔshēng as Grand General of Cavalry.
Five days after raising the army,
those who submitted from near and far reached tens of thousands,
and he then led his forces towards Bālíng.
Jǐngzhēn sent Xú Déjī to lead several hundred local heroes from the commandery to welcome him.
Before meeting Xiǎn,
Liǔshēng conspired with his associates, saying:
"I was the first to serve the Duke of Liáng,
my merit is foremost.
Now, the generals of Bālíng
all hold high positions and command many soldiers.
If I enter the city,
I will end up beneath them.
It's better to kill Déjī,
holding his head as a pledge,
and I alone will usher the Duke of Liáng to take the commandery city,
then no one will surpass me."
So he killed Déjī.
He entered and reported to Xiǎn,
who was greatly alarmed and said:
"Now we wish to restore order from chaos,
but suddenly you kill each other.
I cannot be your lord."
He then walked out of the camp gate.
Liǔshēng was greatly frightened,
prostrated himself and begged for forgiveness.
Xiǎn rebuked him but pardoned him,
then deployed his troops and entered the city.
Jǐngzhēn said to Xiǎn:
"Xú Déjī was a meritorious minister who initiated this righteous cause,
yet Liǔshēng wantonly killed him without reason.
If this is not punished,
how can you govern!
Furthermore, Liǔshēng has been a bandit for a long time;
though he now follows our righteous cause,
his savage and perverse nature is unchanged.
Living together in one city,
a rebellion is inevitable.
If we don't act now,
regret will be too late!"
Xiǎn again agreed.
Jǐngzhēn arrested Liǔshēng
and beheaded him;
his followers all dispersed.
On the bǐngshēn day,
Xiǎn built an altar and performed a burnt offering,
declaring himself King of Liáng,
and changed the era name to Míngfèng.
18 On the rényín day,
Wáng Shìchōng crossed the Luò River at night,
and encamped at Hēishí.
The next day,
he divided his troops to guard the camp,
and personally led elite soldiers to array on the north of the Luò River.
Lǐ Mì heard of this,
and led his army to cross the Luò and engage in battle.
Mì's army suffered a great defeat,
and Chái Xiàohé drowned.
Mì led the elite cavalry under his command to cross to the south of the Luò River,
while the remaining forces fled east to Yuèchéng.
Yuèchéng
was likely a crescent-shaped city built overlooking the Luò River,
corresponding to Cāngchéng.
Mì, from the south of the Luò River, spurred his horse directly towards Hēishí.
Those in the camp were frightened,
repeatedly raising six beacons.
Shìchōng abandoned the siege of Yuèchéng,
and hastily went to his own rescue.
Mì returned and fought him,
thoroughly defeating him,
beheading over three thousand.
In the 19th year, *jiǎchén*,
Lǐ Yuān commanded his various armies to attack the city,
issuing an order,
"No one is allowed to violate the Seven Ancestral Temples or the imperial clan of the Prince of Dài.
Those who transgress will have their three kindreds exterminated!"
Sūn Huá died from an arrow wound.
In the eleventh month,
on the *bǐngchén* day,
the army commander Léi Yǒngjí was the first to ascend.
The *Kǎoyì* states: The *Shílù* of Emperor Gāozǔ of Táng records
"Léi Shào."
We now follow the *Chuàngyè Zhù*.
The Prince of Dài was in the Eastern Palace;
his attendants scattered,
with only the Imperial Lecturer Yáo Sīlián remaining by his side.
When the soldiers were about to enter the hall,
Sīlián shouted sternly,
"The Duke of Táng raised an army of righteousness to rectify the imperial house!
You must not be disrespectful!"
Everyone was astonished
and stood arrayed in the courtyard below.
Yuān welcomed the prince in the Eastern Palace
and relocated him to the rear of Dàxīng Hall.
Dàxīng Hall
was the main hall of the Suí palace.
Since he had not yet assumed the revered position,
he resided in the rear of the hall.
He bowed tearfully and departed.
Sīlián
was the son of Chá.
Yáo Chá
served the Chén dynasty
and was renowned for his literary talent and erudition.
He lodged him in Chánglè Palace
and established twelve articles of law with the people,
abolishing all the harsh prohibitions of Suí.
When Yuān raised his army,
the officials guarding the city exhumed his ancestral tombs
and destroyed his five ancestral temples.
According to Suí regulations,
all dukes established five ancestral temples.
Wèi Wénshēng had already died.
On the *wùwǔ* day,
Yīn Shìshī and Gǔ Yí, among others, were apprehended.
They were accused of greed and cruelty
and of resisting the righteous army.
All were executed;
more than ten people died,
but no others were interrogated.
Lǐ Jìng of Sānyuán, Assistant Administrator of Mǎyì Commandery,
had long been at odds with Yuān.
The *Suí Zhì* states that
Sānyuán County belonged to Jīngzhào Commandery.
Emperor Yáng renamed Shuò Prefecture to Mǎyì Commandery.
The *Kǎoyì* states: Liǔ Fāng's *Táng Lì* and Jìng's biography in the *Táng Shū* say:
"Gāozǔ attacked the Tujue beyond the frontier.
Jìng perceived that Gāozǔ harbored ambitions for the four directions,
and therefore, he chained himself and submitted a memorial reporting the matter,
intending to go to Jiāngdū.
Upon reaching Cháng'ān,
the road was blocked and impassable, so he stopped."
However, when Tàizōng planned to raise an army,
Gāozǔ was not yet aware of it.
Even when he knew, he did not agree.
At the time of attacking the Tujue,
he had no other ambitions.
How could Jìng have perceived this?
Moreover, when submitting a memorial reporting such a matter, one should travel by post-horse to be swift.
Why would he chain himself?
We now follow Jìng's *Xíngzhuàng*, which says:
"In the former Suí dynasty,
he once displeased the emperor.
When the city fell,
Gāozǔ called him to account for his past words.
The Duke debated fearlessly and directly,
and was exceptionally pardoned."
However, the *Xíngzhuàng* attributes its authorship to Wèi Zhēng,
which is incorrect.
According to records, Zhēng died in the 17th year of Zhēngguān,
while Jìng died in the 23rd year.
It was probably written by later generations,
attributing it to Zhēng.
Furthermore, the account of Jìng's deeds is extremely fantastical and unreliable;
only this part can be used as evidence.
He was about to be executed.
Jìng cried out loudly,
"Your Grace raised an army of righteousness,
intending to pacify the tyranny and rebellion.
Are you going to kill a brave man because of a personal grudge?"
Shìmín pleaded earnestly for him,
and so he was spared.
Shìmín then summoned him to his staff headquarters.
Jìng had displayed ambition and spirit from a young age
and possessed both civil and military talents.
His maternal uncle, Hán Qínhǔ, would often pat him and say,
"Among those with whom one can discuss strategies for generals and commanders,
only this child is capable!"
Wáng Shìchōng, after his defeat north of Luò,
fortified his defenses and did not venture out.
Yuè Wáng Dòng sent an envoy to console him.
Shìchōng was ashamed and fearful,
and requested battle at Mì.
On the *bǐngchén* day,
Shìchōng and Mì arrayed their forces across the Shízihé river.
Mì's formation stretched over ten *lǐ* from north to south.
Zhái Ràng first engaged Shìchōng in battle,
but retreated after suffering a disadvantage.
Shìchōng pursued him,
but Wáng Bódāng and Péi Rénjī cut across from the side to sever his rear.
Mì then commanded his central army to attack,
and Shìchōng was greatly defeated,
fleeing westward.
The *Kǎoyì* states: *Bǐngchén* and *wùwǔ* days have already appeared previously.
To narrate the events of Xījīng and Dōngdū separately
and prevent confusion,
they are repeated here.
According to the *Tōngjiàn* text below, it records:
"On the *wùwǔ* day,
Zhái Ràng was killed."
The *Kǎoyì* also mentions this here.
Zhái Ràng's Sì Mǎ (Steward) Wáng Rúxìn
persuaded Ràng to appoint himself Grand Chancellor (dà zhǒng zǎi), to take overall charge of all affairs,
and thereby seize Mì's power.
Ràng did not agree.
Ràng's elder brother, Zhù Guó (Pillar of State), the Duke of Xíngyáng, Hóng,
(A textual variant notes: The Hélùo Jì records it as
“Hóng.”
We now follow the Púshān Gōng Chuán.)
said to Ràng:
"You should be the Son of Heaven yourself.
How can you give it to someone else!
If you don't take it,
I will!"
Ràng merely laughed heartily,
not taking it seriously.
Mì heard of this and disliked it.
Zǒng Guǎn (Governor-General) Cuī Shìshū had first defected to Mì from Yānlíng.
(Yānlíng Xiàn [county],
in the Suí dynasty, belonged to Yǐngchuān Jùn.)
(Yān [Yānlíng],
read as yèwǎn,
also as yújìan,
also pronounced yǎn.)
Mì demanded goods from him,
but Shìshū had not yet managed to procure them.
Mì was about to inflict punishment immediately.
Ràng summoned Yuán Shuài Fǔ Jì Shì (Secretary of the Marshal's Residence) Xíng Yìqī to gamble.
Yìqī procrastinated and did not come forward,
so Ràng had him beaten with eighty strokes of a staff.
Ràng said to Zuǒ Cháng Shǐ (Left Chief Clerk) Fáng Yànzǎo:
"You previously conquered Rǔnán
and obtained a great deal of treasure.
You gave it all to the Duke of Wèi,
and nothing to me!
I established the Duke of Wèi;
who knows what will happen!"
Yànzǎo was frightened
and reported the situation to Mì.
Consequently, he and Zuǒ Sī Mǎ (Left Marshal) Zhèng Tíng jointly advised Mì, saying:
"Ràng is greedy, stubborn, and inhumane.
He has the ambition to depose his lord.
You should deal with him early."
Mì said:
"Now, our safety is not yet assured.
If we immediately start killing each other,
how will we show our intentions to those far away?"
Tíng said:
"When a poisonous snake stings a hand,
a brave man will cut off his arm.
What is preserved is the greater good.
If he gains his ambition first, it will be too late to regret."
Mì then agreed,
and arranged a banquet, inviting Ràng.
On the day Wùwǔ,
Ràng, together with his elder brother Hóng and his nephew Móhóu, who was Sī Tú Fǔ Cháng Shǐ (Chief Clerk of the Minister of Education's Office), went to see Mì.
Mì sat with Ràng, Hóng, Péi Rénjī, and Hǎo Xiàodé,
while Shàn Xióngxìn and others stood by as attendants.
Fáng Yànzǎo and Zhèng Tíng moved about, inspecting.
Mì said:
"Today, we are drinking with high-ranking officials.
We don't need many people;
(Dáguān [high-ranking officials]
is synonymous with xiǎn guān [prominent officials].)
just attendants."
All of Mì's attendants withdrew,
but Ràng's attendants remained.
Yànzǎo reported to Mì, saying:
"Now, we are enjoying ourselves,
and the weather is very cold.
Please give wine and food
to Sī Tú's attendants."
Mì said:
"Let Sī Tú decide."
Ràng said:
"Very good."
Thereupon, Ràng's attendants were all led out.
Only Cài Jiàndé, a strong man from Mì's retinue, stood by with a knife.
Before the food was served,
Mì took out a good bow
and practiced archery with Ràng.
As Ràng drew the bow to its fullest,
Jiàndé chopped him from behind,
and he fell before the couch,
his cry like the roar of an ox.
Hóng, Móhóu, and Rúxìn were also all killed.
Xú Shìjì ran out,
and the gatekeeper chopped him, wounding his neck.
Wáng Bódāng shouted from a distance, stopping him.
Shàn Xióngxìn kowtowed and begged for his life,
and Mì spared him.
Mì's retinue was alarmed and confused,
not knowing what to do.
Mì loudly declared:
"I raised this righteous army with you all
originally to eliminate tyranny and chaos.
Sī Tú engaged in tyranny and brutality,
insulting his colleagues
and disregarding hierarchy;
now, only his family has been punished.
None of you are involved."
He ordered Xú Shìjì to be helped into a tent,
and personally dressed his wound.
Ràng's subordinates wanted to disperse,
so Mì sent Shàn Xióngxìn to go and reassure them.
Soon after, Mì rode alone into Ràng's camp.
(Dúqí [rode alone]
is synonymous with dānqí [single rider].)
(Qí [ride],
read as qí jì.)
He ordered Shìjì, Xióngxìn, and Bódāng to separately command Ràng's troops,
and thus stability was restored both internally and externally.
Ràng was cruel and merciless,
Móhóu was suspicious and jealous,
and Rúxìn was greedy and unrestrained.
Therefore, on the day of their deaths,
none of their subordinates mourned them.
However, Mì's generals and assistants began to feel uneasy.
Initially,
Wáng Shìchōng knew that Ràng and Mì would not remain in harmony for long,
hoping that they would plot against each other,
so he could take advantage of the situation.
When he heard of Ràng's death,
he was greatly disappointed
and sighed:
"Lǐ Mì's natural talent is discerning and decisive.
Whether he becomes a dragon or a snake,
he is indeed unfathomable!"
On the 21st day, Rénxū,
Lǐ Yuān prepared the imperial carriage to welcome the Prince of Dài (dài wáng) to ascend the throne as emperor in the Tiānxīng Diàn.
(Tiānxīng Diàn [Heavenly Prosperity Hall]
should be Dàxīng Diàn [Great Prosperity Hall].)
A general amnesty was declared, and the era name was changed.
The era name was changed to Yìníng.
On the day Jiǎzǐ,
Yuān entered Cháng'ān from Chánglè Gōng.

Yuān was appointed Jiǎ Huángyuè (Acting Imperial Axe-Bearer), Shǐ Chíjié (Imperial Commissioner), Dà Dū Dū Nèiwài Zhū Jūnshì (Grand Commander of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside), Shàngshū Lìng (Director of the Imperial Secretariat), Dà Chéngxiàng (Grand Chancellor),
and was further enfeoffed as the King of Táng.
Wǔdé Diàn was made the Chancellor's Office,
and his directives were referred to as "Lìng" (orders).
He presided over affairs daily at Qiánhuà Mén.
(Qiánhuà Mén [Gate of Earnest Transformation]
was in the eastern section in front of Dàxīng Diàn.)
On the day Yǐchǒu,
Yúlín, Língwǔ, Píngliáng, and Āndìng Commanderies all sent envoys to request their appointments.
On the day Bǐngyín,
an imperial edict decreed that all military and state affairs,
whether great or small,
the establishment of civil and military offices,
whether noble or humble,
and the regulations for rewards and punishments,
all belonged to the Chancellor's Office;
only the suburban sacrifices to Heaven and Earth,
and the seasonal dì and xiá sacrifices were to be reported to the emperor.
Officials were established for the Chancellor's Office.
(A textual variant notes: The Táng Dì Jì places this in the 12th month, Guǐwèi.
We now follow the Chuàngyè Zhù.)
Hé Pānrén sent Lǐ Gāng to meet Yuān,
who retained him
and appointed him as the Chancellor's Office Sī Lù (Recorder).
(Lù [Recorder]
means to oversee all affairs of an office.)
(After Emperor Wén of Suí received the abdication,
there was no longer a Chancellor's Office,
nor were there its officials.)
(The Duke of Táng assisted in governing,
his position surpassing all others,
so all his officials were specially appointed.)
Also, former Kǎo Gōng Láng Zhōng (Director of Merit Evaluation) Dòu Wēi was made Sī Lù Cānjūn (Adjutant-Recorder),
tasked with establishing rites and ceremonies.
(Wēi was the son of Chì.)
(Dòu Chì was one of the three Dukes [Sān Gōng] at the beginning of the Suí dynasty.)
The state's finances were insufficient,
so Yòu Guānglù Dàfū (Grandee of the Right, Glorious Dignitary) Liú Shìlóng offered a plan.
(In the Suí dynasty, this was an honorary title,
Yòu Guānglù and Zuǒ Guānglù
were of the second rank.)
"Now, our righteous army numbers tens of thousands,
all in the capital.
Firewood is expensive, while cloth is cheap.
Please fell trees in the six streets and the imperial park for firewood.
(The six streets within Cháng'ān city;
the imperial park enclosed the former Hàn capital,
reaching the Wèi River.)
This can yield hundreds of thousands of bolts of cloth."
Yuān followed this advice.
On the day Jǐsì,
Lǐ Jiànchéng was made the Crown Prince of Táng,
Lǐ Shìmín was made Jīngzhào Yǐn (Magistrate of Jingzhao Prefecture) and the Duke of Qín,
and Lǐ Yuánjí was made the Duke of Qí.
22 All the commanderies of Hénán had submitted to Lǐ Mì,
except for Xíngyáng Prefect Shúnyáng Wáng Qìng and Liángjùn Prefect Yáng Wāng, who still held out for the Suí.
Qìng
was the son of Héjiān Wáng Hóng;
Hóng
was a distant cousin of Gāozǔ.
Emperor Yáng changed Sòngzhōu to Liángjùn.
Shún,
pronounced Xún.
Wèi,
pronounced yúwěifān;
similarly below.
(Mì) explained the advantages and disadvantages to Chén,
and furthermore said:
"The King's family ancestry
originally resided east of the mountains,
and their original surname was Guō,
not of the Yáng clan.
The fragrant orchid burns while the common grass laments (an idiom meaning that the innocent suffer along with the guilty),
but the situation here is not like that."
Originally,
Qìng's grandfather Yuánsūn was orphaned early
and was raised by his maternal uncle's clan with his mother, Lady Guō.
When Emperor Wǔyuán (Yáng Zhōng) started his campaign in Guānzhōng with Zhōu Wén,
(Yáng Zhōng,
posthumously titled Emperor Wǔyuán.)
he feared being executed by the Gāo clan,
(The Gāo clan of Northern Qí.)
so (Mì) secretly said this.
Qìng was terrified upon receiving the letter,
and immediately surrendered the commandery to Mì,
restoring his surname to Guō.
23 In the twelfth month,
on the guǐwèi day,
posthumous titles were conferred: Táng Wáng Yuān's great-grandfather, Xiānggōng, was posthumously titled Jǐng Wáng;
his father, Rén Gōng, was posthumously titled Yuán Wáng,
and his wife, Lady Dòu, was titled Mù.
Xiānggōng
was Hǔ.
Rén Gōng
was Bǐng.
Lady Dòu
was the daughter of Yì,
and she became Empress Tàimù.
Shì,
pronounced shénzhìfān.
24 Xuē Jǔ dispatched his son Rén’guǒ to raid Fúfēng,
and Táng Bì, based in Qīnyuán, resisted him.
Qīnyuán County,
in the Suí dynasty belonged to Fúfēng Commandery.
Qīnyuán,
pronounced kǔjiānfān.
Bì then killed Lǐ Hóngzhī
and offered to surrender to Jǔ.
Táng Bì established Lǐ Hóngzhī, as seen in volume 182, Dàyè 10th year.
Shǐ,
pronounced shūlìfān.
Jiàng,
pronounced hùjiāngfān.
(Jǔ) launched a surprise attack and defeated them,
absorbing all their troops.
Bì fled with several hundred cavalry to Fúfēng to surrender,
but Fúfēng Prefect Dòu Jìn killed him.
Jǔ's power grew even greater,
with his forces numbering three hundred thousand. He planned to capture Cháng'ān;
but upon hearing that Chancellor Yuān had already secured Cháng'ān,
he instead besieged Fúfēng.
Yuān sent Lǐ Shìmín to lead troops to attack him.
He also sent Jiāng Mó and Dòu Guǐ together out of Sǎnguān,
(Dàsǎnguān,
located southwest of Chéncāng County in Fúfēng Commandery.
Sǎn,
pronounced xīdǎnfān.)
while Zǎo Guānglù Dàfū Lǐ Xiàogōng pacified the area south of the mountains;
and Fǔhù Cáo Zhāng Dàoyuán pacified the area east of the mountains.
(Dàoyuán
was the Hùcáo of the Chancellor's office.
He was a paternal cousin of Yuān.)
On the guǐsì day,
Shìmín attacked Xuē Rén’guǒ in Fúfēng,
decisively defeating him.
He pursued the fleeing enemy to Lǒngchí and then returned.
Xuē Jǔ was greatly alarmed
and asked his officials:
"Has there ever been a case in history where an emperor surrendered?"
Huángmén Shìláng Qiántáng Chǔ Liàng said:
(Suí Zhì,
Qiántáng County belonged to Yúháng Commandery.)
Jiàng,
pronounced hùjiāngfān;
similarly below.
"Zhào Tuó submitted to the Hàn,
(This event is recorded in the annals of Emperor Gāozǔ and Emperor Wéndì of Hàn.)
Tuó,
pronounced túhéfān.
(This event is recorded in the annals of Wèi and Jìn.)
and is still honored to this day.
This refers to the children of the Xiāo clan.
It has happened since ancient times."
Wèiwèi Qīng Hǎo Yuàn quickly stepped forward and said:
"Your Majesty has asked wrongly!
How perverse are Chǔ Liàng's words!
In the past, Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn repeatedly suffered defeats and fled,
(See the main annals.)
(See the annals of Emperor Xiàndì of Hàn.)
Jí,
pronounced qùlìfān.
How can Your Majesty, after one unfavorable battle,
immediately contemplate a plan for the downfall of the state!"
Jǔ also regretted his words and said:
"I was merely testing you all."
He then generously rewarded Yuàn
and appointed him as his chief strategist.
25 On the yǐwèi day,
Píngliáng Liúshǒu Zhāng Lóng,
on the dīngyǒu day,
Héchí Prefect Xiāo Yǔ, and Fúfēng and Hányáng Commanderies successively surrendered.
Emperor Yáng changed Chéngzhōu to Hányáng Commandery,
which was the land of Wǔdū and Qiúchí.
Shǒu,
pronounced shìyòufān.
Jiàng,
pronounced hùjiāngfān.
Xiāo Yǔ was appointed Lǐbù Shàngshū and Sòngguó Gōng.
26 Jiāng Mó and Dòu Guǐ advanced to Chángdào,
(The Northern Wèi divided Shànglù to establish Chángdào County;
in the Suí dynasty, it belonged to Hányáng Commandery.)
and then retreated.
Yuān sent Tōngyì Dàfū Lǐquán Liú Shìràng to pacify Táng Bì's remaining forces,
(Tōngyì Dàfū,
a nominal official position in the Suí,
fourth rank, upper grade.)
(Suí Zhì,
Lǐquán County belonged to Jīngzhào Commandery,
formerly Níngyí County of the Later Wèi,
renamed in the 18th year of Kāihuáng.)
but he was defeated in battle
and captured by Jǔ.
27 Lǐ Xiàogōng defeated Zhū Càn,
and his generals requested to kill all the captives.
Xiàogōng said:
"That is unacceptable.
From now on,
who would be willing to surrender again!"
Thereupon, he marched from Jīnchuān into Bā and Shǔ,
and wherever his proclamations reached,
over thirty prefectures surrendered and submitted.
(Suí Zhì,
Jīnchuān County,
belonged to Xīchéng Commandery,
territory of Hàn Xīchéng County;
in the early Liáng, it was called Shànglián,
later Jíyáng,
Western Wèi renamed it Jí'ān,
then in the Later Zhōu, Xīchéng was incorporated;
in the 3rd year of Dàyè,
it was renamed Jīnchuān,
because gold was produced in its territory.
From Jīnchuān, one enters Bāzhōng,
and from Bāzhōng, one reaches Shǔ.)
28 Qūyú Tōng (屈突通) and Liú Wénjìng (劉文靜) faced off for over a month.
Tōng (通) again sent Sāng Xiǎnhé (桑顯和) to raid his camp at night.
Wénjìng (文靜) and Zuo Guanglu Dafu (左光祿大夫) Duàn Zhìxuán (段志玄) fought with all their might.
Xiǎnhé (顯和) was defeated and fled.
All his troops were captured.
Tōng's (通) situation became increasingly dire.
Someone advised Tōng (通) to surrender.
Tōng (通) wept and said:
"I have served two masters,
the two masters
refer to Emperor Wén (文帝) and Emperor Yáng (煬帝).
The character '說' (shuō)
is pronounced 'shì ruì' (式芮).
The character '降' (jiàng)
is pronounced 'hù jiāng' (戶江);
the same applies below.
To receive a man's emolument and then shirk his difficulties,
I will not do it!"
He often rubbed his neck and said:
"I must take a blade for the state!"
He encouraged and consoled his officers and soldiers,
never failing to shed tears,
and people consequently respected him.
Prime Minister Yuān (淵) sent his household servant to summon him.
Tōng (通) immediately beheaded him.
When he heard that Cháng'ān (長安) could not be defended,
and his family members had all been captured by Yuān (淵),
he then left Xiǎnhé (顯和) to guard Tóngguān (潼關),
led his troops east,
intending to proceed to Luòyáng (洛陽).
As Tōng (通) had just left,
Xiǎnhé (顯和) immediately surrendered the city to Wénjìng (文靜).
Wénjìng (文靜) dispatched Dòu Cóng (竇琮) and others with light cavalry to pursue him with Xiǎnhé (顯和).
They caught up with him at Chóusāng (稠桑).
In Húchéng (湖城) County, Guó (虢) Prefecture, there was Chóusāng Yì (稠桑驛).
The character '琮' (cóng)
is pronounced 'cú zōng' (徂宗).
The character '將' (jiāng)
is pronounced 'jí liàng' (即亮),
and also sounds as written,
meaning to lead.
The character '騎' (qí)
is pronounced 'jī jì' (奇寄).
Dòu Cóng (竇琮) sent Tōng's (通) son, Shòu (壽), to persuade him.
Tōng (通) cursed, saying:
"Why has this scoundrel come!
Formerly we were father and son,
now we are sworn enemies!"
He ordered his左右 (attendants) to shoot him.
Xiǎnhé (顯和) said to his troops:
"The capital city has now fallen.
You are all people from Guānzhōng (關中).
Where do you intend to go?"
All the troops laid down their weapons and surrendered.
Tōng (通) knew he could not escape.
He dismounted, faced southeast, bowed twice, and cried out, saying:
"This minister's strength is exhausted to this point;
I do not dare to betray the state.
Heaven, Earth, and the spirits truly know this!"
The soldiers seized Tōng (通) and sent him to Cháng'ān (長安).
The 'Kǎoyì' (考異) states: The 'Gémìng Jì' (革命記) says:
"Gāozǔ (高祖) ordered his generals to attack Tōng (通).
Tōng (通) fled out of Tóngguān (潼關).
He then ordered Tōng's (通) son, Shòu (壽), to follow the army and call his father.
When they reached Chóusāng (稠桑),
they caught up with him.
Shòu (壽) told Tōng (通), 'The empire has now perished.
The King of Xiang (相王) has raised a righteous army
to pacify the turmoil;
your excellency must turn misfortune into fortune
to preserve yourself.
Alone on horseback, with light baggage,
where do you intend to go?'
Tōng (通) cursed Shòu (壽), saying, 'How can this scoundrel be tolerated!'
He drew his bow and shot him.
Shòu (壽) called out to Tōng's (通) soldiers,
and they all laid down their weapons and surrendered.
Shòu (壽) then rushed forward and embraced Tōng (通),
'Please, your excellency, bend your will and return to righteousness.'
Tōng (通) then turned his head southeast,
tears streaming down his face as he cried out,
repeatedly calling out the Emperor's title: 'This minister's strength is exhausted to this point.
It is not that this minister dares to tarnish his reputation
or betray the state's grace.'
Only then did he wipe away his tears and proceed to the army
to meet King Táng (唐王)."
We now follow the 'Táng Shū' (唐書).
The 'Táng Péi Jǔ Zhuàn' (唐裴矩傳) states:
"When news of Qūyú Tōng's (屈突通) defeat reached Jiāngdū (江都),
Emperor Yáng (煬帝) asked Jǔ (矩) for a strategy.
Jǔ (矩) said, 'There is rebellion in Tàiyuán (太原),
and the capital region is not peaceful.
To make arrangements from afar
might miss the opportune moment;
only if the imperial carriage returns early
can things be pacified.'"
It is observed that the fall of Suí (隋) was
entirely due to Jǔ's (矩) flattery.
How could he dare to advise the emperor to return west!
Probably because Jǔ (矩) served the Táng (唐) dynasty,
his descendants and the historians added these words
to cover up his evils.
This is not adopted here.
He was granted the title Duke of Jiǎng (蔣公).
Jiǎng (蔣)
is the name of an ancient state.
Yuān (淵) sent Tōng (通) to the city of Hédōng (河東) to persuade Yáo Jūnsù (堯君素).
When Jūnsù (君素) saw Tōng (通),
he sighed and could not control himself.
Tōng (通) also shed tears that dampened his lapels,
and then said to Jūnsù (君素):
"My army is defeated.
Wherever the righteous banner points,
none fail to respond.
The situation is thus;
you should surrender early."
Jūnsù (君素) said:
"You are a great minister of the state.
The sovereign entrusted you with Guānzhōng (關中),
and the Prince of Dài (代王) entrusted you with the altars of soil and grain.
How can you betray the state and surrender alive,
and then become a persuader for others!
The horse you are riding
was bestowed by the Prince of Dài (代王).
How can you have the face to ride it!"
Tōng (通) said:
"Alas,
Jūnsù (君素),
I came here because my strength was exhausted!"
Jūnsù (君素) said:
"Your strength is not yet exhausted now;
what need is there for many words!"
Tōng (通) was ashamed and withdrew.
29 In Dōngdū (東都), a dou (斗) of rice cost three cash,
and two or three tenths of the people died of starvation.
30 On the day of Gēngzǐ (庚子),
some of Wáng Shìchōng's (王世充) soldiers deserted and surrendered to Lǐ Mì (李密).
Mì (密) asked:
"What is Shìchōng's (世充) army doing?"
The soldiers said:
"Recently we saw him recruiting more soldiers
and twice feasting the officers and men;
we don't know the reason why."
Mì (密) said to Péi Rénjī (裴仁基):
"I almost fell into that slave's trap.
Does Guanglu (光祿) know this?
I have not sent out troops for a long time.
Shìchōng's (世充) fodder and grain are about to run out.
Unable to seek battle,
he therefore recruits soldiers and feasts his men,
intending to attack Cāngchéng (倉城) during the new moon.
We should prepare for it quickly."

He then ordered Píngyuán Gōng (平原公) Hǎo Xiàodé (郝孝德), Lángyá Gōng (琅邪公) Wáng Bódāng (王伯當), and Qíjùn Gōng (齊郡公) Mèng Ràng (孟讓) to lead their troops and camp separately near Cāngchéng (倉城) to await him.
That night, at the third drum,
Shìchōng's (世充) troops indeed arrived.
Bódāng (伯當) encountered them first.
He fought,
but was unsuccessful.
Shìchōng's (世充) troops immediately assaulted the city.
Zǒngguǎn (總管) Lǔ Rú (魯儒) repelled them.
Bódāng (伯當) gathered his troops again and attacked them.
Shìchōng (世充) suffered a great defeat,
beheading his fierce general Fèi Qīngnú (費青奴),
and over a thousand soldiers drowned in battle.
Shìchōng (世充) repeatedly fought Mì (密),
but did not win.
The 'Kǎoyì' (考異) states: The 'Púshān Gōng Zhuàn' (蒲山公傳) says:
"From the defeat north of Luò (洛) to this point,
there were over seventy battles."
The 'Héluò Jì' (河洛記) says:
"Over forty battles,
with repeated losses."
Here, it only says that he repeatedly fought Mì (密).
Shìchōng (世充) complained that his troops were few
and exhausted from many battles.
Dòng (侗) reinforced him with 70,000 troops.
31 Liú Wénjìng (劉文靜) and others led their troops east to seize territory,
taking Hóngnóng (弘農) Commandery,
and thus pacified the area west of Xīn'ān (新安).
The 'Suí Zhì' (隋志) states: Shǎn (陝) County of Hénán (河南) Commandery
formerly established Hóngnóng (弘農) Commandery.
In the early years of Dàyè (大業), Hóngnóng Gōng (弘農宮) was established.
There was also a separate Hóngnóng (弘農) Commandery,
which governed counties like Hóngnóng (弘農), Lúshì (盧氏), Chángquán (長泉), and Zhūyáng (朱陽).
Xīn'ān (新安) County also belonged to Hénán (河南) Commandery,
and its territory was east of Shǎn (陝).
Thus, taking Hóngnóng (弘農) Commandery also meant taking Hóngnóng Gōng (弘農宮).
On the Jiǎchén day of the 32nd year,
Lǐ Yuān dispatched Zhān Jùn, the Magistrate of Yúnyáng, and Lǐ Zhònggǔn, the Xiànzhèng of Wǔgōng County, to tour Bā and Shǔ,
and pacify them.
The Suí Zhì states: Yúnyáng and Wǔgōng Counties both belonged to Jīngzhào Commandery.
Emperor Yáng changed the Xiànwèi to Xiànzhèng.
Zhān,
is a surname.
There was Zhān Fù in the Zhōu dynasty,
and Zhān Yǐn in the Chǔ state.
The Kǎoyì says: The Chuàngyè Zhù states:
"In the eleventh month, on the Jiǎzǐ day,
envoys were dispatched to console and pacify Bā and Shǔ."
The Shílù records it as the twelfth month, Jiǎchén day,
and the Táng Lì records it as the twelfth month, Bǐngwǔ day.
It is unknown whether what the Chuàngyè Zhù referred to was Zhān Jùn and his group,
or different envoys.
We now follow the Shílù.
On the Yǐsì day of the 33rd year,
Fāngyǔ, along with the bandit leader Zhāng Shàn'ān, attacked and captured Lújiāng Commandery.
The Suí Zhì states: Fāngyǔ County belonged to Péngchéng Commandery.
Emperor Yáng changed Lúzhōu to Lújiāng Commandery.
Fāngyǔ,
pronounced Fángyù.
Shuài,
pronounced 'suǒ lèi fān'. (Fāngyǔ) returned Lín Shìhóng to Yùzhāng;
Lín Shìhóng suspected him,
and camped above Nántáng.
Emperor Yáng changed Hóngzhōu to Yùzhāng Commandery.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states: Nántáng in Nánchāng County,
originally connected to the Dàjiāng (Great River),
during the Yǒngyuán era of the Hàn dynasty,
the Grand Administrator Zhāng Gōng built an embankment to open up the southern route.
Dàjiāng,
is also called Nánjiāng. (Fāngyǔ)
attacked and defeated Lín Shìhóng,
burned his outer and inner cities, and left.
Lín Shìhóng moved his residence to Nánkāng.
Xiāo Xiǎn dispatched his general Sū Hú'ér to attack Yùzhāng,
captured it,
and Lín Shìhóng retreated to defend Yúgàn.
Emperor Yáng changed Qiánzhōu to Nánkāng Commandery.
Yúgàn County belonged to Póyáng Commandery.
Punctuation by Wáng Chóngwǔ, reviewed by Róng Zhàozǔ and Niè Chóngqí.
